10565-watch-dogs-ship-s-company-part-5:
W. W. Jacobs published this comic tale as the fifth part of Ship's Company, opening with the oldest inhabitant enjoying beer and a pipe at the Cauliflower inn. With few teeth left, he prizes pleasures that need no chewing, and he tells a wayfarer that kindness to fellow creatures matters more than kindness to animals alone.

A London gentleman's prize for kindness to animals, a landlord's refilled mug, and a spill of precious beer frame his rambling talk. The old man argues, with crafty humor, that people waste kindness on dumb beasts. Readers get a short, warm Jacobs tale of village talk, beer, and human nature.
10602-the-poetical-works-of-edmund-spens:
Edmund Spenser, the Elizabethan poet of The Faerie Queene, appears here in the fifth volume of his collected poetical works, printed in 1860. This volume gathers his shorter pieces, called Complaints, with The Ruines of Time, The Teares of the Muses, Mother Hubberds Tale, and the Fate of the Butterflie. It also holds his beloved love poems.

Among them are the Amoretti sonnets, the wedding song Epithalamion, Prothalamion, and the Four Hymns on love and beauty. An appendix adds variant readings and two letters to Gabriel Harvey. Readers meet Spenser beyond his great epic, in lyrics and satires that show his range, music, and moral seriousness.
10706-the-history-of-rome-volumes-1-5:
Theodor Mommsen's History of Rome, in this complete form, gathers all five books of the German scholar's masterwork in Dickson's English translation. Book one covers Rome before the kings fell, and book two runs to the union of Italy. Book three reaches the defeat of Carthage and the Greek states. Book four tells the Revolution, and book five sets up military monarchy.

Together the volumes trace Rome from a small city to a Mediterranean empire, through law, war, and civil strife. Mommsen's blend of scholarship and narrative made the work famous across Europe. Readers get the whole arc in one place, a classic history still worth reading for its sweep and judgment.
10785-matrimonial-openings-sailor-s-knot:
W. W. Jacobs's "Matrimonial Openings," the fifth tale in Sailors' Knots from 1909, opens by a kitchen fire where Mrs. Dowson scolds her husband Joe. She fears their daughter Flora will follow her sister Jenny and marry a man she must then work herself to skin and bone to keep. Joe's mild replies only stir his wife further.

The comedy grows from married talk: warnings, contradictions, and the small wars of a household. Jacobs keeps the scene short and sharp, in plain working speech. Readers get a domestic farce complete in itself, funny without needing any other tale in the book.
10799-clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of:
Samuel Richardson's Clarissa Harlowe, told wholly in letters, is one of the great English novels, and this fifth volume of nine carries the story through its middle crisis. Letters pass between Lovelace and his friend Belford, and between Clarissa and Miss Howe, as Lovelace plots, deceives, and watches Clarissa's feelings with cold delight.

The volume's summaries name an airing, a plot with ipecacuanha, and Clarissa's acknowledged tenderness for a man of errors. Richardson builds suspense through small details and long, searching letters. Readers meet the novel at its tensest, as virtue and villainy close in on each other.
10871-at-sunwich-port-part-1-contents-ch:
W. W. Jacobs's At Sunwich Port opens in this first part, covering chapters one through five, with drawings by Will Owen. The ancient port basks in July sunshine, cranes and winches rattling in the harbor, while the town itself half sleeps. Somnolent shopkeepers veil their faces in red handkerchiefs against flies, and small boys mind shops under the church clock.

Sunwich is proud of its fine church, whose tall grey tower, a landmark at sea, rises suddenly above huddled roofs with a black-faced clock and gilt numerals. Jacobs sets his seaside comedy here, among sailors and townsfolk. Readers get the novel's sunny opening, complete in these first chapters.
11185-bob-s-redemption-captains-all-book:
Jacobs's night-watchman opens this story by scoffing at gratitude, recalling men he helped who repaid him with blows or betrayal. One man, Harry Thomson, had the watchman write his love letters for six months, then attacked him weeks after the wedding. Another, Bill Clark, asked him to end a courtship with a lie, then blamed him when the girl moved on. Bob's own redemption grows out of similar tangles.

The humor rests on the gap between the watchman's self-pity and his talent for making trouble worse. Every favor curdles, and every explanation starts a fight. Readers get a compact example of Jacobs's method: a talkative narrator, a small cast of sailors, and a plot that unravels through misunderstandings.
11250-journeys-through-bookland-vol-5:
Charles H. Sylvester's Journeys Through Bookland, volume five of a 1922 reading plan for children, anthologizes the world's best literature in adapted form. Contents include Gulliver's Travels, the Ballad of Agincourt, Tennyson's Geraint and Enid and Passing of Arthur, the Holy Grail from Malory, Scott on Robert Bruce. Longfellow's Skeleton in Armor, Browning's ride from Ghent to Aix, and Tom Brown at Rugby, with American pieces from Franklin to the Battle Hymn of the Republic.

Sylvester's plan was to lead children through literature by journeys rather than lessons, with illustrations and pronunciation help. The volume's range, from Arthurian romance to pioneer reminiscence, shows what educators counted as essential reading a century ago. It works now as both an anthology and a record of the canon taught to children.
11437-stories-by-american-authors-volume:
Stories by American Authors, volume five from 1884, collects Henry James's Light Man, F. D. Millet's Yatil, Park Benjamin's End of New York, George Arnold's Why Thomas Was Discharged, and E. P. Mitchell's Tachypomp. James's opener follows Maximus Austin, resuming old notes in a new world at thirty-two with a net income of considerably less than nothing. walking Broadway and wondering what he is, wishes, tends toward, and believes, beset by impertinent whisperings.

The volume's range, from Jamesian introspection to Mitchell's scientific romance, shows American short fiction's breadth in the 1880s. Its authors were magazine leaders. Readers sampling the period will find James's story the most literary and the others lively companions.
11475-the-convert-deep-waters-part-5:
Mr. Purnip, warm and earnest, walks arm in arm with his new recruit Mr. Billing, praising him as a bright lamp whose example will draw others like sheep. Billing, a jolly man with a quick temper, accepts the praise with modest pride.

The joke turns on the new rule Billing has taken up: no more fighting, and turn the other cheek when struck. He doubts it will work, since he can hit a man hard, and Purnip must talk him round. Jacobs makes the comedy from a convert trying, with goodwill and some doubt, to live by a rule he barely trusts.
11955-a-popular-history-of-france-from-t:
Volume 5 of Guizot's History of France is richly illustrated. Its steel engravings show Gabrielle d'Estrées, Marie de Medici, Richelieu, Louis XIV, and Turenne, with woodcuts of Henry IV at Ivry. Its famous image shows Henry urging his men not to lose sight of his white plume in battle.

The volume covers the era of Henry IV, Marie de Medici, Richelieu, and Louis XIV, when France moved from religious war toward centralized monarchy. Guizot's narrative follows kings, ministers, and generals through court intrigue and battlefield alike, using portraits and battle scenes to keep a long political story vivid for general readers.
11975-dialstone-lane-part-5:
Part 5 of W. W. Jacobs's Dialstone Lane follows the Fair Emily month by month as she creeps down south, with the Great Bear and other constellations giving way to southern skies. Chalk tries hard not to feel disappointed with the arrangement of the stars in the Southern Cross. Pressed by the triumphant Brisket, he admits it is at least as much like a cross as he expected.

This final portion brings the treasure voyage to its southern waters, where the comedy of mismatched sailors, maps, and hopes plays out under unfamiliar stars. Jacobs keeps the tone light even at sea, letting Chalk's literal-minded astronomy stand for the whole expedition, brave, muddled, and cheerfully out of its depth.
12125-cupboard-love-the-lady-of-the-barg:
Part 5 of Jacobs's Lady of the Barge stories, Cupboard Love, opens in the comfortable living-room at Negget's farm. The room is half parlour and half kitchen, where three people sit at tea in the waning light of a November afternoon. Conversation, brisk at first, languishes as Mrs. Negget glances at frequent intervals toward the door, convinced the servant is listening behind it.

Cupboard love, affection for the sake of food and comfort, drives the comedy that follows, as suitors, servants, and farm folk maneuver around the tea table. Jacobs keeps the farce domestic and small-scale, finding humor in eavesdropping, jealousy, and the rituals of a farmhouse tea.
12155-stepping-backwards-night-watches-p:
W. W. Jacobs wrote this comic short story for his 1911 collection Night Watches. The narrator, a Thames night watchman, tells of ordinary working men whose vanity leads them into absurd fixes, a pattern across the whole book.

Mr. Simpson, fifty-three and tired of looking old, takes a friend advice to dye his hair, shave his whiskers, and appear years younger. The change fools strangers and flatters him, but at home it breeds confusion: his wife takes the altered man for an intruder. Locked in his own cellar and threatened with the police, Simpson learns that youth bought in a bottle costs more than it saves. The tale turns a barber-shop joke into a neat marital farce.
12205-lawyer-quince-odd-craft-part-5:
Lawyer Quince, so called by his neighbors in Little Haven, sits in a wooden hutch by his cottage making boots in Lawyer Quince, a comic tale from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft. Quince legal lore comes from a few old books, but villagers trust it as law.

The London coach has gone by in dust, the village street slumbers in sunshine, and footsteps bring a client with a dispute that needs Quince brand of justice. Quince pronounces, advises, and settles, with cobbler confidence and book learning in equal parts. Jacobs comedy rests on a man whose authority is invented and yet effective, because neighbors accept it. The story is a small satire on law itself: custom, talk, and trust matter more than statutes.
12592-j-s-le-fanu-s-ghostly-tales-volume:
Volume five of J. S. Le Fanu's ghostly tales gathers stories from 1869 to 1872. Laura Silver Bell opens on Dardale Moss, a bleak, ugly yet savagely picturesque moor of black peat and heath, ringed by birch, hazel and dwarf oak. Wicked Captain Walshaw of Wauling, The Child That Went with the Fairies and The Vision of Tom Chuff follow.

Stories of Lough Guir add the Magician Earl, Moll Rial's adventure, the Banshee, the Governess's Dream and the Earl's Hall, closing with Dickon the Devil. Le Fanu writes Irish and English ghost lore with slow dread, letting place do much of the haunting. The volume is a fine sample of Victorian supernatural fiction at its most atmospheric.
15182-marion-arleigh-s-penance-everyday-:
Charlotte Braeme's Marion Arleigh's Penance, number five in the Everyday Life Library, opens on a sultry June afternoon in London. Heat hazes the sky, flowers droop in street stalls, and roses thirst for dew, while cool streams and sea breezes lie far away. The city setting frames a tale of guilt and atonement.

Marion's penance unfolds through love, secrecy, and suffering, in Braeme's familiar melodramatic style. London heat gives way to moral storm as she pays for past faults. Fans of Victorian sensation fiction will find the novel emotional, plot-driven, and full of period feeling.
17701-the-tales-of-the-heptameron-vol-1-:
Margaret, Queen of Navarre, wrote the tales of the Heptameron, newly translated into English from the authentic text of M. Le Roux de Lincy, with an essay upon the Heptameron by George Saintsbury. This first of five volumes was printed in London in 1894 for the Society of English Bibliophiles. It carries seventy-three full-page engravings by Freudenberg and one hundred and fifty head and tail pieces by Dunker.

Contents open with a memoir of Margaret of Angouleme, Saintsbury's essay, dedications, and a prologue. The first day's tales follow, including the pitiful history of a proctor of Alencon and the fate of a muleteer's wife of Amboise. Readers get Renaissance story-telling at its most frank and lively.
17702-the-tales-of-the-heptameron-vol-2-:
Margaret, Queen of Navarre, wrote the Heptameron in the 1500s, and this second volume of a five-volume English version carries her tales on from the first day into the second. George Saintsbury wrote the essay on the work that fronts the set, and the tales were newly turned into English from the French text.

The stories are short, sharp tales of love, trickery, and pride. A group of travelers tells one tale each to pass the time. Here a wife is caught in a trick of her own making. A lord dies for love of a lady he cannot wed, and a duke is killed to guard his sister's good name. Readers get a frank, lively view of court life in old France, told with wit and bite.
17703-the-tales-of-the-heptameron-vol-3-:
The third of five volumes of Margaret, Queen of Navarre's Heptameron, newly translated from the text of M. Le Roux de Lincy with an essay by George Saintsbury, printed in London in 1894 for the Society of English Bibliophiles, continues the story-telling company through its second and third days. Engravings by Freudenberg and ornaments by Dunker illustrate the set.

Contents continue the second day with tale nineteen, the honourable love of a gentleman who becomes a monk of the Observance while his lady becomes a nun of St. Clara. A lord cured of love for a widow follows, then the third day's prologue and the affecting history of Rolandine, debarred from marriage. Readers get the Heptameron's middle movement, as frank as its opening.
17704-the-tales-of-the-heptameron-vol-4-:
Volume four of this five-volume English Heptameron picks up Margaret of Navarre's tales on the fourth day, in the same 1894 London printing as its sister volumes. George Saintsbury's essay fronts the set. The French tales were newly turned into English for readers who knew the old court stories only by name.

The tales here are darker than the early ones, with friars caught in sly sins, priests unmasked, and husbands who use cool heads to save their wives from shame. One tale turns on a wife made to drink from her dead lover's skull, and one on a lord who poisons his wife in a salad to guard his house. The mix of jest and grim fact gives a sharp, frank look at life in old France.
17705-the-tales-of-the-heptameron-vol-5-:
The last of five volumes of Margaret, Queen of Navarre's Heptameron, newly translated from the text of M. Le Roux de Lincy with an essay by George Saintsbury, printed in London in 1894 for the Society of English Bibliophiles, brings the story-telling company to its sixth day. Engravings by Freudenberg and ornaments by Dunker illustrate the set.

Contents open the sixth day with a prologue and tale fifty-one, on the cruelty of the Duke of Urbino, who hanged a poor lady despite a promise to the Duchess. A merry trick by an apothecary's varlet at Alencon follows, played on a lord and a lawyer who meant to breakfast at his expense. Readers get the Heptameron's close, as witty and frank as its start.
17725-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-:
October 1885 brought this fifth number of the Bay State Monthly's third volume, led by Edward P. Guild's profile of William W. Crapo of New Bedford. Crapo was the son of Henry Howland Crapo, a farmer's son who taught himself, surveyed land, and rose to city treasurer and library trustee.

Guild praises the younger Crapo as a man of mark in public and private life, still in his prime, and sketches the whale-fishery town that shaped him. The issue also runs the magazine's usual serial fiction, in which a young woman wakes before dawn to wrestle with her conscience. Together the pieces show a Boston magazine honoring solid, local worth.
19203-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
The February 3, 1898 number of The Great Round World was a weekly paper for boys and girls. It sold at five cents. It reported world news in short, clear pieces for young readers. Subscription rates covered a year, six months, and libraries. The paper came out each Thursday from New York.

One number quotes former President Cleveland on Hawaii. He calls annexation a departure from America's mission. He calls American interference in its overthrow disgraceful and wrong. Such plain talk teaches history as news. Young readers get a window on 1898 debates, as a children's paper framed them.
2151-the-works-of-edgar-allan-poe-volume:
This fifth volume of Poe's works gathers his essays on furniture, the poetic principle, and old English poetry. Tales such as Hop-Frog, The Man of the Crowd, and Some Words with a Mummy join them. Poems of later life follow. The Poetic Principle, Poe's famous lecture, argues that a poem should aim at beauty alone.

The Raven, The Bells, Ulalume, and Annabel Lee sit beside poems of manhood and youth, from Lenore to Al Aaraaf and Tamerlane. The volume gives a full shelf of Poe, showing poet, critic, and storyteller in one place. The Raven and Annabel Lee, placed among later poems, show Poe's mastery of sound and refrain.
22234-aunt-jo-s-scrap-bag-volume-5:
Louisa May Alcott issued the fifth volume of Aunt Jo's Scrap-Bag as her scrap-bag series of stories grew. Volume 5 gathers tales for the young from her magazine writing. One opens on a boy sitting despondent on a doorstep. His eyes are fixed on a pair of very shabby shoes, and his elbows hide the big patches on his knees.

Alcott's scrap-bag held stories of poor children, proud children, and children learning kindness. She wrote them fast, for money and for love, between her larger novels. The moral warmth of Little Women runs through these shorter pieces. Readers who know only the March family will find the same Alcott here in miniature.
22777-history-of-the-united-states-volum:
This fifth volume of a History of the United States, dated 1899, carries the national story from the earliest discovery of America down to the politics of the 1890s. The catalog record names no author. Where the fourth volume ended with Appomattox, this one faces Gilded Age money, tariffs, and pensions.

The contents march through the era's headlines: the so-called Billion Dollar Congress, its Dependent Pensions Act, the McKinley Tariff with Blaine reciprocity, and a new international copyright law. Mr. Blaine appears as Secretary of State. Then come darker notes: a Mafia murder and riot in New Orleans. The Itata affair at San Diego follows. So does American sovereignty assumed over Tutuila in Samoa. The volume is a period summary of a booming, quarrelsome republic.
24942-the-nursery-november-1873-vol-xiv-:
A November 1873 issue of The Nursery, Shorey's Boston monthly for youngest readers, offers prose and verse for small children. The Aunt and the Niece leads. Aunt Ruth is only nine, while her niece Mary is nineteen, yet Ruth keeps up an aunt's dignity and treats Mary as if she were the little girl.

Other pieces include A Field-Day with the Geese, where Joseph, wanting to be a soldier, drills his uncle's geese on parade, flag in hand, with cousin Richard as trumpeter. Fido the dog eyes Mary's basket while the geese march single file. The issue keeps the magazine's gentle humor and homely charm.
26401-buchanan-s-journal-of-man-june-188:
Buchanan's Journal of Man for June 1887, volume one, number five, is a reformist miscellany with education at its heart. Its lead pieces hail a marvellous triumph of educational science, stage a grand symposium of wise men, and press the burning question in education. Verse replies from figures such as Sir John William Dawson of McGill and J. Sterry Hunt debate belief in eternal life.

The miscellaneous intelligence ranges widely: bigotry and liberality, religious news, abolishing slavery, legal responsibility in hypnotism, Pasteur's cure for hydrophobia, land monopoly, and marriage in Mexico. Psychometric claims and old fogy biography sit beside notes on extinct animals and tobacco bills. The journal's own enthusiasms, including psychometry, are presented as its claims, not settled fact.
29906-modern-painters-volume-2-of-5:
John Ruskin's Modern Painters, volume two, appears here in the Library Edition of his complete works, from the National Library Association. A landscape from a painting by J. M. W. Turner fronts the volume. This volume holds part three, sections one and two, on the imaginative and theoretic faculties, under the heading Of Ideas of Beauty. The theoretic faculty takes the first section, with chapters on its rank, its pleasures, and its errors.

Chapters on typical beauty follow: infinity, unity, repose, symmetry, purity, and moderation, each read as a type of a divine quality. Vital beauty, first as relative, then as generic, and thirdly in man, closes the theoretic part. Then come the three forms of imagination: associative, penetrative, and contemplative, with the superhuman ideal. Ruskin writes with force and system, and the volume is a central piece of his art theory.
29907-modern-painters-volume-1-of-5:
John Ruskin's Modern Painters, volume one, appears here in the Library Edition of his complete works, from the National Library Association. Ruskin signed the work A Graduate of Oxford and dedicated it to the landscape artists of England. His preface to the first edition tells how the book began: in indignation at the shallow, false criticism of the periodicals on a great living artist.

Ruskin meant a short pamphlet, rebuking the matter and style of those critiques and their perilous sway over public feeling. Point after point forced him to amplify the letter into something very like a treatise on art. He gave it more consistency and completeness because it argued opinions that would sound heretical to the ordinary connoisseur. The volume is the bold opening of Ruskin's lifelong defense of true painting.
30495-a-history-of-science-volume-5:
Henry Smith Williams, assisted by Edward H. Williams, closes a five volume history of science with Aspects of Recent Science, copyrighted in 1904 and published in November of that year. The volume opens with the British Museum, from the purchase of Sir Hans Sloane's collection to its home in Montague Mansion.

Later sections follow the Hamilton collection, Egyptian antiquities taken by the English, the present museum building, and the Mesopotamian department. The South Kensington natural history museum, its novel structure, and exhibits arranged to show evolution and protective coloring also feature. Williams surveys recent science through institutions, collections, and display.
30992-the-esperantist-vol-1-no-5:
The March 1904 number of The Esperantist, the Esperanto gazette for spreading the international language, was edited by H. Bolingbrooke Mudie and published by the London Esperanto Club at Outer Temple, London. Single copies sold for fourpence net, and the annual subscription was three shillings. Its contents show the movement's writers at work in Esperanto and in translation.

Pages include The Accent Problem by the editor, A February Walk, Italian Folklore by Clarence Bicknell, and Spanish Proverbs. The Tempest, translated by A. Motteau, continues, with Mateo Falkone by Elise Bauer and Tom Bowling, also translated by Motteau. Later pages bring The Birth of Esperanto, translated by John Ellis, Our Holidays, The Language of Flowers by Ben Elmy, and two fables from Lafontaine. It is a lively snapshot of Esperanto in 1904.
31623-modern-painters-volume-4-of-5:
John Ruskin's Modern Painters, volume four, Of Mountain Beauty, appears in the Library Edition of the complete works of John Ruskin, published by the National Library Association of New York and Chicago. The volume is illustrated with the Kapellbrücke at Lucerne, from a drawing by Ruskin himself. Part five opens with a chapter on the Turnerian picturesque, setting the tone for Ruskin's study of mountains as Turner painted them and as nature made them.

Ruskin treats mountain beauty as a subject for both art and science, moving from geology to the painter's eye. His prose, long and loving, asks readers to look closely at peaks, clouds, and light. Readers of art criticism will find volume four among Ruskin's most sustained achievements, where landscape painting and natural history meet in a single, passionate argument.
32617-the-galaxy-may-1877-vol-xxiii-may-:
The Galaxy, volume twenty-three, May 1877, number five, opens with A Progressive Baby, a letter from Ober Lahnstein dated January 16, 1875. Its writer recalls solitary artist days travelling second class from Dresden to London for fifty thalers, stopping at Frankfort, Weimar, Heidelberg, and Antwerp along the way.

Now travelling first class with a husband, a baby, and a nurse, she writes of comfort, nerves, and small miseries between Blackwall and Rotterdam. The issue shows the Galaxy's blend of fiction, letters, and commentary, moving from a Rhine journey to the wider reading of an American monthly magazine.
32747-travels-in-tartary-thibet-and-chin:
M. Huc, a Lazarist missionary, tells of travels in Tartary, Thibet, and China during the years 1844, 1845, and 1846, translated from the French by W. Hazlitt. The first volume, illustrated with fifty engravings on wood, appeared from the National Illustrated Library in London.

In 1844 the Pope established an Apostolic Vicariat of Mongolia, and Huc and M. Gabet were sent from the mission of Si-Wang to survey it. They reached Lha-Ssa, capital of Thibet, hoping to convert the Talé-Lama, but the Chinese minister Ke-Shen had them deported to China. Huc's narrative follows deserts, lamaseries, and market towns, with his guide Samdadchiemba, through countries then almost unknown to Europeans.
33269-travels-in-tartary-thibet-and-chin:
M. Huc's travels in Tartary, Thibet, and China during 1844, 1845, and 1846, translated from the French by W. Hazlitt, form the second volume of a famous missionary journey. Illustrated with fifty wood engravings, the book follows Huc through lands few Europeans had seen, from Tartar steppes to Tibetan lamaseries and Chinese towns. Its pictures of a Buddha and a grand lama's mausoleum hint at the wonders within.

Huc writes as both priest and traveler, noting customs, faiths, and the hardships of the road with a keen, humane eye. The volume's value lies in its first-hand detail of a world soon to change. For readers of travel and Asian history, it remains a classic account, vivid, curious, and full of the strangeness of a distant age.
3370-a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-5:
William Dean Howells closes A Hazard of New Fortunes with its fifth part, after the storm. On the surface, Every Other Week returns to its old routine, and Fulkerson looks fully restored to favor. March, though, senses nothing will last after recent events, and feels a strange shame toward Lindau, the elderly German socialist.

March did not sympathize with Lindau's opinions, and thought his remedy for existing evils wildly impracticable. Yet the shame lingered, and the magazine's quiet surface hid a moral debt. Readers finishing the novel here get Howells's verdict on success: a business restored, a conscience unsettled, and a hero who has learned what his new fortune cost.
33804-the-mysteries-of-paris-illustrated:
Eugène Sue's Mysteries of Paris reaches its fifth volume in this de luxe edition, illustrated with etchings and limited to one thousand copies. Eleven chapters open a few days after the murder of Madame Séraphin, the death of the Chouette, and the arrest of desperadoes surprised at Bras-Rouge's house. His aim is to practice artifice against Jacques Ferrand, discover hidden crimes, force reparation, and inflict punishment if guilty.

Chapters follow a presentation, Murphy and Polidori, a clerk's office, advice to avoid temptation, La Force prison, Pique-Vinaigre, Maître Boulard, François Germain, a lions' den, a story-teller, and Gringalet and Cut-in-Half. Etchings show Cecily's name murmured, a dance whirling, a touch through a grating, and a staggering skeleton. Sue's serial gathers its villains and victims toward reckoning.
3851-memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-mo:
Madame de Montespan's fifth book finds her taking the waters at Bourbonne with a small company, soon joined by arrivals come to see her and Mademoiselle de Nantes. Chancellor Hyde exchanges his agreeable house for hers. The Prince de Mont-Beliard of Wurtemberg pays his respects as if to a king's daughter, recalling the king's first Flanders journey and praising her increased beauty. Diplomacy hums beneath the compliments, with a duchy in the air and the domain of Navarre promised.

A court debate lightens the volume, as Monsieur prefers Marcus Aurelius for sharing his throne with Verus, while the king calls the act generous but inconsiderate. Montespan reports the exchange with a courtier's ear. Readers who like the memoirs' middle years will find spa talk, flattery, and statecraft in one flow.
3951-cinq-mars-volume-5:
Alfred de Vigny's fifth volume of Cinq Mars carries the conspiracy against Richelieu to the king himself. Plotters propose to get rid of the Cardinal as the Marechal d'Ancre was got rid of, who deserved it less than he. The queen, the nobility, and the parliaments are on their side, they say, and the thing is done once his Majesty is not opposed.

The king answers as Concini is named, and refuses outright. It must not be, he says, for Richelieu is a priest and a cardinal, and they shall be excommunicated. But if any other means exist, he is very willing. Readers who like Vigny's court intrigue will find a volume where murder is proposed, refused, and replaced by subtler plots.
4105-the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1:
Azel Ames's Mayflower history reaches its fifth volume with the vexing problem of quarters, cooking, and provisions aboard two crowded ships. Governors and assistants had to allot berths, with the needs of women and children weighing large in every choice.

The volume works through food, water, cooking gear, and sleeping space, showing how a small ship held a whole village for ten weeks at sea. Ames grounds each detail in records, making daily life vivid. Readers who enjoy social history will find this the most intimate volume, close to the Pilgrims' cramped, smoky world.
4410-the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volum:
Book Five of George Meredith's The Ordeal of Richard Feverel opens in July, on the Solent, where a young bridal pair breakfast by an open window above green waves. Gay yachts flash past like foam, and roses nod at the brine. The scene is bright, but Meredith's irony keeps its edge.

The book's chapters run from the conquest of an epicure and Clare's marriage through a dinner party at Richmond, Mrs. Berry on matrimony, and an enchantress. Richard's ordeal, begun under his father's system at Raynham Abbey, now meets marriage itself. This volume carries the novel toward its painful later acts.
4417-sandra-belloni-volume-5:
Book Five of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni opens too late for Lady Charlotte, who goes to speak for Wilfrid and finds only the youth Braintop resting against a tree. He mutters that he has no notion where he is, an excuse for standing still, while the person he should have detained has gone. Emilia has fled.

The book's chapters mark the degradation of Brookfield, with proceedings of the yacht, Mrs. Chump's epistle, and another pitfall of sentiment. Emilia's flight follows, with her clinging to her voice, and then her voice failing. This volume is the novel's dark middle, where sentiment costs Emilia her art and her place.
4425-rhoda-fleming-volume-5:
Book Five of George Meredith's Rhoda Fleming opens late in the afternoon, with Farmer Fleming sitting motionless in Robert's lodgings since noon. He shows no sign of expecting anyone, mute in limb and mind, alone with his thoughts. The stillness carries the novel toward its end.

The book's chapters bring Dahlia home, a freak of the money demon, Dahlia's frenzy, and Anthony in a collapse. Rhoda pledges her hand, the enemy appears, and the farmer is awakened. When the night is darkest, dawn is near, and the conclusion follows. This final volume resolves the sisters' long trial with mercy and severity.
4431-evan-harrington-volume-5:
Book Five of George Meredith's Evan Harrington opens with Mrs. Mel, the last person her children thought of, reviewing them seriously after a letter from Mr. Goren. The tailor's widow, long ignored, takes stock of her family with a mother's eye. Her bed-making for herself and her family gives the chapter its title.

The book's chapters show Rose's generalship, Evan's performance on the second fiddle, and the wretchedness of the countess. Tom Cogglesby's proposition follows, with a prelude to an engagement and the battle of the bull-dogs in two parts. Evan's love and his birthright collide, with comedy and feeling.
4439-vittoria-volume-5:
Book Five of George Meredith's Vittoria opens with a duel in the pass, while Captain Weisspriess rouses the gendarmerie along the routes to Meran. He guesses Vittoria has rejected the Adige valley for the Valtelline, tempted to cross the Stelvio or a pass into southernmost Tyrol. The hunt for the singer is on.

The book's chapters promise a new ordeal and the escape of Angelo. Vittoria flees through mountain passes, pursued by Austrian police, while her lover and her cause pull her in different directions. This volume is the novel's chase at its most urgent, with the Alps as both refuge and trap.
4448-the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-vo:
Book Five of George Meredith's Adventures of Harry Richmond opens after a duel, with a surgeon admiring the mutual delicacy of two men who spared arteries and vital organs. A bullet, Meredith notes, cuts a rougher path than neat steel, and Harry lies prostrate as the prince presses his hand before leaving for Laibach. The duel's unreason stands exposed.

The book's chapters follow what came of a shilling, a perception of princely state, and the scene in the lake-palace library. Homeward and home again follow, with Janet renouncing Harry and his bankers' book. Harry's fortunes, tied to his father's schemes, turn serious here, and love pays the price.
4457-beauchamp-s-career-volume-5:
Book Five of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career opens with the face of Renee, then a ride in the wrong direction and pursuit of Mr. Romfrey's apology to Dr. Shrapnel. Cecilia conquered follows, with Lord Avonley, and chapters between Beauchamp and Cecilia, a trial of him, and a lame victory. Love and politics pull Nevil both ways.

Renee, his first love, returns to his thoughts, while Cecilia Halkett tests his constancy in England. Meredith balances the two women against Beauchamp's public fight. This volume brings his private life to a point, as apology, conquest, and trial leave him neither wholly victor nor wholly beaten.
4469-diana-of-the-crossways-volume-5:
Book Five of George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways opens with a verdict on the heartlessness of women with brains, then an exhibition of champions of the stricken lady. The convalescence of a healthy mind distraught follows, with nature and one of her cultivated daughters, and a short excursion in anti-climax.

Nature makes of a woman a maid again, Meredith notes, in a chapter thrice whimsical, with a revelation of the origin of the tigress in Diana. The penultimate shows a final struggle for liberty and running, before the conclusion. This last volume restores Diana, chastened and still brilliant, to herself.
4475-one-of-our-conquerors-volume-5:
Book Five of George Meredith's One of Our Conquerors opens with Nesta and her father, on the day of Nesta's return. Victor has been kept from his westward walk by Lady Grace Halley, who wins his politeness with flattery to take her calls. The small theft of time signals larger losses ahead.

Later chapters bring the mother and the daughter, Nataly, Nesta, and Dartrey Fenellan, and a chapter in the shadow of Mrs. Marsett. An expiation follows, with the night of the great undelivered speech and the last chapter. This final volume closes Victor's career, as his conquests give way to reckoning and grief.
4481-lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-5:
Book Five of George Meredith's Lord Ormont and His Aminta opens with lovers mated, as the old soldier thinks of his girl, now his countess, as pardonably foolish. Woman for woman, he judges, she surpasses the world's ordinary pattern and might rival the finest in society. The martial, paternal tone suits Ormont.

Later chapters bring preparations for a resolve, visits of farewell, a marine duet, and the plighting. Aminta to her lord and the conclusion close the book. This final volume settles the marriage that society doubted, as Ormont and Aminta meet its tests together, with Meredith's comedy giving way to tenderness.
4487-the-amazing-marriage-volume-5:
Book Five of George Meredith's Amazing Marriage opens with the red warning from a son of vapour, as Fleetwood grants a deferred audience at home, desiring loneliness or Lord Feltre's company. A record of minor incidents follows, with the fates seen and a choice of refuges from them. The retarded courtship proceeds.

Later chapters follow the road to the act of penance, the earl, the countess and her brother, and a silver cross. A record of what was feared, what was hoped, and what happened leads to undercurrents, surface flashes, and the last chapter, with a concluding word by the dame. This final volume ends Fleetwood's amazing marriage.
5238-the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-:
Charles James Lever's Harry Lorrequer continues in this fifth volume, covering chapters twenty-nine through forty-one. Captain Trevanion's adventure opens the volume, followed by difficulties, explanations, Mr O'Leary's first. Second loves, a duel, early recollections, wise resolves, a proposal, thoughts on matrimony in the army, and Mr O'Leary's capture follow.

The volume holds only this late stretch of Harry's confessions, and its comedy turns increasingly on love and marriage. Readers following the novel in order will find the usual mess-table humour, now mixed with the question of whether Harry himself will ever settle down.
5465-the-sisters-volume-5:
An astrologer climbs to the roof of the pylon tower by the Serapeum gate in the fifth volume of Georg Ebers's The Sisters. From the temple's highest point he hopes to observe the stars. Black clouds sweep again and again across the part of the heavens he needs, and at last he grows impatient. The sky refuses his reading.

The failed observation sets a mood of omen and uncertainty for the volume, where temple, stars, and human plans collide. Ebers uses the Serapeum's height and the cloudy night to frame coming events. Readers get a brooding, atmospheric stretch of the romance, where even the heavens seem to withhold their counsel.
5471-joshua-volume-5:
Prisoners of state being transported to the mines make slow progress in the fifth volume of Georg Ebers's Joshua. Even the experienced captain of the guards has never faced a more toilsome trip, full of annoyances, obstacles, and mishaps. One of his prisoners, Ephraim, has escaped, his faithful hounds are lost, and his troop has been terrified and drenched by a rare desert storm.

The volume follows a harsh desert march, where escape, weather, and discipline test captors and captives alike. Ebers writes the journey with attention to hardship and landscape. Readers get a grim, adventurous stretch of the biblical romance, far from palace ceremony.
5812-following-the-equator-a-journey-aro:
Part five of Mark Twain's Following the Equator covers chapters thirty-nine through forty-nine, approaching India. A Pudd'nhead Wilson maxim jokes that by trying we can easily learn to endure adversity, another man's, and the narrative then lets long-ago dreams of India rise in vague, luscious moonlight. Forgotten details of an earlier vision light up softly above the horizon of consciousness.

The trip with Twain toward Indian ports, temples, and colonial society, with memory and expectation shaping every arrival. The part favors reverie and anticipation, as India appears first as a dream before it appears as a place. It suits readers following Twain's world tour, and it offers a poetic prelude to the sharper Indian chapters that follow.
5822-the-gilded-age-part-5:
Part five of The Gilded Age, by Twain and Warner, covers chapters thirty-seven through forty-five, opening with a chairman nowhere in sight. Such disappointments seldom occur in novels, the narrator notes, but they always happen in real life, so Laura makes a new plan. She sends a note asking a gentleman to call in the evening, receives Buckstone with a sunny smile, and wonders aloud how she ever dared to send it.

Readers watch Laura maneuver Washington society with charm and calculation, as love, lobbying, and reputation intertwine. The part shows her at her most resourceful, turning absence into opportunity and a note into an evening. It suits readers following Laura's arc, since her social skill here carries both promise and danger for the chapters ahead.
5840-sketches-new-and-old-part-5:
Part five of Mark Twain's Sketches New and Old opens with The Siamese Twins, written about 1868. Twain says he does not wish to write only of their personal habits, but also of curious details of their private life that have never crept into print. Knowing the twins intimately, he promises anecdotes beyond the public show, in his usual deadpan style.

Here Twain gives his curiosity writing at its most playful, as a famous pair becomes a study in habit, fame, and human oddity. The part gathers further sketches around it, each turning a small subject into comedy. It suits readers sampling Twain's short work, since every piece stands alone and rewards a few minutes of attention.
5858-personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-vo:
Volume two, part five of Sheridan's Personal Memoirs covers chapters six through eleven, in the war's final campaigns. Headings treat the Battle of Dinwiddie Court House, Pickett repulsed, reinforcement by the Fifth Corps, and the Battle of Five Forks, turning the Confederate left. Relieving General Warren, the Warren court of inquiry, and Sherman's opinion follow, with Lee's retreat and Amelia Court House ahead.

Readers follow Sheridan's cavalry through the battles that broke Lee's lines, told by the commander who fought them. The memoir balances praise for success with the controversy over Warren's relief, giving a participant's case in full. It suits Civil War readers seeking the Appomattox campaign from a Union general's perspective, with detail on orders and outcomes.
5864-personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-:
Part five of Grant's Personal Memoirs covers chapters fifty-two through sixty-one, in the Overland Campaign. Headings treat the Battle of Spotsylvania, Hancock's position, assaults by Warren's and Wright's corps, and Upton promoted on the field, with good news from Butler and Sheridan. The narrative opens on the Mattapony River, formed by the Mat, Ta, Po, and Ny rivers, rising south and east of its junction.

Readers follow Grant through some of the Civil War's hardest fighting, where assaults, positions, and promotions mark a grinding campaign. The memoir's spare prose suits the subject, recording decisions and losses without sentiment. It suits Civil War readers seeking the 1864 Virginia campaign from its commanding general, in the voice that made his memoirs famous.
6178-pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-:
Antoine and Angelique opens Parker's fifth volume, with birds going south early and winter promising long. Angelique hears a child cry in the night and cannot sleep, while Antoine calls it a devil-bird and says summer is dead. Rushing wings, wild geese, vanished squirrels, and a cold hand at her heart follow.

Antoine answers each fear with plain northern sense: geese know their night way, squirrels hide with bears, and frost brings sleep. The Cipher, A Tragedy of Nobodies, and A Sanctuary of the Plains complete the volume. Only the fifth and final set of tales receives treatment here, with earlier sets kept out of view.
6190-northern-lights-volume-5:
The Error of the Day opens Parker's fifth Northern Lights volume. An Admiralty note defines it as the gap between range set on sights to hit a target and actual distance from gun to target. A great naval gun never fires twice alike, varying with atmosphere, ammunition, and wear.

Expert allowance must be made in sighting every time, and the tale turns from gunnery to a street scene where voices ask a pretty fellow's price in the open market. Billy Goat, William Goatry, sings of cold world, street, nothing to wear, and nothing to eat. The Whisperer and As Deep as the Sea complete the volume.
6228-the-seats-of-the-mighty-volume-5:
Dawn breaks over the battered roofs and ruins of the Lower Town as Moray wakes to bells from the Jesuit College and bugle calls from the garrison. Starved peasants creep about the cathedral hoping for crumbs, while soldiers and stragglers fill the streets. This final volume moves through the cathedral itself, a secret behind a tapestry, a side wind of revenge, and a last reckoning with Doltaire.

Parker ends Moray's memoir where its threads pull tight, with lovers hidden, old scores settled, and a devil cheated yet again. An appendix draws on a study of the Scot in New France, grounding the romance in its setting. The closing chapters give the long siege of one man's life its end, in prayer, stealth, and hard-won release.
6234-the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-:
Ranulph comes home to St. Aubin's Bay after dark to find his little house black, with no light, no fire, and the blinds undrawn. He fears for his father at once, and Dormy Jamais plucks at his sleeve with news he will tell only to Ranulph and the wind. The chapters here run through a botched hanging, where a rope leaves a man's toes touching the ground, and a crowd watches in horror as a slow strangling replaces a clean drop.

Parker's fifth volume is dark with law, punishment, and island justice, as old wrongs come due in public. The Vicomte gives the fatal word, the hangman falters, and only one cool head in the crowd sees what must be done. Through it all Ranulph seeks his father, and the private grief of a son runs beside the spectacle of the scaffold.
6279-the-money-master-volume-5:
However far Jean Jacques went after leaving the Manor Cartier, he could not escape the bells of memory, ringing at the touch of a hand that accepts no philosophy but its own. At Montreal, for one hallowed instant, he regained his lost Carmen, only to turn from her grave with a strange burning at his heart. The mourners were himself, two small chattering ladies, and a barber who had dressed her wonderful hair once a week.

This final epoch gives Jean Jacques work to do, a camp of his own, and the question of what the reader would have done in his place. An epilogue closes the tale, after a madman's humouring and a pistol asked for in a tense talk. Parker ends a long rise and fall with memory, not money, as the last creditor, and a man left to reckon with love lost and life still owed.
7002-life-of-george-washington-volume-1-:
Washington Irving's life of George Washington opens its first volume with the genealogy of the Washington family. The family springs from ancient English stock, traced to the century after the Conquest, holding landed estates and manorial privileges in the county of Durham. Such rights belonged only to those who came from Normandy with the Conqueror or fought under his standard.

When William laid waste the country north of the Humber after the Northumbrian rising, he shared estates among his followers and raised Normans to high church places. Durham, among the wealthiest sees, had received the bones of St Cuthbert from Lindisfarne. Only this first volume's matter is told here, as Irving roots his hero in deep English ground.
7137-the-great-conspiracy-volume-5:
Logan's fifth part of The Great Conspiracy opens at chapter eighteen, Freedom Proclaimed to All, with Lincoln revolving emancipation now coming to a head. No small part of his perplexity grew from his assumption that physical difference between Black and White, African and Caucasian, barred living together as free men and equals. His Lincoln Douglas speeches advanced that idea often, as did later presidential utterances.

In July 1862 he appealed to border state delegations. He held out hope freed people would not be reluctant to go to a projected South American colony once their numbers gave company and encouragement. A later August address pressed the same plan. Only this fifth part's course is followed here, as proclamation meets the president's doubts about what freedom should mean.
7158-the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-5:
Part five of Twain's Prince and the Pauper opens at chapter fifteen, Tom as King, with foreign ambassadors arriving in gorgeous trains the next day. Tom, throned in awful state, receives them, and the splendors delight his eye and fire his imagination at first. But the audience drags long and dreary, as do most addresses, so pleasure grows into weariness and homesickness by and by.

Tom speaks words Hertford puts into his mouth from time to time. He tries hard to acquit himself well, but he is too new to such things and too ill at ease for more than tolerable success. He looks sufficiently like a king, yet cannot feel like one, and feels cordially glad when ceremony ends. The larger part of his day wastes, as he terms it, in labors of royal office, and even princely pastimes burden him.
7197-the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-5:
Part Five of Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer holds Tom's great secret: the plan to return home with his brother pirates and attend their own funerals. The boys paddle to the Missouri shore on a log at dusk and sleep in woods at the town's edge. Then they creep through back lanes to finish the night among invalided benches in the church gallery.

Monday breakfast brings a warm change, as Aunt Polly and Mary grow loving and attentive to Tom's wants, unaware of the joke ripening around them. Twain plays the funeral scheme for both mischief and tenderness, letting the boys savour a grief they caused. This part alone carries the secret return and the morning after.
7246-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur:
Part Five of Mark Twain's Connecticut Yankee turns to the restoration of the fountain, where Merlin still burns smoke-powders, paws the air, and mutters gibberish at the dry well. Saturday noon finds the Yankee watching a magician down-hearted after failing to raise even a perspiration in the well, and the Yankee greets him as partner with cool cheer.

Merlin answers that he labours at the most powerful enchantment known to princes of the occult arts in the East, and begs for peace until he finishes. His smoke darkens the whole region, yet the well stays dry, setting up the Yankee's own turn at miracle-working. This part holds the contest of wonders at the fountain's mouth.
735-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Edward Gibbon reached the medieval world in this fifth volume, with notes by H. H. Milman. It opens with the Franks' conquest of Italy and the temporal power of the popes. It follows the rise and coronation of Charlemagne, then the decay of Roman rule in the West and the rise of the Germanic states. A long section turns east to Arabia.

There Gibbon describes Arabia and its peoples, the birth and doctrine of Mahomet, his preaching at Mecca, and his flight to Medina. The volume thus joins West and East in one sweep, from Frankish kings to the prophet of Islam. It shows Gibbon at his most wide-ranging, and it is vital for readers following Rome into the Middle Ages.
7754-godolphin-volume-5:
Lucilla pauses at Godolphin's door toward evening in the fifth volume of Lytton's Godolphin, then summons courage to enter. His servant, amazed and glad, says his master is out but returns tomorrow, and Lucilla delights to learn her letter worked faster than she hoped.

Trunks half-packed mark a coming departure in a long Italian room, where she waits trembling and walks to and fro. At last her eye falls on an open letter on a table. Joy and despair share the chapter's title, and both fill these pages of love at a crossroads.
77882-life-of-george-washington-volume-4:
Washington Irving wrote this life of George Washington, in five books of which this is the fourth. A cheap shape for the folk came out in 1884. A cut at its front shows Washington from the bust by Ceracchi, taken from life. The list of parts of this book shows where the tale stands. The first part treats of the pains of the army at Morristown, in a hard cold season.

The ill state of the coin of the land, the mess of the food store, and the forced take of goods fill that part. The brave acts of the folk of New Jersey are praised in it. The bay of New York froze over that year. Lord Stirling led a raid on Staten Island, and Knyphausen broke into the Jerseys.
8170-gargantua-and-pantagruel-illustrate:
Book five of Rabelais's Gargantua and Pantagruel completes the voyage begun in earlier books, as Pantagruel and his companions sail toward Lanternland and the Oracle of the Holy Bottle. Motteux's rendering of books four and five followed in 1708, after Urquhart's translation of the first two books in 1653 and his third book posthumously in 1693. Passages omitted by Motteux have been restored from the 1738 edition edited by Ozell, as the front matter explains.

The final book brings the great quest to its answer, when the Bottle speaks its single word, Trinch, drink. Rabelais's satire of churches, courts, and sects reaches its height among strange islands. For readers who have followed the giants from Gargantua's birth, this volume closes the sequence with mystery, comedy, and a toast to the reader.
8475-life-on-the-mississippi-part-5:
Part 5 of Life on the Mississippi reaches chapter 21, A Section in My Biography, where Twain's younger self gets his pilot's license at last. Full fledged, he drifts into casual work, then steady engagements. He supposes he will follow the river the rest of his days and die at the wheel, a plan the later book will gently undo.

This section captures the pilot's pride and the river's routine, after training and before return. Readers get Twain's working life on the Mississippi, with its pay, its dangers, and its satisfactions. It is memoir at its warmest, the young pilot sure of his craft and his future, writing with the older Twain's fond irony.
8515-the-three-cities-trilogy-lourdes-vo:
Volume 5 of Émile Zola's Lourdes, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, covers the fifth day, opening with egotism and love. Pierre, at the Hotel of the Apparitions, cannot sleep. He called at the hospital to inquire after Marie, who, since her return from the procession, has been enjoying a deep, restoring sleep, like a child's.

The final volume of Lourdes follows the pilgrimage to its close, as hopes resolve or fail, and Pierre's own faith is tested. Zola's naturalist eye stays on crowds, sickrooms, and priests, while the love story between Pierre and Marie deepens. Readers finishing the trilogy get its resolution, in a novel that never preaches, only observes.
8586-roughing-it-part-5:
This fifth part of Mark Twain's Roughing It opens at chapter forty-one, with Captain Nye laid low by spasmodic rheumatism. Twain paints him as kind and agreeable when comfortable, and a roaring wildcat when a spasm strikes, filling the gaps in his groans with elaborate swearing. The comedy of a sick, profane captain sets the tone for a stretch of frontier life told in Twain's loosest voice.

Beyond the sickroom, the part follows mining camps, stage travel, and the schemes and disappointments of men chasing quick wealth. Twain mixes tall tales with sharp looks at greed, luck, and self-deception, never letting the moral slow the joke. Readers coming from the overland journey will find the same talkative narrator, now settled long enough in the West to laugh at it from inside.
8705-the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-5:
This fifth volume of Gustave Dore's Bible gallery opens with Isaiah, introduced as the earliest and most sublime of the four greater Hebrew prophets. The note places him as son of Amoz, speaking during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz. Hezekiah, from about 760 to about 700 BC, married with three sons, living near Jerusalem. It adds that most critics now hold the last twenty-seven chapters of Isaiah to be the work of a later writer.

Later scenes include the destruction of Sennacherib's host, Ezekiel prophesying and his vision, the fiery furnace. Belshazzar's feast, Daniel in the lions' den, the prophet Amos, Jonah calling Nineveh to repentance. Daniel confounding the priests of Bel. The volume pairs prophecy's stern warnings with its vivid visions, and it gives readers the prophetic books in short, dramatic passages matched to Dore's art.
8725-the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-volum:
This fifth and final volume of Emile Zola's Rome, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, opens in the Borgo before the Vatican at half-past eight in the evening. Pierre, early for his nine o'clock audience in the papal apartments, waits twenty minutes by a sonorous clock stroke in the deep silence of the dark, sleepy district. Relief mixes with grief: that tragic afternoon he spent in a chamber of death, where Dario and Benedetta now sleep the eternal sleep in one another's arms.

The audience itself, long sought through four volumes, finally tests Pierre's book and his hopes for a renewed Christianity. Zola brings the priest's Roman journey to its verdict, with love, death, and church politics converging. Readers who have followed Pierre from his arrival will find the ending both moving and unsparing, and the trilogy's Roman panel complete.
8794-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
This fifth and final part of Cary's Purgatory covers cantos twenty-six through thirty-three, the summit of the mountain. Canto twenty-six walks the rim singly, with Virgil warning Dante to look well, as the sun turns the west from azure to white and Dante's shadow makes the umber flame burn ruddier. Spirits marvel that he seems no insubstantial frame, stretching toward him without overpassing the burning pale.

Lust purged by fire, the Earthly Paradise, the pageant of the Church, and Beatrice's stern welcome and Dante's confession follow, ending with his washing in Lethe and Eunoè. The part closes the canticle in beauty and judgment together. Readers finishing Purgatory here will feel the long climb resolve: Virgil departs, Beatrice takes Dante's hand, and the pilgrim, made new, stands ready for Paradise.
894-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Volume five of Gibbon's history moves from the fall of Rome to the rise of new powers. The Franks conquer Italy, the popes gain temporal rule, and Charlemagne is crowned, restoring a Roman name in the West while Germanic states take shape. Then the narrative turns east, to Arabia and its peoples.

There Gibbon tells of Mahomet, his preaching at Mecca, his flight to Medina, and the spread of Islam, which would reshape three continents. Milman's notes guide the reader. The volume joins West and East in one sweep, and it is essential for following Rome's legacy into the Middle Ages.
9106-the-elson-readers-book-5:
William Elson and Christine Keck compiled this fifth school reader for American children, mixing nature, humor, home, and country. Its sections gather poems and stories by well-known writers. Theodore Roosevelt writes on the buffalo here. Lucy Larcom writes on the brown thrush, and tales such as The Blind Men and the Elephant add jest.

Each part opens with a forward look and closes with a backward look, so pupils can review what they read. The mix aims to build taste as well as skill, joining science notes to verse and jest. The book now shows what American schools put before children in the early twentieth century.
9168-the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-volu:
Book Five of Zola's Paris, called The Guillotine, comes in this volume of the Three Cities trilogy, translated by Ernest Vizetelly. Guillaume insists on watching the execution of Salvat, and Pierre, anxious for his brother's safety, spends the night at Montmartre to guard him. From a friend's house nearby, the scaffold can be seen.

The brothers sit up past half-past four, drowsy, speaking little, as dawn nears and the hour draws on. Zola sets brotherly love against the horror of state killing, in stark and moving scenes. The volume is among the trilogy's most intense, facing justice, terror, and pity head on.
9319-a-doctor-of-the-old-school-volume-5:
Ian Maclaren closed his Doctor of the Old School with Book Five, The Mourning of the Glen. Dr. MacLure was buried during the great snowstorm still spoken of as Drumtochty's standard for a century. Snow lay deep on Monday, fell again Tuesday to Thursday, and the north wind banked it at Glen Urtach's mouth in drifts of lovely shapes.

Men giving notice of the funeral struggled to reach distant patients through the storm. On Friday the wind sank, and the glen gathered to mourn its doctor. The volume is a fitting farewell, tender, snowy, and full of the love of a whole countryside.
9447-samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-:
Part five of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren finds Samantha still at war with a proud, unjust meeting house. In this part, she spars with Josiah over a church steeple, and over a man who kept his place while his victim was cast out. Sister Filkins and other church folk crowd the scenes. Holley's farm dialect keeps the comedy broad and the moral point sharp.

Josiah shrugs off his wife's talk as mere wind, yet Samantha presses on, naming wrongs plainly and seeking funds for fair work. The chapters mix home talk, church politics, and sly jokes at male pride. A reader gets a vivid slice of Holley's reform humor, where a farm wife's voice claims a right to judge church deeds.
975-ethics-part-5:
Baruch Spinoza's Ethics closes in Part Five, of the power of the understanding, or of human freedom, translated by R. H. M. Elwes. Spinoza now passes to the way leading to freedom, treating the power of the mind over the emotions and the love of God that follows from true knowledge.

He argues that freedom is not free will, but understanding necessity, and that the mind that knows God finds blessedness in that knowledge. His geometric proofs reach their summit here, austere and hopeful at once. Part Five completes Spinoza's system, and it rewards readers who have followed him from God to freedom.
9754-night-and-morning-volume-5:
Volume five of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning opens on Mr. Roger Morton, alderman and twice mayor of his town, behind his counter. Portly and thriving, Morton drinks brandy and water each night with mechanical care, yet never calls himself drunk. His digestion troubles him, and he blames joint, pudding, and vegetables in turn. The final book's comedy and fate gather around such figures.

Book five closes the novel's arc, as old scores settle and fortunes find their end. Lytton's prose mixes satire with moral gravity. A reader gets the last book of a Victorian tale of ambition, where a mayor's small vanities mirror larger falls.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
Part 5 of Mark Twain's A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court stages the restoration of the fountain. Merlin sweats over smoke-powders and spells for days while Hank's men quietly repair the broken pipe underground, then fireworks announce the water's return to a crowd of pilgrims. Merlin, beaten at his own trade, is put to sleep by a new magic — a wire, a battery, and a Yankee who understands both.

Afterward Hank holds a competitive examination for army commissions, judging officers on knowledge instead of birth, and starts the kingdom's first newspaper. Each triumph teaches the same lesson in a new field: trained skill beats inherited rank. Yet the Church and the old order watch his reforms closely, and a reader can feel the reckoning being stored up.
a-doctor-of-the-old-school-volume-5: The fifth volume of Ian Maclaren's Doctor of the Old School buries Dr. MacLure in a great snowstorm. Snow deep on Monday falls again till Thursday, when wind sweeps it into the hollows of upland roads. Men giving notice of the funeral struggle to reach distant patients. The volume closes the doctor's story in the glen he served.
a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-5:
William Dean Howells opens the fifth and final part with the affairs of Every Other Week settled, on the surface, into their wonted form. Basil March, though, feels impermanency in everything, and shame toward Lindau, the old socialist his candor failed. He never told Lindau plainly whose money paid them both.

The closing volume gathers the novel's reckonings: a streetcar strike, the Dryfoos family broken by grief, and the Marches weighing their own comfort against their conscience. Howells ends without trumpets, in talk and quiet decisions. The full novel stands as his deepest study of American money, labor, and the literary life built on top of both.
a-popular-history-of-france-from-the-ear: François Guizot follows France from Henry the Fourth through Louis the Thirteenth into the age of Louis the Fourteenth in this volume. The narrative passes Henry at Ivry, his abjuration, and his ministers. Concini, Mary de Medici, and the rise of Richelieu follow, with Turenne among the figures of the later wars. Engravings of the castle of Pau, Gabrielle d'Estrees, Marie de Medici, Richelieu, and Louis the Fourteenth mark the road from civil war to absolute monarchy.
ancient-records-egypt-breasted-1906-vol-:
Volume five of Breasted's Ancient Records of Egypt, published in 1906, is the indices volume for the whole corpus. It holds no new narrative inscriptions; its work is to unlock the four volumes before it. Breasted indexes kings, gods, places, titles, and Egyptian words across thousands of translated records.

A scholar tracing one pharaoh or one temple town can find every mention in the set from these pages. Such apparatus decides whether a corpus serves daily research or sits admired and unused. Breasted, a exacting organizer, understood that and built the indices with care. The volume completes the foundational English corpus of Egyptian historical texts. Libraries still keep the five volumes within arm's reach of the reading desks.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-5:
Hippolytus and Cyprian anchor volume five of the Ante-Nicene Fathers, in the Roberts and Donaldson edition of 1885. Both were third-century churchmen who quarreled with bishops of Rome. Caius and Novatian, smaller figures of the same stormy age, fill out the volume with an appendix.

Hippolytus gives the Refutation of All Heresies, a guided tour of every error he could name. Cyprian of Carthage writes on the unity of the church and the lapsed who fled persecution. His letters show a bishop holding his flock together under Decius's terror. The volume is the early church at its most argumentative and brave.
arabian-nights-payne-1883-vol-5:
In 1883 Payne's fifth volume of the Thousand Nights and One Night joined the growing shelf. The tales from the Calcutta edition grow ever more tangled and strange, as Shahrazad's store seems bottomless. John Payne's complete English version, the first of its kind, holds its course without expurgation.

Halfway through the set, the reader has crossed seas of story: islands of magnets, brass cities, and fish that speak. Each tale resets the pattern of wonder, danger, and narrow escape. Volume V stands at the center of Payne's nine, proof of his patience as a translator of the vast Arabic cycle.
at-sunwich-port-part-1-contents-chapters:
Part 1 of W. W. Jacobs's seaport novel holds chapters one through five, with drawings by Will Owen. Sunwich opens basking in a July afternoon: cranes rattle over the shipping while shopkeepers doze and boys watch the church clock. Jacobs sets his ancient port gently, then lets its captains, stewards, and sharp-tongued families start their quarrels.

Early scenes bring ex-steward Sam Wilks and young Master Hardy together in a painful encounter on the beach. Miss Nugent watches the boy get a beating with a stick and approves the justice of it, repressing her sympathy. Feuds between households, old scores from shipboard days, and the port's love of gossip are all launched here, in Jacobs's dry dialect comedy.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-5:
Volume five of Michael L. Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud holds Tract Pesachim, the laws of Passover. Rodkinson's set, in its 1918 edition, was the first complete English Talmud. Passover is the great feast of the Exodus, and its rules fill daily life for weeks before it comes.

The rabbis work through the search for leaven, the burning of what is found, and the slaughter of the Passover lamb. Then comes the seder itself: the four cups, the telling of the story, and the order of the meal. Hard cases crowd in, from dough left rising to a lamb roasted whole. The volume is the Talmud's fullest picture of a festival kept at home and in the Temple.
bancroft-history-us-vol-5:
Independence is declared and defended in the fifth volume of Bancroft's History, from 1856. The early campaigns of the Revolutionary War unfold in harsh detail. George Washington emerges as the central figure of the American story.

Bancroft's democratic epic reaches its heroic phase in these pages. Defeats teach the raw army its trade, while endurance wins the day. He honors the common soldier beside the great commander. The volume shows why his history shaped how Americans pictured their founding war. It was a people's struggle, blessed by purpose and led by a man of rare virtue.
beauchamp-s-career-volume-5:
The fifth volume of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career runs from chapter thirty-four to chapter forty-one. The face of Renée, Nevil's French wife, returns to trouble his English courtship. A ride in the wrong direction turns pursuit into farce and danger. Old Dr. Shrapnel, assaulted and defenceless, demands an apology from the Earl of Romfrey.

Cecilia Halkett is conquered, chapter by chapter, by Nevil's blunt devotion. Rosamund, the loyal housekeeper, carries messages and warnings between the camps. A trial of Nevil ends in a lame victory, honour satisfied at a limp. Meredith entangles the apology plot with the love plot until neither can move alone. These chapters show his gift for scenes where pride must kneel and cannot. The Romfrey temper remains the true antagonist.
bob-s-redemption-captains-all-book-5:
Bob's Redemption is a comic tale by W W Jacobs, issued as book five of his Captains All set. Jacobs frames it through his night-watchman, who holds forth on gratitude and how ill his help has been repaid. Two old cases, told at length, warm up the main story.

George, Gerty, and young Ted go to the music hall, where cheap seats turn dear and George pays twelve shillings in a fluster. Gerty's calm handling of the night undoes his temper. Next morning she sets things right, and a quiet evening at the furniture shops ends the row. Jacobs writes the dockside talk in thick dialect. Courtship, money, and pride get a gentle comic working-over in a short space.
carlyle-friedrich-vol-5:
Survival, not conquest, marks the fifth volume of Carlyle's Frederick the Great, in the 1897 printing. The Seven Years' War grinds to its close at last. Frederick, battered but unbowed, also takes his share in the partition of Poland.

Odds that should have crushed Prussia fail to finish it. Carlyle honors sheer staying power as the highest proof of greatness. The hero ages before our eyes, victorious yet alone. His epic of endurance draws toward its end here. The king's fame stands secured, and his kingdom is hardened by seven years of fire and want. He never pretends the cost was small or the glory clean.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100080009-5:
Memorandum marked Secret gives comments on a draft STIC charter, and opens bluntly. The writer is less than enthusiastic about the draft. Members of BMIS to whom he had sent copies reacted even less warmly, he reports. Some of their thoughts are folded into his own comments here.

The proposed reorganization looked to him like a blend of the IC Staff and PSTD, he writes. Priority groups seemed taken straight from the PSTD charter, with the life sciences thrown in at the bottom as a gesture. Major problems the intelligence community would face were ignored outright, he argues. A passage lists them: disaster areas in developing countries, and the false but powerful image of Soviet technological parity. It also names unusual phenomena such as UFOs, new farm and food technology, and dissent inside the USSR. Limiting the body's scope so severely would mean presiding over its demise, he warns.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100110005-5:
Booklet from the Educational Testing Service, dated February 1, 1979, sets out its principles, policies, and working guidelines for ETS products and services. Contents run from accountability and confidentiality of data to product accuracy, research, and test development. Copyright is held by ETS for 1979.

The opening principle states the firm answers for careful stewardship of its resources. It lists to whom: the New York Board of Regents that issued its charter, the boards that sponsor its programs, and the advisers who guide its policy. Institutions using its tests are named, and so are the people who sit them. Later policies require fair treatment inside test materials themselves. Biased or offensive wording must be avoided, the text states. Illustrations and practice items should show men and women, and majority and minority groups, with respect.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100130003-5:
Memorandum of March 1980 to the Deputy Director for Administration attaches a staff response to Chapter IX of the Inspector General's draft report on recruitment. That chapter covers the Professional Applicant Test Battery. The response was prepared by three agency staff psychologists holding doctorates, the memo states, with three outside consultants.

Two of those consultants were nationally known experts, named on the report's title page. The sender fully endorses their comments, conclusions, and recommendations. He hopes the response will go forward with the Inspector General's report to the Deputy Director and the Director, he writes. The introduction sorts the inspection's output into four papers, from a draft chapter to appendices on test data. Only the first is answered here, it says. A later passage defends the test battery's essay: many agency jobs need good writing, it argues, so an actual writing sample is the honest check.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100130012-5:
Chapter text on the Professional Applicant Test Battery, or PATB, presents the inspection's findings in plain terms. The battery was an eight-hour series of written tests, used for more than twenty years to select new professional employees. It was run by the Psychological Services Staff of the Office of Medical Services, the chapter states.

Two outside experts in psychological testing handled the evidence on reliability and validity. Their full report forms an appendix, and this chapter gives only their main findings in non-technical form. The use findings rest on a survey of 900 recent employees and 500 supervisors, plus interviews, it states. One consultant point is singled out as the gravest flaw: almost all data on hand tied the tests to success in training, not success on the job. The absence of job analyses beneath the selection system topped their list, the chapter reports.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100010006-5:
Routing packet of March 1980 handles a National Security Council request for access to CIA documents at the Lyndon Baines Johnson Library. A covering note, reference ISS 80-212/1 and dated 25 March 1980, passes the request to the History Staff. Similar requests had been handled there before, it states.

The Chief of the Information Services Staff asked the historians to draft the reply, using earlier letters as models, the note says. The letter would go out over his signature to the Archivist at the LBJ Library, with a copy to the Council. A suspense date of 27 March 1980 is flagged. The drafted letter, dated 26 March 1980, is addressed to Richard A. Jacobs. He was Deputy Assistant Archivist for Presidential Libraries at the National Archives in Washington. The Council's own letter, attached, sought material on the growth of the NSC system under Presidents Kennedy and Johnson.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100040030-5:
Approval to hire a retired officer as a contract writer is sought in a memorandum dated 6 October 1982 from the CIA History Staff. The subject is Richard L. Lehman, lately Vice-Chairman of the National Intelligence Council, whose post-retirement contract work for the Director's office had just ended. The file moves through the Executive Secretary and the E Career Service chairman.

Lehman would spend twelve months, from October 1982 to September 1983, researching and writing a history of William E. Colby's time as Director of Central Intelligence. Such studies of past directors formed part of a History Staff program cleared the year before. The Chief Historian would guide the scope and focus of the work as it went forward.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100070028-5:
Minutes record the first meeting of the CIA History Advisory Board, held at 10 in the morning on Wednesday 15 December 1982 in the Director's conference room. Charles Briggs chaired, with senior officers from each directorate present and Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald as executive secretary. The board had been set up that month to approve new historical studies and rule on their circulation.

The first item was a planned study of Congress and the CIA, with a prospectus by a staff historian. McDonald said his main test in picking topics was their use to senior management, and he ranked Agency ties with Congress as the most pressing subject. Discussion of the study's design follows in the minutes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100080018-5:
Work in hand at the CIA History Staff fills a two-week report dated 27 April 1984, sent to Executive Secretary Tom Cormack. One item covers the transfer of OSS records to the National Archives. Foreign governments tied to the OSS were being assured by cable, and an agreement with the Archives awaited final approval.

Other items track live tasks across the staff. A court had ruled that a draft chapter of the Helms history did not have to be released for the Westmoreland case against CBS. Letters had gone to five retired officers asking for interviews, among them James Critchfield and James Angleton. Staff writing honors, retirements, and records processing are also noted in passing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp02-06298r000900060004-5:
Fisher 9500 Series butterfly control valve bodies are the subject of an instruction manual, Form 2433, dated September 1976.
