The manual gives installation, adjustment, and maintenance steps for the valve body assemblies. Separate manuals cover the power actuators, brackets, linkage, and positioners used with them.

The valves come with keyed shafts for linear-motion actuators such as the Fisher Type 480-15 and 656, or splined shafts for rotary actuators such as the 1051 and 1061. Linkage is set at the factory when the valve ships as a full assembly. Removal steps warn that the disc must be shut before the valve leaves the pipeline, so the disc and liner are not damaged.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100070001-5:
Brazil's fight for financial stability is tracked in a secret intelligence assessment dated April 1984, ALA 84-10035. The Office of African and Latin American Analysis prepared the paper, coordinated with the operations directorate. It rests on information available as of 15 March 1984 and looks ahead at the rest of that year.

Four main findings open the paper, drawn from forecasts of Brazil's economy and its ability to follow an IMF-backed stabilization program. A revised accord aimed to cut inflation to 100 percent and the current account deficit to 6 billion dollars. Money supply growth was to slow sharply. The paper notes that holding IMF and creditor support meant keeping unpopular steps that squeezed the middle class.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100160001-5:
Cuba's changing ties with Latin America are assessed in a secret intelligence paper dated September 1984, ALA 84-10092. The Office of African and Latin American Analysis prepared it, coordinated with the operations directorate. It rests on information available as of 1 September 1984.

Key judgments describe a two-track policy in Havana: revolutionary goals on one side and diplomatic gains on the other, with the stress shifting as wider policy demands. Later sections turn to multilateral work. The paper reports Cuban efforts to raise its standing in the Nonaligned Movement and to warm ties with Western Europe. Those moves, in the paper's account, were meant to support the improving links with Latin American governments.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000201230001-5:
China's turn to fiscal and monetary tools is described in a confidential memorandum dated 24 February 1984. The summary opens with a shift: Beijing's direct grip on the economy has weakened as decision power has moved to lower levels. The government has begun testing Western-style demand management in reply.

The banking system has been fully restructured to make monetary policy workable, the paper reports. Treasury bonds and changes in state spending have also been put to use. The experiment is expected to run for some years, but without major price reform the paper expects Beijing to stay unhappy with the results. Later pages cover tax trials, including taxes on fixed assets and value added in a few areas.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100080001-5:
Peru's cocaine industry is studied in a secret research paper dated March 1985, carrying three report numbers from global issues, Latin American, and imagery analysis offices. The operations directorate coordinated the work. It rests on information available as of 28 February 1985.

A summary calls the Peruvian drug trade a dynamic industry with powerful economic and political effects. Later pages argue that a depressed economy deepens the coca trade's grip on local and regional life. That weight, the paper reports, makes at least some officials think twice before cracking down during a deep slump. Imagery analysis among the authors points to the paper's use of overhead evidence on growing areas.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100530001-5:
How China makes foreign policy is the subject of a secret research paper dated January 1985, EA 85-10010. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it. The paper opens with a flat claim: decision making in China is, and always has been, highly centralized.

Since his return to power, Deng Xiaoping has called most of the shots, above all in foreign policy, the paper reports. In recent years he has passed more power to picked successors, party chief Hu Yaobang and Premier Zhao Ziyang, with Hu named the real heir. The armed forces are treated with care: the paper says there is no hard evidence the military as an institution has pushed or blocked a foreign policy line.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201150001-5:
Japan news for the first days of 1985 is gathered in a memorandum dated 16 January 1985, covering 1 to 13 January. The Japan Branch prepared the roundup, using information available as of 13 January. It carries the number EA M 85-10011 and a note marking it as a duplicate of another file copy.

The lead item covers the summit between Prime Minister Nakasone and the President on 2 January. Press reports before the meeting said Nakasone had much to gain, and later comment held that he won his aims. Those aims included closer personal ties with the President and a private sounding of American policy toward the Soviet Union. Holiday television coverage at home also served him well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201330001-5:
Japanese attitudes toward the MOSS trade talks are traced in a memorandum dated 5 March 1985. MOSS stands for market-oriented sector-specific talks with the United States. The Japan Branch prepared the paper, using information available that day.

Despite American press claims of foot-dragging in Tokyo, parts of the Japanese bureaucracy moved fast to head off payback, the summary reports. They tackled visible import barriers in the chosen sectors. Pressure at home is also pushing the more cautious ministries for forestry and telecommunications toward a better stance. One risk is named: former prime minister Tanaka's stroke could turn his party inward for weeks, slowing work on the trade front.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201600001-5:
China's anticorruption campaign is weighed against its reforms in a memorandum dated 30 April 1985. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared the paper. Public growth in corrupt acts by officials forced reform leaders to reassert central control over some spending and goods flows.

Steps announced at a recent National People's Congress session aim to stop speculation in scarce goods, excess bonuses, and unapproved price rises. The paper judges that reformers began the drive themselves, but conservative critics have used it to attack the reforms. Reformers still hold the upper hand and call the problem receding. The likely cost is slower progress on firm freedom and on the marketing of scarce goods.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000301960001-5:
A new succession package in China is reported in a memorandum dated 22 July 1985. The Domestic Policy Branch of the China Division prepared the paper. Deng Xiaoping seems to have had second thoughts about the succession plans built over five years, the text reports.

Party chief Hu Yaobang and Premier Zhao Ziyang, once set to lead China after Deng, may now leave their posts as early as September. Under the reported package, Hu would take the party military commission chair and Zhao would become state president. Hu Qili would rise to party chief and Li Peng to premier. Deng would keep the Central Advisory Commission chair, joined by elders who have opposed parts of his reforms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302130001-5:
China is building an antiship missile much like the French Exocet, in a memorandum dated 20 November 1985, EA M 85-10170C. East Asian and weapons research analysts shared the work, using information available that day. The weapon is the C-801, in development since 1978.

The solid-propellant missile may be ready for use as early as 1987, the paper reports. It is likely the fruit of close study of an air-launched Exocet that Beijing obtained. Export sales are hoped to offset the cost of fitting out China's own navy. Success would show that China can reverse-engineer some advanced weapons, the paper judges. Fielding the missile would sharply strengthen China's coastal defenses.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302220001-5:
China's balancing act in Burma is traced in a memorandum dated 29 October 1985. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared the paper, using information available that day. Earlier this year, the text reports, China cut off all arms and ammunition to the Burma Communist Party.

Beijing even took the party's hidden radio station off the air. The steps aimed to reassure Burma and to show Southeast Asia that China wants better state-to-state ties. Then China resumed some arms shipments, the paper reports, likely to keep the Burmese communists from turning to Moscow or Hanoi. Neighbors such as Indonesia and Malaysia, already wary, will likely read the renewal as proof that China stays a long-term threat.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302400001-5:
China's textile industry is briefed in a paper prepared for the United States Trade Representative, sent as a package on 16 August. A routing form from the China development office heads the file. No year is printed on the brief itself.

China ranks as the fourth largest supplier of textiles and apparel to American markets, the brief states. Reforms meant to raise output and exports, a vast pool of cheap labor, and a pricing system that seldom reflects real costs have lifted production sharply since 1980. Beijing's opening of commerce to foreign participants has also drawn bargain-hunting Western importers. Growth may now slow: a reorganization of the textile and apparel bureaucracy leaves the roles of its bodies unclear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000100040017-5:
The Inspector General gives his personal thoughts on a Bar Association questionnaire in a memorandum dated 23 January 1984. He writes to the Associate General Counsel for Intelligence Community Affairs. The reference is a General Counsel memorandum of 13 January 1984 on the same subject. A routing sheet with the same date heads the file.

His comments are keyed to the questionnaire itself, question by question. On the opening criteria he is firm on one point and divided on another. There is no question, he writes, that intelligence agency activity should face congressional oversight. He sharply disagrees, though, with keeping the intelligence budget subject to the controls of the authorization process as at present. Thanks for being asked close the short cover note.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000701540015-5:
Annotated pages from a United States Code volume make up a legal reference file catalogued as Foreign Gifts and Decorations. The pages reproduced in the opening carry case notes under a statute on political activity, section 7324. The notes concern federal workers and elections in the District of Columbia.

One line of cases asks whether District residents employed by the federal government could challenge a Civil Service Commission rule. The rule exempted campaign work for independent candidates in local partisan elections from the usual bans. The courts found standing, since the rule both freed one kind of campaign work and withheld freedom from another. Evidence questions in such challenges are also noted in the annotations.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000100030094-5:
Admiral Stansfield Turner, Director of Central Intelligence, addressed the American Association of University Professors on 10 June 1978. The released text heads him as the second speaker of the day. His theme is kinship: the intelligence profession and the academic profession rest on the same ground.

Both, he argues, are founded on good research, on searching out information, and on analysis that adds to the fund of knowledge. Both publish their data for those who need it. Turner notes that the intelligence community holds more doctorates than any other part of government. He calls for a more comfortable and mutually supportive relationship between the two professions, and says good intelligence matters more now than at any time since the Second World War.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000100030148-5:
Notes from a symposium with Seweryn Bialer fill a memorandum for the record dated 19 February 1981. Bialer, director of a Columbia University research institute on international change, spoke at the Council on Foreign Relations on 17 February. Poland's crisis forms the whole subject.

When Gierek took power in 1970, he borrowed abroad to build export industry, the notes report. Output rose 10 to 12 percent and living standards gained for five years. From 1975 the plan failed: oil prices rose, the West slumped, and imported technology could not be matched by management change. Two years of negative growth followed in 1978 and 1979. The notes list further causes: collapsed party credibility, special shops for party people, and unfair housing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200480003-5:
Stansfield Turner writes to Professor Vincent Davis at the University of Kentucky in a letter dated 14 July 1977. He thanks Davis for several July notes and for advice sent on 8 July about reorganization. Nothing new has moved on that front, he reports.

A newspaper story that morning would suggest their decks are awash, Turner jokes, but hull integrity holds for now. Davis is the only reader so far to react to an article on the naval intelligence program, and Turner hopes it stirs reasoned debate in the community. A rival article will be left alone, since answering would only raise interest in it. A spring public lecture is favored, with dates left for Davis to propose.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200480012-5:
Vincent Davis explains why he should stay close to the Patterson School in a memorandum dated 1 May 1977. The memo goes to Admiral Turner at the Old Executive Office Building. It recaps points made in conversation on 26 April, with a few more added.

His first reason is commitment: academic life has been his main calling for twenty years, chosen as an end in itself and not as a fallback. Davis contrasts scholars like himself with figures who treat universities as stepping stones. He names Kissinger and Brzezinski as men never truly oriented toward academic careers. Their reputations among policymakers, he argues, mattered more to them than standing among fellow professors.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000300730004-5:
Budget issue studies touching the national foreign assessment center are forwarded in a note dated 30 October 1978. The writer serves the Deputy to the Director for Resource Management. One study inside asks whether more resources should go to CIA production to raise the quality of analysis.

For fiscal year 1980, the only major increase proposed is Project SAFE, the background states. SAFE should free analysts from drudgery and open richer data to them, but it will not come online until fiscal 1984. Long-range forecasting trials and electronic presentation work were left out of the program. Apart from SAFE and personnel costs, the production budget fails to keep pace with inflation, the study concludes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401040008-5:
Long Range Schedules, October 1977 to June 1978 list the Director's known commitments months ahead. The Director was the Director of Central Intelligence. The October entries include a Business Council meeting at the Homestead. A press day at the Agency is listed. So is an address to a military reserve officers unit. The Navy Ball appears. So does the launching of the destroyer Hancock at Pascagoula, Mississippi. November brings addresses at DePauw and Wabash universities in Indiana. A Chicago Council on Foreign Relations appearance is listed too.

The December and January entries are sparser in the released copy. They note the Christmas and New Year holidays. A Conference Board event appears. The schedule reads as a planning aid. It mixes official travel, speeches, and ceremonies. Social obligations are mixed in as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501190038-5:
Commencement Address, Bryant College, 21 May 1977 preserves a speaking text. Director of Central Intelligence Stansfield Turner delivered it to the graduating class. The outline honors the graduates' commitment. It then contrasts their college years with an earlier era. Their years were the mid-1970s. The earlier era was the late 1960s and early 1970s. In those years, protest made young people choose sides in black-and-white terms. The pressure to oppose "the government" was at its greatest then.

Turner argues that few things are all one way. He says the American government has shown two centuries of resiliency. His own thirty-one years of service have been exciting and rewarding, he says. He urges each graduate to serve the government at some point. At minimum, each should be an informed citizen. Such a citizen follows public officials, writes to them, and advises them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501280001-5:
September 1979 press clippings fill a Central Intelligence Agency file of that month's news. A form at the front notes stock moved in 2002. The stock went to the CIA declassification center. A New York Times report leads the news pages. It is dated 13 September 1979. It covers the row over a Soviet brigade found in Cuba.

Writers doubt the White House grip on policy. They look back to past Cuba crises. The 1962 deal gets fresh print. So does work at Cienfuegos Bay. The file shows a scare that mixed old fears with new claims. Soviet subs and missiles close to home shores drove the scare.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601420031-5:
Herbert H Tarson wrote on 29 December 1980 with an invite. He wrote from National University in San Diego. He asks Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, to give the commencement address. A high school classmate of the director urged the ask. The school had in fact invited him once before.

The date set is Sunday 14 June. The place is a new campus in Vista. Vista sits 40 miles north of San Diego. Tarson would urge the board to act on a degree. The degree would honor Turner's work over 25 years. A scheduling slip logs the ask in the file. It marks the item as received on 5 January 1981.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601450056-5:
A E Majendie wrote from the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London in July 1978. The letter goes to Turner at the agency. It sends on a copy of a July 7 letter from the institute. That letter told him a place was held for him at the 20th annual conference at Oxford.

One part of the old letter no longer holds, Majendie notes. A double room at the Randolph Hotel in Oxford has been booked for Turner and his wife instead. Space in hall at Christ Church was tight, the letter adds. His wife could not take lunch and dinner with the conference, though she was welcome at other parts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601470018-5:
Limits of obsession is the theme of this law review piece from 1976. Its full title fences in the national security claim. Harlan Cleveland and Stuart Gerry Brown wrote it. It ran in the Administrative Law Review, volume 28, in the summer of 1976.

A quote from William Rogers opens the argument. The land must not grow so fixed on security that laws are freely broken, he said. Watergate drives much of the case that follows. The authors urge a public-gaze test for secret acts. Secret acts tend to come out in time, they note. The piece sat in the Aspen workshop file on secrecy, kept with Central Intelligence Agency papers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601480026-5:
Economic Club of Detroit sets out its speaker's table for April 13, 1978. The luncheon that day honored Admiral Stansfield Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence,. The file lists the men seated at the top table by name and firm. Bank, car and power company chiefs fill the list.

Names from the Detroit Free Press and state office appear too. The roll runs to dozens of city leaders. Such a list served the club and the guest alike: it showed who would be in reach at the meal. Turner spoke that day on new directions in intelligence. The file is the seating record for that Detroit appearance.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601480035-5:
American Universities and Colleges, 11th edition of 1973, supplies this excerpt. The entry treats Ohio State University at Columbus. It calls the school a coeducational state university and a land-grant college. Branch campuses at Marion, Mansfield, Newark and Lima get a mention.

Pages before it cover Ohio Northern, with staff and enrollment counts. The Ohio State entry lists its colleges and degree paths. The excerpt gives the school in the plain terms of a standard reference book: its size, its reach and its standing. Graduate-level extension programs run through the university's graduate center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base get a mention too.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601490007-5:
Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, wrote on 17 March 1978 to Robert J Dixon about a retirement rite. The ceremony was set for the 20th of April. Turner had just received the invitation. He writes at once because he will be out of town for two weeks.

Both he and Pat hope to attend, and the accept card goes back with the letter. One snag stands out: he is set to testify on the Hill that morning. If that changes, they will be there for certain. Staff on both sides would keep in touch. If they cannot come, he asks that their warm thoughts be known as Dixon closes a distinguished career.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601560072-5:
Houston Clubber for November 1977 fills this Central Intelligence Agency file as a club magazine. The Houston Club published it for its members. Early pages carry an advertisement for a Texas gas firm and its coal work in the Midwest. Member news fills much of the issue.

New junior members get short sketches of their work and families. Lawyers, oil men and accountants fill the lists. Firms such as Superior Oil and United Gas Pipe Line appear in the rolls. The magazine shows a city club at work: meals, members and standing in Houston business life, all recorded month by month for the house.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200430038-5:
Turner wrote to the Michigan Daily on 14 November 1978 to answer an editorial. The student paper's piece of 24 October was called The CIA on Campus. It claimed no one holds authority over the CIA. It claimed the agency had long acted outside civilian control. Its verdict was that the agency had got out of control.

That claim is wrong, Turner replies, in history and in fact. He cites the Senate panel chaired by Senator Church. Its final report's first book treated oversight at length. The letter then walks through the watch that Congress and the President keep. The file is a spy chief's public rebuttal, sent to a campus editor.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200470016-5:
Joseph E Leary wrote on May 24, 1979 from Sebastopol, California. He signs from the Sonoma County Stump, a small paper he co-publishes. He was sorry Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, missed the Laguna Beach Arts Festival last summer. He had stood ready to come down if Turner made it, he writes.

Leary became co-publisher the past February. He wrote the article on hydrogen fusion in the enclosed issue. He asks Turner to read it and respond. The country waits for ideas to break its dependence on foreign fuel, he suggests. The letter is a small-town editor's pitch to a spy chief: energy, print and a personal word in one envelope.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200660024-5:
Director of Central Intelligence agenda for 18 November 1977 runs from 1430 to 1530. Morale in the Directorate of Operations leads the hour. Twenty minutes are set for it. The future of that directorate takes ten minutes next. Issues in the directorate take fifteen.

General discussion fills the last quarter hour. A memo of 17 November backs the first item. The operations arm has a vital, lasting mission, it says. High achievement in that mission is essential to the security of the United States, it holds. The file pairs a timed agenda with a plea: the arm that felt the cuts most still carried a core task.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200680013-5:
Director of Central Intelligence meeting with summer interns gets an agenda for 14 July 1977. It is marked for internal use only. Topic one is the tie between the CIA and the academic community. Twenty minutes are set for it. Agency problems take fifteen.

Intern program suggestions take the last fifteen, with an addendum after. Under the first topic, a plain question is posed. How can the CIA improve its rapport with universities, students and faculty? Analysts joining conferences and seminars is one path listed. The agenda shows interns, the most junior people in the building, asked to judge the house and its campus standing to its chief's face.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200690012-5:
Renewable way of life is the theme of this article on green plants as energy. Harlan Cleveland and Alexander King wrote it together. Rising cost and shaky supply of oil and gas turn eyes to plants, they argue. Firewood, grain alcohol and methane are only a small part of the store.

Bioresource is a new word, they note, for an old subject. Hunting, fishing and farming are as old as mankind. The 1970s shifted how men see renewable flows, the piece argues. Sun, soil and growth look fresh and attractive as fuel and food sources. The article makes the case for living off income from nature, not capital. It was kept in Central Intelligence Agency files with the Aspen papers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200770004-5:
South African minerals material moves in this file under a sensitive tag. A form notes material relocated to the declassification center in 2002. A memo dated 24 February 1981 sits beneath it. The chief of the Agriculture and Materials Branch in the Office of Economic Research signs the memo. Material Admiral Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, had asked for is attached.

A recent study goes with it, matched to his interests. Its title is The Importance of Southern African Minerals to the Free World. The file shows the economic research arm feeding the top a live concern of the day: how much the West leaned on one region for key metals and ores.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200780030-5:
Nob Hill News serves guests at a San Francisco conference in this file. Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, was the luncheon speaker for the event. The news sheet treats Monday and the opening ceremony. A change in plans is flagged at the head. Readers are told to read with care.

Breakfast in the Fairmont Terrace Room starts at 6:45. The Sutter Street Stompers would serenade from 7:45. Music would lead the crowd to the Grand Ballroom by 8:45. A welcome from the chairman follows. The event was the 28th Annual University for Presidents. The sheet is a cheerful guide for executives at a school week by the bay.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300850013-5:
Harvard, Fletcher and Duke speaking invitations get a staff memo dated 10 May 1978. The memo goes to the Director of Central Intelligence from his office. Advice is crisp: tie the Harvard and Fletcher trips to a 13 November 1978 address in New York. The Fletcher invitations are attached at Tab A. Duke's invitation sits at Tab B.

Taking Harvard and Fletcher in November, with Chicago in October, would fill that stretch, the memo warns. Duke should be told to look at February 1979, with a southern trip in winter. Marks on the memo record the decisions: accept Harvard, accept Fletcher on the plan, regret Duke. The file is diary management at the top.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300860030-5:
American College of Trial Lawyers program fills this file for its 25th annual spring meeting. The meeting sat at the Boca Raton Hotel and Club in Florida. Dates were March 11 to 14, 1979. Officers lead the printed program. Emil Gumpert is named as chancellor-founder of the college.

Marcus Mattson serves as president, with Samuel E Gates as president-elect. James E S Baker is secretary and John C Elam treasurer. A board of regents from many cities follows. The program came to the Director of Central Intelligence as a guest of the meeting. It sits in his trip file beside the Pascagoula commissioning papers of the same March days.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300960002-5:
Memorandum for council members, guests and wives heads this Business Council file. It treats the October 1979 meeting at The Homestead, Hot Springs, Virginia. The council's letterhead opens the pack. Its office sat at 888 Seventeenth Street in Washington. A roll of active members follows on the sheet.

Names new to this copy appear among the chiefs. Frank Borman and Charles L Brown stand in the list. The memo form addresses three audiences at once: members, guests and wives. Such packs, kept in Central Intelligence Agency files, carried the practical word for a council weekend: who comes, where to be, and what the days would hold at the resort.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301090007-5:
Amherst reunion letter from Bob Finsthwait fills this Central Intelligence Agency file, dated 1980. He writes to fellow forty-fivers, his class name. Everyone he has talked to calls the 35th reunion the best yet, he says. It was the most gemutlich, the most warm and easy, of them all. The young had a great time too.

Thanks go to the reunion committee for a well run show. Polly and Charley Gadsden and George Starkweather get special thanks. The highlight was Gene Reilly's poetic dissertation, he writes. A powerful moment for the memory book, he calls it. The letter is a classmate's warm postscript to a college weekend.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401130010-5:
An invitation form for the Director of Central Intelligence invitation form 79-331 logs a Christmas party in this file. The form shows a date received in December 1979. A letter from Edward F Terrar Jr brought the invitation. The event was the annual Christmas party of Republicans Associated for Mutual Support. RAMS is its short name on the form.

Hours were noon to 1430 on Wednesday 19 December 1979. The Capitol Hill Club is the place. A suspense date of 13 December is marked. Replies went to a named staffer by phone. The file is the scheduling sheet for a party invitation, one of many that crossed the director's desk that season.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401130074-5:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) invitation form 79-270 logs an after-dinner speaking ask for 3 December 1979. A letter from Gene E Bradley brought it. Bradley chaired the International Management and Development Institute. The event was the annual meeting of that institute. Turner was asked to give after-dinner remarks.

Dinner would start at 6 p.m. that evening. The room was the Benjamin Franklin Dining Room, on the eighth floor of the State Department. The form was received on 15 October 1979. The file is the staff record of the ask, one of the many dinner invitations weighed by the director's office that fall.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401150054-5:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) scheduling item 80-79 logs a keynote luncheon ask for 23 October 1980. A letter from Mrs Edward J McNamara brought it, received on 25 March. The event was the 23rd United States Day Luncheon and Flag Ceremony. The Women's Auxiliary of the Chamber of Commerce of the New Orleans Area hosted it. Turner was asked as keynote luncheon speaker.

A suspense date of 11 April 1980 is marked. A New Orleans phone number stands on the form as the contact. The file is the staff sheet for a patriotic rite in the south: a flag ceremony, a ladies' auxiliary and a spy chief billed to speak at lunch.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401150081-5: Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) invitation form logs an annual Oxford and Cambridge dinner for Wednesday 2 April 1980. A flyer brought the invitation, received on 5 March. Cocktails would start at 1900, with dinner after. The place was the International Club at 18th and K Streets in Washington. Attire was black tie. The price was 23 dollars a person. An RSVP envelope went with the flyer, the form notes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401160026-5:
Herbert E Hetu wrote to Atlee W Wampler III on 10 June 1980 for the Director. Wampler was United States Attorney for the Southern District of Florida, in Miami. Hetu thanks him for a letter of May 21. Wampler had invited Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, to address the South Florida Chapter of the Federal Bar Association.

The answer is a regret, in courteous form. The Admiral's schedule is so crowded into the foreseeable future, Hetu writes, that no new commitments can be taken on. He appreciates the invitation all the same. The file is a public affairs reply of the standard kind: thanks, the reason in one line, and the door left warm.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601570001-5:
National Intelligence Estimate NIE 4-1-78 weighs how a Warsaw Pact war in Europe might start. The estimate was issued by the Director of Central Intelligence with board backing. It asks what signs NATO could expect before an attack and how much warning time might exist.

Sections work through Soviet views of war, pact readiness, and steps to ready forces. Political moves come first in the account, from party briefings to broad public messaging. The text also weighs how East European allies would be drawn into a choice for war. Judgments are framed as assessed likelihoods, with gaps and dissent noted in the text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601690008-5:
Executive Order 11905, signed 18 February 1976, is printed in full as a Federal Register text. The order bears the title United States Foreign Intelligence Activities. Its stated aim is to lift the quality of intelligence, clarify who holds which duties, and set firm oversight.

Eight sections lay out purpose, key terms, and control of intelligence bodies. Duties are then set agency by agency, for the Central Intelligence Agency, State, Treasury, Defense, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, among others. Later sections set limits on intelligence work, oversight steps, and secrecy rules. The print runs from page 7703 in volume 41, number 34, dated 19 February 1976.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601720040-5:
Processing times for Career Training recruits are set out in a memo from John F. Blake. Blake wrote as Acting Deputy Director to the Director, with no date legible in the header. The memo answers a query on how long it takes to bring a recruit into the operations side.

Stages run from first file review to final entry on duty. A first choice to reject or go on can take three working days, the memo states. Interviews and tests then take four to five weeks in the east and up to three months in the west. Medical and security checks add one and a half to two months more.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601730003-5:
Agency promotion policy is summed up in a briefing paper held in Agency files. Promotion is described as a contest judged each year against peers in the same field. Judges weigh work done, skills, time served, and value to the Agency.

Staff who rise above their post grade must move to a fitting post within two years. The paper traces a 1973 review that cut 23 career services down to five. Figures for fiscal 1976 show 26 percent of staff promoted, with 10 percent on a fast track. Later pages cover a talent program that grooms staff from GS-13 up for top posts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601730030-5:
Follow-up on staff rated lowest for poor work is reported in a memo from Harry E. Fitzwater. Fitzwater, Director of Personnel, wrote to the Deputy Director with career service replies attached. The cases came from the fiscal 1979 Annual Personnel Plan, Phase II.

Career services report what was done for each worker in the lowest group. Outcomes listed include better work, moves within a service, moves between services, training, and in some cases an end to service. One service reports no such cases at all. Fitzwater notes that thin case detail made sorting hard and that staff often fit more than one group.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000200230001-5:
Renamed as the Handbook of Economic Statistics, the 1975 volume is marked (ER) 75-65 and dated August 1975. Queries go to the Chief, Economic Accounts Section, Office of Economic Research, the front pages state. Scope covers chosen non-Communist lands and all Communist lands.

Most data run from 1965 to 1974, with figures tuned where needed so lands can be matched. Summary tables add West Germany to the main state and bloc pages. One table tracks electric power output from 1965 to 1974 in billion kilowatt-hours. OECD output in that table reaches 4,350 in the final year shown.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-00105r000403770001-5:
Keeping signal links working in the Far North is treated in a Soviet article by two officers. Authors are Lieutenant-General of Signal Troops D. Loloko and Lieutenant-Colonel I. Pliskin. Harsh cold, rock, marsh, and few roads open their account of the region.

Gaps between command posts can reach 500 kilometres in that country, they state. Fixed wire lines are slow to build and of little use at modern attack speeds. Field cable laid from cross-country trucks is urged instead for long links. A trial used helicopters to place five R-401 relay sets on high ground along a 220 kilometre route.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-01569r000100010005-5:
Winding up the Strategic Services Unit is ordered in C.I.G. Directive No. 6, copy number 24. The Central Intelligence Group issued it in April 1946 under National Intelligence Authority action. Enclosed texts carry the War Department order and the first directive to the unit chief.

A War Department memo dated 3 April 1946 orders the wind-up to go on at once. The work must end no later than 30 June 1947, that memo states. Wind-up steps must match the growth of the lasting peacetime intelligence program. During the wind-up the unit must still serve the agencies under coordination, as far as it can.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-01569r000100040002-5:
Policies and steps to govern the Central Intelligence Group are proposed in N.I.A. 1, dated February 1946. The report comes from the Director with board concurrence. It answers the President's letter of 22 January 1946 that set up the Authority.

That letter fixed the Group's broad tasks but left policy points open, the report states. An enclosed directive is meant to close those gaps at the start. Sound policy, the report argues, will help the Group work well and with effect. Members of the Authority are asked to approve and sign the directive. The text that follows is partly garbled in the scan held here.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10m02313r000704000005-5:
Joint study of remote sensing systems is the thread of a short file from June 1979. A note dated 27 June 1979 tells B. C. Evans that Dr. Cook will stay on the study. Cook had acted for Admiral Turner in Phase I of the work.

Presidential Directive NSC-42 ordered the joint study, a NASA letter in the file states. The study weighs ways to merge remote sensing systems into one national system. The NASA chief wrote to Turner on 15 June 1979 as Phase I neared its end. A draft report treats skill and cost points for set grades of merger. Routing slips show the file moving through the Director's office that month.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100170001-5:
Cape Verde Islands and their place in Allied plans are treated in a short wartime paper. The islands lie 480 miles due west of Dakar, the paper states. Sea lanes and air routes vital to Allied supply pass close by them, it argues.

Three islands nearest Africa hold first-class airfields, the paper states. Sal, Santiago, and Maio are named, with Sal able to take the heaviest planes. Enemy submarines and bombers could strike supply routes from such bases, the paper warns. Taking the islands would be easy but holding them hard, it judges. A report on a job interview dated 14 November 1941 is bound with the paper.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100420003-5:
Far Eastern affairs fill a large correspondence file from 1941 with a clear opening memo. A Far East Desk memo dated 2 December 1941 treats postings to that region. It urges contact with International Harvester, International Telephone and Telegraph, and United States oil firms there.

No United States oil men are now in Vladivostok, the memo notes. A past I.T. and T. man in Japan and the Philippines is praised but his name is lost to John Wiley. Charles Russell, a past Foreign Service officer then with the firm, is named as fit for British-held areas. A State letter dated 24 November 1941 sends a secret Far East review to Donovan. Later pages track a singer linked to Gestapo chief Himmler and secret radio work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100430002-5:
China reporting fills the legible core of a file whose inner stamps name a twin record number. Hosted text governs here, and its catalogue line names Berlin and Hamburg bombing losses. Chemical and biological warfare and censorship office work are also listed in that line.

A long account treats the Japanese fort policy in China as told by a source. Forts built by forced labor with seized goods ring ground the Japanese then hold, it reports. Garrisons draw food from the local people and sally out only in force. Villages in their path are burned or torn down for building stuff, the account states. Eighth Route Army leaders sought United States observers, it adds, and held that guns alone could crack the forts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100070007-5:
Accomplishments of the U-2 program are summed up in a paper dated 27 May 1960. Copy 12 of 23 is the copy held here, marked for TALENT control handling. Five years of flight are weighed against the risk of surprise attack, the opening states.

Four hard problems drew the main effort of the flights. They are named as the Soviet bomber force, the atomic energy program, the missile program, and the air defence system. Photography is reported to show only a small long-range bomber build still going on. Some bomber plants had likely switched to other work, the paper reports. Later pages treat target data, naval order of battle, and map fixes drawn from the flights.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100100094-5:
A new Office of Statistical Research is proposed in a memo dated 2 December 1955. The memo goes to the Deputy Director (Support) with charts and staffing tabs attached. The office would sit in the Deputy Director (Intelligence) area, the plan states.

Its chief task is statistical study in support of the intelligence program. Past study of Soviet figures had shown great worth in gauging Soviet plant output, the memo argues. Machine methods promise still more gain from pooled data over time. The work phase is named Project AUTOMAT in the plan. The ORR photo reading division would move over as the core of the new office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100210001-5:
Overflight needs for China and Southeast Asia are framed as study tasks in an NRO paper. Task I asks what the present U-2 national capacity is, with costs and timing for updates. It also asks what future U-2 needs exist in any world area.

Task II sets the SR-71 against OXCART on speed, height, and risk from missiles and jets. Task III, named Black Shield, treats proposed flights from Okinawa over Southeast Asia. It asks if OXCART would be spotted and how its boom would be read in China. Task IV asks the state of the first OXCART concept. Target needs for China, North Korea, and the Far East USSR close the set.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100220019-5:
Mission result tables fill an untitled file of U-2 flights from Adana and other bases. One table lists flights by date, mission number, target area, and grade words. Grades shown run from poor and fair to good and excellent, spelled in full.

Rows from August and September 1957 treat Lebanon and Syria flights out of Adana. A strategic mission table then lists Baku, Bulgaria, and Caspian and Black Sea runs. Dirty Bird flights from Adana toward Iran, Iraq, and Syria recur in that table. Camera types are given for each run, such as A-2, B, and System 4. Deep USSR targets named include Tomsk, Novosibirsk, Omsk, and Krasnoyarsk.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100390093-5:
Duties of the Deputy Director (Science and Technology) are set out in a draft paper dated 23 January 1964. The office runs basic and applied research in science and technology for the Agency, the draft states. It also keeps ties with the science world and other agencies.

Technical collection projects fall under the office, with their gear built in house. A centre for all data on foreign missile and space work is also its charge. Six offices report to it, from Research and Development to Computer Services. Foreign weapons study heads the fields listed, ground gear and site layouts included. Three further offices are noted as still in preparation at the head of the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100430007-5:
Project AQUATONE is proposed in a Top Secret paper marked TS 103217. With Air Force help, twenty high altitude aircraft would be bought with photo and electronic gear. Wide overflights of the Soviet Bloc would then be flown for photo intelligence.

Lockheed's CL-282, a jet glider type, forms the base of the plan. It would fly at 70,000 feet, past the reach of Soviet jets of the day. One clear flight could photograph a strip 200 miles wide and 220 long, the paper states. The safe window may last only a year or so, it warns. The Special Assistant for Planning and Coordination would lead, with Herbert Miller as executive officer.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200150025-5:
A Soviet bid for flight rights over Turkey is traced in a Foreign Service despatch dated 16 February 1961. The despatch comes from the American Embassy at Ankara by air pouch. It logs each step since the bid first surfaced in early December.

Moscow sought passage for a set flight from Moscow to Beirut, the despatch states. Repair, fuel, and ramp service at Ankara were asked for as well. Turkish staff saw no bar in Article 23 of the Montreux Straits Convention, it reports. A note dated 3 February and a talking paper were left with the Foreign Minister. Both stress fair return and warn that a Czech pact sets no pattern here.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200200001-5:
Air Force U-2 facts fill briefing pages on the aircraft and its support office. The plane is a single engine, single seat craft built light for long high flights. Its Pratt and Whitney J57 engine gives 11,200 pounds of thrust, the pages state.

Wing spread is 80 feet over 600 square feet of wing area. Design gross weight is 17,750 pounds on a 50 foot frame. Range runs 3,000 nautical miles in normal trim and 4,000 at most. Cruise speed is 425 knots, with flights of eight to ten hours. Cost tables put 35 aircraft at 17,750,000 dollars less engines and gear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200440005-5:
Fourth quarter FY 1972 work is briefed in a memo dated 3 July 1972 to the Chief, Budget and Finance Division, OSA. The operations part of the quarterly review is attached, the memo states. Detachment G at Edwards Air Force Base leads the test list.

Red Dot film trials used varied camera fits in the U-2R over six sorties. A new H lens took twelve sorties to qualify, the briefing states. Detachment H alerted fourteen missions and flew ten in the quarter. All flown missions kept at least 25 nautical miles off the China coast. Three launches were lost to weather and one to a gear fault.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300150042-5:
Two operational missions crown a commander's report dated 7 March 1962, IDEA-0705. February 1962 flying is summed up for the Chief, DPD in its pages. Partner crews are judged at peak skill after the month's work.

The T-33 was flown 41 hours 45 minutes on training through the month. Eleven overlays were drawn from film of the two flown missions. One staff man had bone graft surgery on his left forearm on 15 February. Oil bath storage for small tools fights heavy rust in the damp air, the report notes. A wall tool crib with signed chits keeps track of gear drawn for tasks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400060041-5:
Method of operation paper, control number 4924-63, spells out how the Deputy Director of the National Reconnaissance Office is to work under the 13 March 1963 defence and CIA agreement. His listed duties: stay fully informed on all program activity, supervise ties with the United States Intelligence Board and the exploitation community, and supervise all program tasks the Director assigns to CIA. He also acts for the Director in his absence.

Working detail follows: the Deputy keeps his present office and staff as CIA Deputy Director for Research, with a Pentagon office inside the NRO staff area for part time use. NRO staff must route copies of all incoming and outgoing mail and cables to him as routine. Set informal talks with senior NRO staff keep him current on problems and actions in work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500120025-5:
Draft paper dated 23 February 1968 argues for putting fast, high quality film processing at the airfield where a reconnaissance aircraft lands. Its opening case rests on speed: aerial reconnaissance earns its value by how fast its product reaches users. When film must be packed, flown to a distant plant, and worked there, hours are lost and a mission turns strategic in effect, however tactical its tasking.

Vietnam experience is cited to show a strategic system can serve a tactical role when film is processed in or near the theatre. The plan offered is a transportable, self-contained capability of small cost in staff, space, and support, giving rapid and reliable processing on site. It is not meant to displace the overseas processing centres already standing, but to sit beside them where time matters most.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500390017-5:
Program checkpoint charts dated 4 January 1962 track the 330 program across design, fabrication, testing, and support tasks. The work statement lists parts under study, among them an indicator, power supply, repeater, drum, navigation panel, computer, platform, and coupler. Dates beside each item mark test starts, document delivery, and completion points reaching back to 1960.

Later pages cover spares for two initial systems, ground support gear such as preflight carts and test sets, and field support staffing. A flight test schedule follows, with first flight set for 7 February 1962 and the first inertial navigation flight for 1 May 1962. Charts also record position error and azimuth test results.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500390125-5:
Short unsigned paper GUS-0036, headed Estimates of Required Performance for GUSTO, warns readers not to trust its own figures too far. Calculating the radar cross section needed to blunt a given radar set is called a dangerous occupation. Gaps in knowledge about the sets faced, plus shifting test factors, make any estimate shaky from the start.

Two methods are compared: direct use of the radar range equation, and correction from a set with real flight test history. Theory, the paper argues, credits radar with an ideal operator that human scope watchers cannot match. It ends by backing performance near the Iron Maiden standard, proposing a flying wing study and named measurements.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040087-5:
Use of the unit's U-3 aircraft is covered by Detachment H SOP H-50-16, dated 25 August 1971. The rules apply to all who fly in the aircraft, crew and passengers alike. The Director of Operations watches over compliance with the rules. The pilot in command answers for safe operation of the aircraft and for following the SOP on each flight he makes.

Only pilots who have passed a check as pilot or instructor may command the U-3. Staff may ride on a space available basis with the pilot's approval. Civilian riders must first fill out a DD Form 1381. Later pages treat flight clearances, fuel, oil, upkeep, and a command post monitor for local flights in clear weather.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600050022-5:
Air Force regulation ATTG Reg 60-1, dated 12 April 1971, comes from the 1130th Aerospace Technical Development and Training Group at Edwards Air Force Base, California. Its aim is to keep compromising papers out of U-2 aircraft and off pilots flying operational missions. The Group Operations Officer holds overall charge of the checks.

Each section that puts gear or papers on a pilot or aircraft must certify what it has added. A security guard is posted on the aircraft, logs all who go near it, and bars any late fitting without the certifying officer's approval. The file ends with a signed certificate for the pilot, aircraft, and mission, tying the checks to a 1966 project directive.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600070011-5:
Search and rescue support at a test base is planned in standing operating procedure 50-3064-1, dated 4 October 1966, replacing a September 1964 version. The plan gives steps for an aircraft accident or an emergency with people missing, and is kept in the Base Commander's Guide held by Command Post staff, per the text.

Word of a crash goes at once to Base Operations or the Command Post, which sets off the crash alarm system. Primary stations called include the fire station, base hospital, helicopter rescue, and operations. The Command Post controls all traffic during a mission. Final pages limit who may enter the post during a real mission and control access to the crash scene by badges.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700010007-5:
Short bundled file starts with a sample message form for Project IDEALIST, marked top secret, in the CONCEN series. Its Part III fields call for a mission number, the route flown in lettered legs, and the targets to be covered. Addressees named on the form include air force and defense intelligence staff offices in Washington, with routing notes for the Joint Reconnaissance Center.

Bound after the form is Project Headquarters operations directive 50-10-8, dated 9 November 1967, replacing a February 1966 version. It sets how specified agencies are told of planned IDEALIST missions so they can collect communications intelligence tied to those flights. The IDEALIST Division holds charge of the notices.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700050012-5:
Change sheet dated 30 September 1966 revises Project Headquarters Manual 50-3055-8, the OXCART general instructions first issued 15 June 1966. A list names the changed pages across six chapters. Old pages are to be removed and destroyed under AFM 205-1, with a certificate of destruction required, and the change sheet itself may be destroyed once the revision is posted.

The pages that follow define terms such as denied territory, then move into mission practice. Tanker and receiver crews must be fully briefed before takeoff and given flimsies on the rendezvous and refueling. Weather minima for a rendezvous are stated. A closing table matches system failures, such as loss of inverter power, to abort or continue choices.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800020005-5:
IDEALIST progress report for 1 July to 30 September 1973 is sent 15 October 1973 by Brigadier General Wendell L. Bevan Jr. Only the IDEALIST program is covered this quarter, in three copies. A flight table gives 188 flights and 593.1 hours across four aircraft, numbered 051, 053, 054, and 055, for the quarter just ended.

Payload work centers on the H camera. A mirror was moved from the Detachment H configuration serial 003 into a heat-modified configuration, serial 002, at the contractor's plant. After five good test flights in late August, serial 002 deployed to Detachment H on 4 September and was declared ready after more testing. A life support conference at Brooks Air Force Base is also noted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800050002-5:
IDEALIST progress packet dated 13 January 1971 covers 1 October to 31 December 1970, signed by Harold F. Knowles. Development items lead the report. A tree-lowering device has become a standard part of the RQ-225 parachute assembly, and all parachutes are being modified as they pass through Lockheed for repack. The first two modified chutes reached Detachment H on 16 November 1970.

Heat trouble at high altitude drove another change. Project pilots had suffered heat on the backs of the hands and on the thighs during the past summer. A white outer coverall of fire suppressant Nomex was made and test flown, with hopeful results, and the new coveralls entered service for all project pilots. Status tables close the report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800290024-5:
Memorandum for the record dated 9 July 1965, titled Micrology vis-a-vis the NRO, records one official's view after three years of budget submissions to the National Reconnaissance Office. The writer claims no special vantage point, but sets the comments down for the record. In the fiscal 1963 submission, he writes, CIA's part in the NRO was not cut much, and the small NRO staff could not dig deep into the papers.

By fiscal 1965 the picture had changed, with longer, closer budget justification. The memo then defends CIA's record, listing the U-2 and the SAMOS and CORONA history as cases in point. It closes by asking what act of enlightenment gave the Pentagon sole rights on technical knowledge, and when CIA lost its own sound judgment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800340019-5:
Memorandum DDS&T-183-68, dated 2 February 1968, sends the latest progress report on the DDS&T history program to office historians through their directors. Attachment A reports status as of 15 January 1968 and has been sent to the Agency Historical Officer. A second attachment records a discussion in which 1 July 1968 was judged a realistic deadline for completing the program.

Attachment DDS&T-181-68, dated 19 January 1968, gives the detail. Some offices moved well in the last quarter of 1967, the report says. Others lagged: one historian was pulled to other duties, and the ELINT history's post-1962 half was still in the planning stage. The Scientific Intelligence office, with wide ground to cover, reported itself about eighty percent complete.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800340037-5:
File pairs a short action note with a longer memorandum on a proposed history of the U-2 program. The note, from Albert D. Wheelon, asks James A. Cunningham Jr. for a written status and prospectus, after the Board of Editors of Studies in Intelligence inquired about the paper. Cunningham's memorandum, dated June 1965, admits no forward progress for months, crowded out by daily issues, but sets out his thinking on approach.

Cunningham proposes starting with a controlled agency document, then gathering taped interviews with key early figures, naming Allen Dulles, Richard Bissell, Kelly Johnson, and former U-2 pilots among them. He also suggests a collaborator who has served with the program for years and already written on U-2 operations, and asks for comments on the plan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030004-5:
Bound file opens with a draft memorandum dated 21 July 1947 establishing a Property Survey Board for the Central Intelligence Group. The board would decide, finally, whether an employee owes money for lost, damaged, destroyed, or stolen public property, or is relieved of responsibility. It could also order disposal or destruction of unserviceable and obsolete property in the group's custody.

Survey reports would be made on Form No. 36-18, with a notarized statement from the person responsible. The board could direct an investigating officer to open a report, and would review affidavits and exhibits. Papers bound after the draft give related property routines: requisitions on Form No. 1110 for shipments, personal effects forms, and a property transfer action form used in five copies by accountable officers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030040-5:
Typewriter Repair Procedure splits the repair unit's work into service calls and shop work. Service calls answer requests by phone or requisition, with a repairman sent out to judge the repair on the spot. Minor fixes are done in the office, meant to be completed within sixteen hours. The stated aims are faster service, fewer machines hauled to the shop, and fewer replacement machines issued.

Phone requests are logged at once on Form No. 36-21, the request for pickup and delivery. The repairman signs the form and notes findings on its back. Machines needing more than a call allows go to the shop, where work runs under the supervisor. A monthly report closes the procedure, counting machines repaired, the dollar value of work, and each repairman's output.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050138-5:
Public Law 413, 80th Congress, is the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947, approved 19 February 1948. The act governs purchases and contracts for supplies or services made by five bodies. They are the Departments of the Army, the Navy, and the Air Force, the Coast Guard, and the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics. The buying must be paid for from appropriated funds. The act took effect ninety days after enactment, its text states.

Congress declares that a fair share of government buying should go to small business concerns. Contracts above 10,000 dollars made by negotiation without advertising draw special attention under the act. Progress payments can create a government lien, senior to all other liens. That lien covers the goods contracted for and contract materials. Liquidated damages clauses are addressed, with the Comptroller General given power to act on the agency head's recommendation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050147-5:
Delegation dated January 1947 authorizes the Chief, Services Division, to enter into and sign contracts on behalf of the government. The power is narrow: unnumbered contracts only, where payment is a single remittance and the amount is less than 2,000 dollars. It flows from a memorandum of 6 September 1946 that gave the Executive for Personnel and Administration contracting power with rights of further delegation.

A memorandum of 23 December 1946 to the Office of General Counsel, bound after the delegation, asks approval of the same arrangement for purchase orders. The file closes with a passage on Services Division staffing, noting that work suffers when direction changes hands often. It recommends formal recognition of a named staff member as Acting Assistant Chief, Services Division, so the office can run with steadier direction.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050156-5:
Public Law 515, 79th Congress, makes appropriations for the Military Establishment for the fiscal year ending 30 June 1947. Sums are appropriated out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, the act opens. Early items fund the Office of the Secretary of War and contingencies of the Army, covering emergencies and extraordinary expenses that cannot be foreseen or classified, at home and across the Army.

Line items proceed through the services and bureaus. One item gives 69,000 dollars for operating, repair, and upkeep of the Rock Island bridges and viaduct and the arsenal street joining them. The Chemical Warfare Service section funds buying, making, and testing of gases, toxic substances, incendiaries, and gas masks. Closing provisions govern transfers between appropriations, with quarterly statements sent to the appropriations committees of both houses.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200060038-5:
Letter dated 25 January 1947 answers two work requests sent on Form 10-222 to the Public Buildings Administration. The first asks for lease and installation of an electric water cooler, dated 14 January. The second seeks installation of a janitor board, dated 16 January 1947, its dimensions partly illegible in the scan. For the water cooler, actual or near installation cost and monthly rental must be obtained first. Only then can the form be obligated and returned for release.

Future forms, the letter directs, should each state the actual or approximate cost of the service asked for. That lets the Accounts Unit of the Finance Division set up an obligation on its records. Requests for continuing services are to be made quarterly by fiscal year, with service dates shown. The catalog title of this record speaks of fiscal procedures for a logistic support plan; the scanned page itself is the water cooler letter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200100006-5:
April 1953 operations are reported by the Chief, Records Management and Distribution Branch, in the branch's standard monthly form. Details match the pattern of the run: two staff on special detail all month, one records analyst with the Jackson Commission and one man as full time courier in Transportation. Six new applicants were interviewed, five recruited by Personnel and one by the branch. Four sessions of a records management training course were held during the month.

Work improvement projects close the report. Project 2-53, refiling unbound information reports in indexed folders, stands ninety-eight percent complete. It had paused for a shortage of folders, now back in stock. Project 3-53, conversion to the revised card in the intelligence report inventory control file, is marked complete. Courier and file activity tables fill the middle pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00195a000100010016-5:
Minutes of a Joint Training Committee meeting dated 26 October 1950 record training business for OSO and OPC. A chart comparing the two offices' training load against estimates was presented first, as requested at the prior meeting. OPC training requests were expected to grow, after a ruling that poor field performance by untrained staff would rest on the division chief concerned. OPC expected twenty applicants a month for one course named. Concurrent classes were running in one course, with two more courses set to follow.

Other business included a draft memorandum on special training projects, sent for comment, and instructor staffing items. A memorandum asking for a system to debrief returnees for intelligence information was presented with a draft reply from the Chief, TRD. The committee agreed the draft solved the problem raised. Charts of TRD training load from October 1949 to October 1950 were also shown.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00252a000200030055-5:
Memorandum dated 13 December 1950, to the Assistant Directors for Policy Coordination and for Special Operations, argues against moving TRD out of the covert offices. A reorganization plan raises that chance, the memo says. Training should stay an operational support of OSO and OPC, not part of agency administrative services. The move would cut the value of training for both offices, in the writer's view.

Experience shows training works best closest to operations, the memo states. That closeness explains much of the recognized gain in training quality. Security is the first harm named: current and planned OSO and OPC operations would be exposed to people with no need to know. Research and testing work would also suffer, since sound training studies need close coordination with operations. A routing slip asks both assistant directors to review the paper and then meet jointly with the Chief, TRD.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00252a000200060007-5:
Trainee comment report, its catalog heading reading Administrative - Mail, collects complaints from students in formal training. Handling of personal mail during the training period leads the legible text. Mail arrived with no adequate explanation of the handling, students say. Some packages had been opened and re-sealed with Scotch tape, pointing to censorship. Students subject to these measures objected to them, the report states, in partly degraded lines.

Pool arrangements for students awaiting formal training are also criticized. Many felt little real thought had gone into their work activities while they waited. Morale closes the report. The major factor named is personnel disposition of those who resign from the program: students believe dropping out of paramilitary training speeds a career, since dropouts seem favored over those who finish. The scan is rough throughout, but these points read clearly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00355a000100020035-5:
Course outline for Section I, The Basic Conflict for World Power, frames a sixteen lecture series, each lecture followed by discussion. Its purpose is to present the elements of national power in the present world conflict, building the setting in which intelligence work is done. Three fields are covered: the opposing outlooks of the United States and the USSR, estimates of basic power factors on both sides, and the security commitments of each.

Lecture entries name the giving office and a short precis. The first, by the Geographic Division of O/RR, treats geography and national security, frontiers, and climate in military operations. Department of State lectures then trace the aims of the United States from 1789 through 1951 in three parts. Closing lectures treat the USSR and its satellites, their political structure, and the Russo-Chinese Treaty of 1950 with its commitments and likely results.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100150005-5:
Memorandum from the Chief, Plans and Policy Staff, reports a survey on building a Professional Administrative Officer Program. Several offices saw a need for more trained professional level support staff, and would back a course with material and instructors. Named support is quoted. L. K. White, ADD/A, calls the need definite. F. Trubee Davison of Personnel offers lecturers and teaching material.

Other voices qualify their backing. Sheffield Edwards of I&S would use the training for staff on duty, but can offer no instructors or material. Suggested course content is then listed at length. It runs from fiscal and budget theory to staff coordination, buying under GAO and GPO rules, and general services practice, in a list of more than twenty lettered subjects.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00011a000100070003-5:
Proposed CIA regulation, dated 29 December in its legible heading, governs training at outside facilities under Public Law 110. The statute is quoted first. Any agency officer or employee may be sent for special study, research, or training. The venues named are schools and firms, at home or abroad, and courses under the National Military Establishment. The agency pays tuition and other costs, on top of pay and allowances, under rules the Director sets.

Authority under the law is given by the Director of Central Intelligence to the Director of Training. Office heads must support staff in training with office services. They must also send a yearly statement, before mid March, of training needs for the next two fiscal years. Trainees must follow the office and security measures set for the training. Payment runs on Standard Form 1031 vouchers to the Finance Division.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100020008-5:
Official report on the Seventh Agency Orientation Course covers the program of 8 to 11 July 1952, run three hours a day, 0900 to 1200, in the Department of Agriculture Auditorium. It was the third course held under the quarterly regulation. The four segments match the pattern used again later: Background, Support and Coordination, the Production Function, and the Impact of Intelligence. The writers call themselves their own most severe critics, and judge the split clearer than in past programs, while refusing to call it perfection.

Speaker notes are candid. One current intelligence talk is judged the best of the course in print, yet the field must be handled in a more practical way live. Another speaker, lacking Harry Rositzke's flair, still earns a vote of confidence for his analysis. A change of dates is recommended, to pull the program clear of the July 4 period, starting with the eighth course in November.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000200040005-5:
Office of Training regulation of the Agency laying down procedures for the Training Evaluation Program, run by the Assessment and Evaluation Staff. Courses are taken up in a set order, in four groups, starting with basic courses and their later phases, then administration and language courses, then all other courses, and last tutorial training. Each course had to send its aims to the staff within thirty days.

Aims must be recast to state what subjects, traits, or skills a student will be rated on. Workshops for instructors cover framing aims, choosing tests, and keeping marks alike across classes. Reports go to a student's division chief as a narrative on knowledge and skill, plus strong and weak points bearing on a CIA career. Rating words run from unsatisfactory through superior.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100020083-5:
Task Force paper on entrance on duty dates. The paper concerns new Agency overseas appointees. An Audit Division memo is attached. A draft change to the CIA Regulations is attached too. Current practice set the date at the start of travel. A new appointee began travel from home on that date. The habit made reports hard to process. Travel accounts and payrolls were hard to audit.

The draft change works in a new way. A person could be appointed before travel began. Travel costs and per diem would still be covered. Pay would start only on reporting in Washington. That reporting day counts as a full day of duty. The audit note gives a reason for change. Roundabout travel and early arrivals caused trouble. Leave without pay was charged before duty began.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100030019-5:
Draft notice dated 5 August 1952. Its subject is allowances and differentials. It cites CIA rules and the Confidential Funds Regulations. Basic salary is full pay for the work itself. Pay ties to the job, not the place. Allowances have a different purpose. They draw Agency staff to an overseas post. They also repay costs that home service would not bring.

Allowances are never open to bargaining. Each case is figured from set rates. Those rates are fair averages, not sums fitted to one person. Three kinds of payment are defined. Incentive payments include quarters and temporary lodging. Protective payments guard staff against loss. Salary differentials form the third kind. They serve posts with harsh or unhealthy conditions. Such posts need extra pay to draw staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100030064-5:
Task Force memorandum dated 13 March 1951. It went to the Assistant Deputy Director for Administration. Per diem policy is the subject. Several papers are attached to it. One is an administrative instruction with supplements. One paper dates from 1 July 1949. That paper fixed per diem rates for Agency covert staff. The rates covered Washington duty and travel overseas.

Later papers deal with changed hiring practice. Pool hiring had grown in volume. That growth made one step vital. Fitness for per diem had to be settled early. It had to be settled before travel began. A draft change gave that ruling to set officials. The Personnel Director was one of them. Assistant directors were named as well. The Task Force offers a set procedure instead. It asks the Senior Review Committee to approve it. Approval would let the procedure be issued at once.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100080014-5:
Working list number one, dated 4 May 1953. The Professional Selection Panel prepared it. It names qualities bearing on career service fitness. Each quality comes with questions to ask. The panel would judge each applicant by them. Technical skill for a set post is left aside. The list runs to at least twenty-two qualities.

Integrity heads the list of qualities. Morality and faithfulness follow close behind. Objectivity and adaptability are also tested. Anonymity matters greatly in this career. A candidate must accept a life without public notice. Acceptance of discipline is probed too. Emotional control under strain is another test. Career desire and discretion both appear. Later items cover money readiness for an Agency salary. Freedom of action closes the visible list. Family, faith, and politics may limit that freedom.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100020002-5:
Budget narrative for Training (General) activities, fiscal 1954. A general statement opens the long file. The Office of Training (General) runs most Agency training. Clandestine methods training sits outside its charge. Sections cover the planning function in detail. Intelligence training gets its own section. The Junior Officer Training Program follows.

Management and clerical training are covered next. Language, area, and technical training follow. Publications close the main sections. Appendices hold related material for the first section. Training liaison officer meetings are recorded. External training needs span fiscal 1954 and 1955. A staff study covers briefing service attaches. A Near East language and area program is described. The narrative also notes deals with the armed services. Agency staff could enlist for military training under them. Their Agency careers stayed protected meanwhile.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000010082-5:
Statement of assumptions and tentative understandings on contractor staff. It concerns staff at a forward base of operations. Their entitlements are the subject throughout. Room and board would come at government expense. Each person hired under the Agency mission qualified. Exchange privileges would match those of troops. Prices would match troop prices at the location. Currency conversion would be provided free.

Staff should draw little of their pay abroad. Only a minimum amount was the advice given. Base details would be shared once chosen. Climate data would be furnished to the contractor. Commodity costs and recreation costs would follow. Those facts would help set the overseas share. Payment particulars fill the second half. The contractor signs the employment agreement itself. Contractor and employee fix the overseas amount together. That amount is listed beside the employee's name.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000080003-5:
Long contract file opening with a short March 1956 memo. The catalog title gives its subject as visa requirements. Distribution ran to Agency project offices and security staff. The bulk of the file is a standard provisions text. An index of general provisions leads that text. Definitions and changes open the numbered list. Limitation of cost comes third in order.

Allowable cost, fixed fee, and payment follow. Records and government property provisions come next. Insurance and inspection clauses are included too. Excusable delays and subcontracts are covered. Patent matters take several long provisions. Filing of applications and patent rights both appear. Copyright and technical data use are covered. Disputes, gratuities, and alien employment close the list. Military security requirements end the index. The provisions run to more than thirty pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000090039-5:
Negotiated Agency contract number HF-1230, in a very long file. The contractor was a company on Broadway in Buffalo. Its name reads poorly in the scan. Target price is given as 507,906 dollars and five cents. Ceiling price is given as 555,778 dollars and twenty-six cents. The parties executed the contract in 1956. The schedule controls over general provisions in any clash.

The contractor must furnish facilities under the deal. It must deliver supplies and perform services too. Those duties are set out in the attached schedule. Corporate certification pages follow the contract face. An officer certified due signing for the company. The bulk of the file is standard provisions text. Litigation evidence duties appear deep in that text. The contractor must share evidence on request. Government expense rules govern that sharing duty. Indemnity cases form an exception to the rule.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000090084-5:
Report of a visit to Hycon Manufacturing Company in Pasadena. The visit also covered the project site itself. The report dates from 4 April 1956.
