It went through the Agency Contracting Officer for the record. Time at Hycon ran from 4 to 11 March. Time at the site ran from 13 to 19 March. Findings and problems at both places are reported.

Personnel met at Hycon are described in the report. Site talks covered the Hycon task group. Detachment A members were also met there. A tracker camera section leads the findings. Five or six 70-millimeter cameras sat at the site. Their malfunctions were of a minor nature. A maintenance manual for that camera is named. Its title names the Model 111 data recording camera. Design changes for a later mode are discussed. Wider overlap and a wider angle are projected.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000110135-5:
Agency letter contract number RA-101 with General Precision Laboratory. The company sat at 63 Bedford Road in Pleasantville. That town is in New York state. The letter is numbered SAPC-5257 in the file. An order is placed with the contractor by it. Supplies and services in Exhibit A are covered. The exhibit is made part of the contract.

On acceptance, the contractor must proceed at once. Necessary materials must be procured without delay. Manufacture or services must start right away. Work must go forward with all diligence. Earliest practical delivery is the stated aim. Procurement regulation clauses are built in by reference. Definitions, changes, and extras clauses are named. Inspection and payments clauses appear in the list. Later terms alter one records clause. The Comptroller General is replaced in that clause. The Contracting Officer takes that role instead. Claim assignment needs written approval first.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000130043-5:
Negotiated Agency contract number EQ-1806 with Eastman Kodak Company. The company sat in Rochester, New York. The contract amount reads as 1,361,850 dollars. A schedule of items forms the visible body. Lot and job amounts are listed in the schedule. One lot reads as 160,000 dollars even. Other lots read as 94,000 and 30,000 dollars.

Delivery terms are set item by item. Items one through thirteen carry April dates. Most of those dates fall in April 1956. Later items run through the summer of 1956. Item sixteen completes in November 1956. Item seventeen completes in August 1956. Item nineteen splits across three months. One unit falls in August, two in September. Two more units fall in October 1956. Item twenty-two completes in November as well. The file is short, at a few pages. Its face and schedule carry the whole record.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000140123-5:
Negotiated Agency contract entered into on 1 January 1956. The file head names a national aeronautics committee address. That address is 1724 F Street, Northwest, in Washington. The contractor was a corporation in Burbank, California. Its name is redacted in the contract text. Article one states the work required. Pilot services are the heart of the deal.

Fully qualified airplane pilots must be furnished on request. About thirty pilots at any one time is the estimate. Pay is 833 dollars and thirty-three cents per pilot monthly. A portion of a month is paid pro rata. An administrative charge of 850 dollars monthly is added. That charge repays the contractor's direct costs. Indirect costs and fees are covered by it too. Transport of pilots from Burbank is government paid. Other expenses of the service fall on the government. Fair compensation language closes the visible text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000190010-5:
Agency letter contract with the contractor unnamed in the head. An order is placed by the opening introduction. Supplies and services in Exhibit A are covered. The exhibit is made part of the contract. On acceptance, the contractor must proceed at once. Materials must be procured without delay. Manufacture or services must start right away. Earliest practicable delivery is the stated goal.

Procurement regulation clauses are built in by reference. Definitions, changes, and extras clauses are named. Variation in quantity and inspection appear too. Responsibility for supplies is covered in the list. Assignment of claims and bond security follow. Federal, state, and local taxes are named. Disputes clause closes the visible list. Termination terms run long in the later text. Costs on supplies delivered before termination count. A two percent sum enters the termination formula. That sum applies to unprocessed materials costs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000200110004-5:
Blank student comment form for course evaluation. Students are asked to answer carefully and completely. Answers help instructors judge course results. They also help develop the whole Agency training program. Signing the form is not required of students. That freedom lets praise and criticism flow openly. Legible writing is requested on the form. Ink or a typewriter is preferred.

The first question asks about added knowledge. Four graded answers are offered for it. A student may call the results essential. Lesser grades run down to nothing worthwhile learned. Reasons are requested under that first question. Later questions cover overlap with prior knowledge. Lecture and discussion time is weighed by students. Whether instructors encouraged questions is asked too. Written problems and tests get their own question. Space is allowed for extra sheets.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000600210009-5:
Day-by-day account of an Agency Basic Intelligence Course. The course ran 14 January to 25 February 1953. Sessions are listed with times and speakers. A comment follows each session in the account. Security opened the course on 14 January. Liaison, source protection, and careless talk were covered. The comment praises that talk warmly. Common sense and understated humor held attention.

Types of intelligence filled the next session block. Political, sociological, and biographical intelligence followed. Forms of government and parties were covered there. The comment calls that run-through quick but sensible. Its material was judged very basic in nature. Intelligence production came on Wednesday 21 January. Report types from daily to monthly were described. The Current Intelligence Digest served as an example. Customer needs and consumer guidance were treated. Sorting, evaluation, and synthesis steps were set out.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100030001-5:
Staff study from August 1953 on central processing of travelers. It went to the Acting Deputy Director for Administration. The Chief, Classification and Wage Division, sent it. A survey report of 7 July 1953 came first. That report called for detailed tables of organization. This study proposes one such table in response. The Passenger Movement Branch is the unit covered.

That branch sits in the Transportation Division, Logistics Office. Certain positions would move under the proposal. They would go to the Central Processing Branch. That branch sits in the Personnel Office. The Personnel Office was revising its own table meanwhile. That revision covered the entire processing branch. A simple transfer of existing posts seemed best. The branch would keep its liaison duties as well. Government agencies and commercial firms are named there.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100060017-5:
Management survey of the Graphics Register, dated 23 August 1949. The register sat in the Office of Collection and Dissemination. Its stated functions were found generally sound. Staff showed sincerity of purpose, the survey states. Procedural difficulties were disclosed in the examination. Many such steps were mandatory for records or higher authority. Routine administration was decentralized across the register.

Professional staff lost much time to that administration. About forty percent of their time went there. Organization has an office of the chief. A Photograph Division and Film Division sit below. Similar functions run through both divisions. Material type splits the work between them. Analysis for accession is a major duty. Filling requests is another major duty named. One recommendation concerns reports to other agencies. Agency accession numbers should enter those reports first. That step removes a need to keep copies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200020001-5:
Office memorandum dated 29 April 1952 on building services. The Agency Building Services Officer program is the survey subject. It went to the Chief, Organization and Methods Service. The program aimed to correct supply problems. Distribution and control of supplies were its targets. Other economies were expected from the program. Better property records lead the expected advantages.

Full-time staff would keep records accurate and current. Accountability by buildings would end account confusion. Property moves between accounts caused that confusion. Fewer people would handle property accounting under it. An estimate counted 144 persons then involved. Twenty-three branch accounts were in that count. Turn-ins and requisitions should fall as well. Identical items would be coordinated within each building. Findings note moves made without telling the officer. One move shifted property to I Building entirely. Weekly requisitioning was under consideration by procurement.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200090013-5:
Tab A guidance on a subject file for records. Official records of an Agency office form the file. Correspondence on specific issuances sits outside it. Tables of organization and forms records sit outside too. Present location and staff are judged adequate. Reorganization of the file is recommended nonetheless. Material should follow a logical system there.

The subject-numeric system is then explained fully. It adapts both subject and numerical coding ideas. Alphabetical arrangement of subject titles is retained. Related subjects are brought together under it. File designations balance long titles against short numbers. Primary subjects are shown by actual title words. Secondary and tertiary subjects take numerals instead. Education entries illustrate the scheme in the text. Schools and training for non-federal employees fall there. Personnel is the cross reference for federal employees. Employment of non-federal persons appears later too.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200150007-5:
Symposium account on machine techniques for information selection. An MIT industrial liaison office sponsored the meeting. Sessions ran on 10 and 11 June 1952 at Cambridge. Chemical and Engineering News carried the report. Its issue of 7 July 1952 printed it. MIT had investigated machines for several years. Searching and correlating information was the focus.

James W. Perry led that MIT work program. Analyzing information occupied much of the effort. Indexes searchable by machine were being designed. IBM was developing new machines in parallel. Those machines would have suitable operating traits. A mechanized system is hailed in the report. Literature searching enters a new era thereby. Scanning codes receive detailed treatment later. Luhn devised a code in several series. Two full alphabets are provided by it. Capitals and small letters both appear there. Two-digit numbers, subscripts, and superscripts follow. Only five holes are punched per column.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200150016-5:
Appendix XI of the Agency indexing study lists code dictionaries and terminology files. Files from an earlier appendix generated them. Complete dictionaries sit in Room 1348M. Excerpts of the listings are given here. An English to Code Dictionary Workbook leads. Index terms are listed in alphabetical order there. Semantic factors follow each term in that workbook. Each factor is shown by a four letter code.

Autoclave carries three codes in the sample. Autolysin and autolyzate carry their own factors. Automatic pilot shows four codes in sequence. A Code to English Dictionary Workbook follows. Codes there are arranged in alphabetical order. The term for each code follows it. Semantic factor dictionaries form a third listing. Two listings were prepared for use. Alphabetic order there rests on the codes. Words designating each factor follow its code. Vehicle terms illustrate the grouping in excerpts. Tank, tractor, train, and truck share one code.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100070001-5:
Text of Public Law 507, 81st Congress, on science. The act promotes the progress of science generally. National health, prosperity, and welfare are advanced. National defense is secured among its purposes. Its short title is the National Science Foundation Act of 1950. Senate bill 247 is the vehicle printed.

Establishment of the Foundation fills section two. An independent agency in the executive branch is created. A National Science Board forms part of it. A Director completes the Foundation's named structure. Functions of the Foundation fill section three. A national policy for basic research is directed. Education in the sciences rides with that policy. Basic scientific research is initiated and supported. Mathematical and physical sciences are named first. Medical, biological, and engineering sciences follow them. Contracts and other arrangements are the instruments used. Foreign country contracts appear in the later sections. Defense requested research is also provided for.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100140012-5:
Memo dated 14 May 1953 reporting on a short duty trip. It went to the Deputy Director (Administration). The Acting General Counsel sent the report through channels. A deputy General Counsel made the trip itself. Its purpose was weighing the legal function abroad. Tying steps together was to be developed there. Advice on gains was also sought.

Senior reps abroad were the primary visits. Their missions' sway on legal work was the question. Departure came on 25 March as scheduled. Return to headquarters came on 6 May. Problems met are not listed one by one. Matters of general interest are presented instead. Office and legal interest guides that selection. Property control receives extended treatment later. A central program had been begun locally. Many buying sources make running it hard there. Varied supply channels add to that trouble. Spread of places completes the problem. The Chief, Logistics Office, was briefed on it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100150075-5:
Executive Order text terminating the Office of Strategic Services. An immediate release dates it 20 September 1945. Disposition of the office's functions is ordered. Constitutional and statutory authority is recited first. Title I of the First War Powers Act is cited. Presidential and Commander in Chief roles are invoked. An Interim Research and Intelligence Service is established.

That service sits in the Department of State. Research and Analysis Branch functions transfer to it. Presentation Branch functions transfer there as well. Both branches belonged to the terminated office. Functions within Germany and Austria are excluded. Related functions of the office follow them across. Director and Joint Chiefs functions transfer correspondingly. The Secretary of State receives those director functions. Remaining functions take a different path onward. The Department of War receives the office's residue. The order opens for business 1 October 1945. Harry S. Truman signed it at the White House.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100220004-5:
Memo for the Director on schooling payments. Payments for minor children's schooling are its problem. Staff and employees at foreign stations are concerned. What law should the Agency seek, it asks. Facts bearing on the problem follow the question. No formal policy on such payments exists. No steady practice on them exists either.

School-age children of foreign stationed staff are affected. Legal opinion finds no specific power to spend. Post extra pay ignores children entirely. It rests on hardship factors as salary shares. Being or number of children changes nothing there. Schooling abroad is often unfit for use. Poor or far too costly schooling is common. Leave for the chief to allow payments is weighed later. Territories would be covered alongside foreign countries. A draft bill offers one vehicle for power. The Bureau of the Budget sponsored that draft.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000200090053-5:
Scanned pages carry a pulp adventure story, Donovan of Central Intelligence, issued by Avon Publications. The tale opens in the voice of a man working for a secret service chief he calls Donovan, telling how the service was built during the Second World War. Action scenes follow in quick order: a chase, secret plans that must reach an American consul, and pursuers close behind. Speech balloons and captions drive the story in comic form.

The scan's lettering is heavily garbled by machine reading, so many lines can be followed only in part. What survives is the shape of a wartime spy yarn sold to the public, with central intelligence cast as daring field work. Its place in an Agency file shows officials kept popular tales about their own service, however loose the link to real work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400060045-5:
Instructions for a Personnel Information Card govern how new staff and transfers report their details on joining the Agency. New employees and staff moving from another CIA office must supply every item on the card. New appointments mark the type of change as E.O.D., while transfers mark it as a transfer entry. Administrative officers check whether the name may appear in the CIA telephone directory.

Staff must also report changes at once: name, home or office address, phone number, marital status, or a move to another part of the Agency. Absence over thirty days must be reported too, with the office number of the administrative officer. The card form printed with the text turns these duties into a single sheet kept on file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400120084-5:
Who in the Office of Special Operations had to sign papers in person is the question behind a Legal Staff memorandum dated 13 January 1950. An executive officer's note of 3 November 1949 asked for a review of all directives and instructions touching that office. The review had to show what the Assistant Director or his deputy must sign himself. It also had to say whether such power could be passed further down.

A second part asks what approving power sat in the deputy's own office, with its executive officer and executive secretary. Answering meant combing Agency instructions, the Confidential Funds Regulations, and past grants of authority. The memorandum works through staff policy first, then takes each class of paper in turn.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400180006-5:
Shipment and storage of one officer's household effects draw a General Counsel opinion built on an October 1952 Finance Division memorandum. First checks corrected the man's status: files showed him a Marine Corps officer on detail to the Agency, not the military staff agent first supposed. He would therefore be treated as a member of the military personnel group. His orders for a permanent change of station had allowed shipment at government cost.

The allowance covered goods sent for storage ahead of his later return to the continental United States, up to a stated weight limit. He in fact shipped 12,263 pounds and placed them in storage. Counsel is asked which rules govern such a case, and what share of the cost the Agency may pay. Names in the file are redacted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500020002-5:
Major findings of a Bureau of the Budget and Civil Service Commission report on overseas pay are summarised in a paper sent on 1 April 1952. The report went to the Post Office and Civil Service Committees of both houses under Public Law 201. Its first finding is blunt: federal practice abroad is not built to give staff a career service like the one at home. Sound grading of posts is called vital to fair pay and good hiring.

In practice, the summary says, grading is applied unevenly overseas, so like work draws unlike pay. A stiff allowance structure for the territories has also pushed posts to seek rises by other routes. Further findings cover hiring, leave, and differentials. The summary gave Agency staff a government-wide picture of the faults reformers wanted fixed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500050009-5:
A committee print of August 1950, tied to Union Calendar and a House report, presents an act on pay from dual employments under the United States. The bill had been sent to the House Committee on Post Office and Civil Service in September 1949. It was reported with amendments in August 1950 and ordered printed. Struck-through text and italic inserts show exactly what the committee changed.

Its purpose line promises to simplify and consolidate the scattered laws on second government pay. The rule reaches offices in the federal service and in the District of Columbia government. Government-owned or controlled companies count as well. As a print, the record lets a reader watch a bill being reshaped, line by marked line, before it faced the full House.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500050027-5:
A Comptroller General decision answers the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency on hiring retired Foreign Service officers. The Director's letter of 29 October 1951 had asked for a ruling, and action waited on a report from the Department of State. Two questions run together: may such officers be employed, and may they keep their retirement annuities while employed by other agencies? Section 2 of the act of 31 July 1894 anchors the legal problem.

That section bars a person holding an office paid at twenty-five hundred dollars or more from holding any second paid office, unless law allows it. The first question then narrows to a retired officer whose annuity passes that sum. The decision works through each question on the statutes the Director cited.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500060017-5:
Legal text gathered for a proposed appointment, with the name removed, quotes the statutes that bar holding two well-paid offices at once. The long quotation comes from the act of 31 July 1894, later amended. It bars a person whose office pays twenty-five hundred dollars or more from taking any second paid office unless law allows. Retired officers of the Army or Navy are excepted where voters elect them or the President appoints them with Senate consent.

Retired enlisted men, and officers retired for battle wounds or disability in the line of duty, are also taken outside the bar. A second act quoted bars an officer from holding a civil office in named cases. The surviving pages are the law extracts behind a hiring choice, not the choice itself.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500080051-5:
Two plans for benefits owed to staff on hazardous duty fill a report of the Hazardous Duty Committee. The committee acted on instructions from the Acting Executive, and its members are named in the text. Plan I is the long-range scheme meant for career staff who face hazardous duties at some point in their service. Plan II aims at quick use, shaped for a possible national emergency or war.

Plan II needs no added law, the committee says, and could start at once inside CIA with the Director's approval. It was drawn for real, current needs voiced by the covert offices, not for theory. Three appendices back the two plans with detail. The report shows staff trying to price danger before the next emergency priced it for them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500090005-5:
A House committee study of efficiency rating systems in the federal service, dated 1 February 1950, runs to a full printed volume. It was made under section 903 of Title IX of the Classification Act of 1949. The Committee on Post Office and Civil Service, chaired by Tom Murray of Tennessee, issued the study. A letter of transmittal from the Civil Service Commission opens the text.

Inside, the study surveys how agencies graded their staff, what forms they used, and where the systems failed. Findings lead toward the new performance-rating plan Congress took up that same year. Agency personnel offices kept such a study close at hand: ratings drove pay steps, promotions, and cuts, so the rules for grading work shaped every career in the service.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500120001-5:
Public Law 102 of the 83d Congress, Chapter 178 from H.R. 4654, frees certain senior officers from the Annual and Sick Leave Act of 1951. It adds a new subsection to section 202 of that act. First named are officers appointed by the President, with or without Senate consent, whose basic pay passes the top General Schedule rate. Officers paid under section 411 of the Foreign Service Act of 1946 come next.

District of Columbia officers and those of government-owned companies are covered by the same wording. Further letters in the list take in other classes of senior post. The act recognises that the highest officials do not work to a leave ledger like graded staff. Its short text settles their position in one clause.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500120083-5:
Requests for military leave are traced to their legal roots in a General Counsel paper of 10 June 1952 for the Chief of the Fiscal Division. It answers a memorandum of 20 May 1952 and deals chiefly with leave for training duty. Agency Regulation is cited, then the basic authority itself. For the Naval Reserve, the quoted law at 50 U.S.C.A. 833 grants leave to officers and employees of the United States and the District of Columbia.

That leave runs without loss of pay, time, or efficiency rating for days spent on training duty under proper orders. Like rules for the other reserve branches are set out in turn. The paper gives the fiscal office a firm base for granting or refusing each training leave request.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500120100-5:
Wording for a time and attendance certification by fee-basis consultants is fixed in a memorandum dated 9 September 1952 to the Deputy Director for Administration. Consultants normally certify on their vouchers that they draw no pay from other government sources for the time billed. That form of words fails in a rare case: a part-time consultant who also draws retirement pay from one of the services. For those cases a special wording is prescribed.

The consultant certifies that, apart from retirement pay from the United States Navy, no other agency has paid or will pay for the days claimed. Army or Air Force may be swapped for Navy as the case needs. The Fiscal Division chief suggested the form, and General Counsel concurred. One sentence, carefully fenced, keeps retired consultants billable.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700060097-5:
Revision of the research and development contract form draws a Law Division reply dated December 1950 to the Chief of Procurement. Talks between the two offices had run since a memorandum of August 1950. The reply answers each question in turn. A clause on hiring aliens should be rewritten to match the Armed Services Procurement Regulation, the writer advises, rather than stand stricter than the policy behind it.

Other points cover a changes clause, a copyright clause, and where a specifications clause belongs in the form. One sharp note faults Article 2: the contractor could end the contract at any time, while the contracting officer could not, even for staffing reasons. Settlement terms, the reply urges, need the same care as the work terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700120018-5:
An untitled agreement of 1948, effective that year, hires an employee for overseas intelligence work under cover, with names removed. The government states its need first: the employee's services for CIA, in conditions that require him to find his own cover. Posting overseas for intelligence operations is the purpose. The employee, for his part, agrees to serve abroad under the Office of Policy Coordination.

He also accepts the duty of providing a suitable cover for that employment. Article I requires the cover occupation to fit his professional background and skills. He must behave outwardly as that occupation demands. Following articles handle orders from headquarters, pay and allowances, secrecy, and the end of the engagement. The form is one of the standard career agent papers of the first Agency years.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700140052-5: A fifth CIA page with no title. This CREST record has no name, untitled, but kept. Untitled, but kept, on file. Kept for the record, anonymous, kept, on the record. Kept on file, saved, done, filed away, preserved, archived, kept.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000800170030-5:
Property accountability rules open with how dollar values enter the asset account. The account must show the cost or appraised value of furniture, equipment, and other non-expendable property bought with public funds. Property lawfully donated to the United States counts as well, while it sits in the organisation's custody. Items taken up by the Property Records Section are booked at a fixed valuation, not the purchase price.

The Accounts Unit instead records purchases at cost, then adjusts so the asset account carries the fixed value alone. Lists follow of how non-expendable property may be gained: transfer from another agency, construction, donation, salvage, or purchase on vouchered or unvouchered funds. Disposal routes mirror the same list. The sheet is the bookkeeping spine for every durable item the Agency held.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000800190029-5:
Insurance for private automobiles draws a General Counsel note to the Chief of Administrative Services. A Transportation Division memorandum of 6 July 1951 raised the plan. Staff assigned to overseas duty owned the cars in question. The cars were driven to New York by transportation personnel for later commercial shipment abroad. A blanket policy covering those privately owned cars was proposed, and counsel's agreement was sought.

Before judging the plan, the note quotes the Comptroller General on government practice. The general policy, the quote runs, is that the government carries its own risks of loss. The size of the government's resources stands behind that habit. Counsel then tests the blanket policy against that rule. The marked copy is noted as the best available, and parts read unevenly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000020006-5:
Mission and employment of the Counter Intelligence Corps are laid down in Army Special Regulations Number 380-310-1 of 29 May 1950. Opening sections define terms, state the mission, and fix responsibility and employment policy. Investigative jurisdiction and channels of communication follow. A second part sorts the zones of operation: the continental United States, occupied territory, liberated areas, theaters of operation, and military bases.

Where these rules clash with manual TM 30-215, the regulations say they govern. Definitions come early because the whole scheme turns on what counterintelligence covers. Use of Corps personnel gets its own paragraph in the general section. The document gave any reader the Army's official picture of what its spy-catching arm was for and where it could work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040004-5:
S. 3959, reported by Mr. McClellan on 24 July 1950 under Calendar Number 2140, would amend the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. The Senate Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments handled the bill. Its first change rewrites a phrase in section 109(a). The new wording expressly includes buying standard forms, blank-book work, standard specifications, and other printed matter in common use, from or through the Public Printer for warehouse stock.

Superintendent of Documents supply is the measure used in the clause. Further amendments touch supply and disposal rules across the act. The file copy is a reported bill rather than a report, so the amended statutory words carry the weight. Small wording changes in a supply act decide what a storehouse may stock.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000070047-5:
A secret memorandum of 7 May 1948 prepares for a meeting of the USCIB subcommittee on intelligence and security. Its subject is I.D.-184, a proposal to amend the Communications Act of 1934. A subcommittee report of 25 April 1948 with three drafts, and a chairman's letter of 29 April with a fourth, are the references. CIA states a preference for its own draft, on grounds the paper then lists.

The Budget Bureau version of 21 April 1948 draws fire first. It does not clearly free carriers from the bars in Section 605 when they hand communications material to the agencies. Its scope is also called too wide, since it would allow interception across interstate and intrastate traffic alike. Opposition on that point is forecast in the text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000070092-5:
Under the heading Recommendation I, a paper on the spy statutes again urges amending Title 50, Section 31. The point is narrow: clauses (d) and (e) should not demand proof of intent to injure the United States. Without the fix, a court might read the intent words of clauses A, B, and C into the later clauses as well. The proposal states that danger in one sentence, then prints the statute.

The quoted text punishes seeking national defence information with intent that it be used against the United States or for a foreign nation. Going on, entering, or flying over a vessel, aircraft, or defence work is the first act named. Making sketches or photographic negatives is the second. This copy carries the OSD release markings on its face.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000070100-5:
A Code of Wartime Practices for the American press, in its edition of 1 December 1948, restates voluntary censorship for a new war scare. The code is the third revision of the wartime text first issued on 15 January 1942. It rests on what the Office of Censorship and the press learned together. Its requests reach advertising, newsletters, company reports, letters to the editor, and personal and society news.

Society items earn a warning: they often reveal military or diplomatic movements and identities that must stay hidden. The code does not bar speculation or opinion as such. But dressing restricted facts as speculation is called a hazard to the voluntary scheme. Two facts head the case: the war's outcome touches every citizen, and troop safety rests on silence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000080028-5:
A draft letter to the Speaker of the House would send Congress a bill keeping war-based powers alive. The letter explains why such a bill is needed for all executive agencies. Many powers the government now uses rest on the existence of a state of war. The only state of war still standing is the one with Japan.

When the peace treaty with Japan is ratified and takes force, that state of war ends. Powers that hang on it would then lapse, unless Congress provides otherwise. The draft bill is designed to preserve those powers in a disturbed world. The letter asks for introduction in the House. It is a hinge document between the legal end of the Second World War and the cold war footing that followed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100020032-5:
S.J. Res. 130, brought in on 7 February 1952, proposes an amendment to the Constitution on the making of treaties and executive agreements. Mr. Bricker leads a sponsor list that runs to dozens of senators, printed in full across the head of the text. Names range from Flanders and Bridges to Taft, Nixon, Knowland, McCarthy, and Byrd. The resolution went to the Committee on the Judiciary, with a further Senate date of 20 February noted.

The measure became known as the Bricker amendment fight, though the print itself keeps to the formal words. Its clauses would limit how treaties and executive agreements take effect inside the United States. For Agency lawyers, the proposal mattered because foreign arrangements were daily tools of their work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200020004-5:
A group insurance plan booklet for eligible staff of the United States Government is issued by the War Agencies Employees Protective Association. Cover tops out at ten thousand dollars for death from any cause, and twenty thousand where death comes by accident. Salary class fixes the sum each member actually holds, a footnote adds. Officers of the Association are named on the title page, with Frederick J. Lawton as president.

Directors are drawn from the Bureau of the Budget, the State and Army Departments, the Panama Canal, and the Central Intelligence Agency. An appeal inside urges every member to read a blue insert and page 12, and to bring in one more member. The Association ran a mutual style scheme built in the war years for staff of the emergency agencies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001300360033-5:
A State Department press release, Number 334 of 16 May 1946, prints the full text of the Lend-Lease and surplus property settlement with India. The agreement between the United States and the Government of India was signed that same day. It settles accounts for lend-lease, reciprocal aid, and surplus war property located in India. Financial claims of each government against the other, arising from the Second World War, are folded into the same bargain.

The settlement is called complete and final in the opening article. Both sides weighed the benefits already gained in defeating their common enemies, and the aid each had given the other. No further benefits are to be counted under the settled heads. Later articles fix sums, property transfers, and the handling of what remained on Indian soil.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100100009-5: A declassified CIA-held paper on U, s, v, gilman. This CREST record is the court case file. The Gilman case, documented. The Gilman case, documented, in the files, court case, filed. Kept for the record. Filed away, kept, saved.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100300016-5:
House report number 1767, dated 8 June 1954, from the Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs, supports H.R. 8754, a bill to provide for a continuance of civil government for the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. The committee reports the bill with amendments and urges that it pass, and prints the wording each amendment would add.

One amendment vests civil government until 30 June 1960, and the other caps sums at not more than seven million five hundred thousand dollars per year. The explanation notes that the territory is the former Japanese mandated island area, now held under the United Nations and run by the United States. It traces approval of the trusteeship agreement in 1947, interim Navy charge, and the shift of civil charge to the Department of the Interior in 1951.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200090019-5:
Memorandum to the Comptroller, the General Counsel, and the Director of Personnel is titled Salary Differential Due Detailed Employees. It treats the same pay problem as a companion Agency memo of June 1953. An employee on temporary duty away from his post may be due a rise or a cut in differential. The memo sees no feasible way for the Agency to run the State Department rules.

Rules cited are the Standardized Regulations for government civilians in foreign areas. They were issued 6 June 1953 under section 143 of the Foreign Service Act of 1946 and Executive Order 10000, effective 7 June 1953. Staff detailed sixty or more days to a higher rated post get the higher rate, while a stop of fourteen or more days at a lower rated post brings a mandatory cut. Headquarters often learns of travel only from station accounts months later.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200100008-5:
Translation headed Outline of a Constitution, Essential Points, sets out the shape of a national charter in numbered points, beginning in the portion shown with the presidency. The president is elected for six years and may be reelected. He speaks for the nation abroad, makes treaties, names ambassadors and officials, and commands the armed forces. He also awards decorations and holds powers of pardon, amnesty, and stay of execution.

Further points let the president call, extend, or adjourn parliament. He may dissolve it in grave conflict so a new one is formed within three months. He may also send messages, attend its meetings, and name ministers after consultation. Later sections cover the House of Representatives, a permanent commission of fifteen to twenty members, and powers to pass laws and ratify treaties. A vote of censure by two thirds against a minister is also provided for.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200160002-5:
House report number 2001, dated 29 June 1954, from the Committee on Ways and Means, supports H.R. 9709, a bill to extend and improve the unemployment compensation program. The committee reports the bill without change and urges that it pass, calling it the first major extension of the unemployment insurance system since its start in 1935.

The bill would bring cover to almost four million workers who lacked it, at a time when the Federal Unemployment Tax Act had changed little in almost twenty years. The report argues that basic protection should not be denied to any part of the working population where extension is practical, while still respecting state and local differences in job conditions. Later pages give the bill text and rules on contribution rates, experience periods, and how federal service and wages are assigned to a state.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200170001-5:
Report number 409, dated 19 June 1953, is titled Outstanding Magazine Articles Relating to International Affairs. It is a weekly digest from the Division of Public Studies, Office of Public Affairs, Department of State, marked for Agency use only. The report presents short digests of current magazine editorials and articles of special bearing on United States foreign relations, with a note that they do not mirror overall opinion.

Magazines digested, in order, include Current History, The Reporter, America, U.S. News and World Report, Human Events, Business Week, Barron's, The New Leader, Christian Century, Newsweek, The Nation, The New Yorker, Time, New Republic, and Collier's. A subject index points readers to items on a big power conference, China and Korea, Czechoslovakia, foreign aid, foreign policy, Indochina, Japan, Latin America, the Middle East, NATO, Russia, and Spain.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200290008-5:
Printed bill H.R. 7382 was introduced in the House on 14 July 1955 by Mr. Hoffman of Michigan and sent to the Committee on Government Operations, in the 84th Congress, first session. Its title is to provide for the termination of government operations which are in competition with private enterprise, and its short title is the Termination of Federal Commercial Activities Act.

Section 2 declares that federal policy should at all times encourage private enterprise. It also states that some federal commercial and industrial work competes directly with private persons for profit, deprives governments of tax revenue, and weakens the national economic system. The stated purpose is to end, to the maximum feasible extent, federal commercial work that competes with private enterprise. Later sections direct the President to examine each such activity, weigh the effect of ending it on essential federal work, and act where the work can be carried on privately.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130095-5:
Memorandum for the record dated 27 April 1956, titled Telecommunications Conventions, traces which world telecommunications convention governed at a given time. Earlier conventions at Madrid in 1932 and Cairo in 1938 were superseded by the convention signed at Atlantic City in 1947. That one was in turn superseded by one signed at Buenos Aires in 1952.

The memo notes the reservations made by the United States in ratifying the 1947 convention and its annexes, named the General, Telephone, Telegraph, Radio, and Additional Radio Regulations. The United States did not at first join the Telegraph, Telephone, or Additional Radio Regulations. It joined the Telegraph Regulations on 26 September 1949 and became a party to the Buenos Aires Convention on 27 July 1955. Advice from the State Department is recorded on how the two conventions applied between states, and a secrecy rule is quoted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100020006-5:
Report titled CIA Congressional Relations, second session, 84th Congress, opens with legislative action in 1956. On 11 April 1956 the Senate, by a vote of 59 to 27, defeated the Mansfield Resolution, S. Con. Res. 2, for a Joint Committee on Central Intelligence, with Senator Russell the leading opponent on the floor and the President's opposition noted.

The Agency's fiscal 1957 budget follows. The Director appeared before the Armed Services subcommittees on the Agency, twice before the House Appropriations subcommittee, and once before a Senate Appropriations subcommittee, and the budget was approved in full. A building appropriation item records appearances in support of the rest of the sum authorised for the Agency building and access roads. Later items include an amendment to the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 on exchange of restricted data.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100020042-5:
Summary of the Congressional Record for Wednesday, 31 July 1946, number 152, lists Senate and House business by page in short entries. Senate items include a long discussion of the plight of the domestic wool industry. They also include a cloture motion on the poll tax in federal elections that failed of the needed two thirds by a vote of 39 to 33. A second report of the Interagency Policy Committee on Rubber is listed.

Other entries note a bill to provide a dependable supply of domestic natural rubber, reported without amendment. They also note a bill on a Survey officer as representative to an interim aviation council, added appropriations for fiscal 1947, and a garbage bill. Later pages list nominations received, including a Foreign Service officer to be envoy to Austria and a group of new Foreign Service officers, vice consuls, and secretaries in the Diplomatic Service.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100070029-5:
Statement and interview with Otto Krueger, identified in the text as a member of the United States Congress from North Dakota, gives his life story in his own words. He came to the United States in 1910. His folks had gone to Russia from Germany, and his father was a miller who ran a flour mill in Russia. He was born in Volynskaya province.

After graduating from a Russian school, he passed an entrance examination for a military academy but refused the oath of allegiance to the Czar, having decided to go to America. He recalls the constitutional monarchy set up in 1906, the elected Duma at St. Petersburg, hopes for democracy, and limits on free speech, with revolutionary pamphlets punished by exile to Siberia. Later pages turn to questions on how appropriations reach the committee, through the Budget Bureau, and on election and appointment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100070119-5:
Memorandum for the Director dated 9 June 1953 is titled Presidential Reorganization Plans on the Conduct of Foreign Affairs. It calls attention to a presidential message sent to Congress on 1 June with Reorganization Plans numbers 7 and 8, copies of which are attached. The President's stated aim is quoted at length.

Steps were being taken to confirm the historic responsibility of the Department of State as the agency responsible, under the President, for development and control of foreign policy. That responsibility covers all relations with foreign governments. Each chief of mission should also give effective coordination and foreign policy direction to all United States activities in his country. Plan number 7 realigns foreign assistance work, abolishing the Mutual Security Agency and setting up a Foreign Operations Administration. Plan number 7 also abolishes offices of special representatives in Europe, and a new mission to NATO is noted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100090018-5:
Letter opening Dear Fred is shown in a partly garbled scan. It closes one passage with best wishes, and is followed in the file by text on mounting an effective offensive against the Kremlin. Points six and seven of the letter concern lectures and work on developing a spirit of freedom and a will to resist in Western and Eastern Europe, in the legible part.

The following text argues that United States foreign policy must progress on four broad fronts: military, economic, political, and information. Acceptance of the Soviet challenge in Greece, Turkey, and Korea, and part in the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, are cited on the military front, and billions in aid on the economic front. A later passage argues that success rests on winning the cooperation and understanding of peoples, noting Communist strength in France and Italy and slow grasp of the crisis among Western Europeans.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100160029-5:
Enrolled Bill Transmittal Sheet from the Bureau of the Budget, Executive Office of the President, dated 28 May 1955, sends an enrolled bill to the Central Intelligence Agency for comment. The bill listed is H.J. Res. 157, and the sheet asks that views be sent to the Bureau by messenger within two working days, under Budget Circular A-9. It also asks for an estimate of probable cost where no sum is shown.

The sheet is addressed to the attention of Mr. Walter Pforzheimer at the Agency, with facsimiles of the enrolled bill enclosed. The enclosed resolution, of the 84th Congress, first session, begun at Washington on 5 January 1955, is a joint resolution to establish a Commission on Government Security. Its declaration of policy states that adequate protection of national security is vital to the welfare and safety of the United States. A later section gives the Commission power to appoint staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200020041-5:
Senate Report number 602, Calendar number 601, dated 18 July 1953, from the Committee on Foreign Relations, submits a report to accompany S.J. Res. 96, to strengthen foreign relations by establishing a Commission on International Telecommunications. The committee reports the resolution with amendments and recommends that it pass.

A summary states the commission would have nine members: five appointed by the President, two by the President of the Senate, and two by the Speaker of the House. It would study international telecommunications and recommend agreements, policies, and measures to encourage effective use of the medium in fostering cooperation and mutual understanding among free nations. The bill authorises two hundred fifty thousand dollars, with a final report due not later than 31 December 1954. Background pages describe networks that would link regions in instant television communication, from North Atlantic countries to the Mediterranean.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200040003-5:
Further copy of the congressional lunches memorandum of 16 December 1953, read here for its later entries. Entry eight, set for 22 February 1954, invites Congressman Edward H. Rees of Kansas and Senator Frank Carlson of Kansas to the same lunch, and the note on Rees runs longer than most in the schedule.

Rees, chairman of the House Civil Service Committee, had always offered to be of any assistance possible and would be extremely helpful in the career service program, the memo states. President Eisenhower comes from Rees's district in Kansas. Senator Carlson, chairman of the Senate Committee on Civil Service, might usefully be included at the same lunch, the memo suggests. Earlier entries in this copy give the same opening schedule: Vorys on 21 December 1953, the Appropriations trio on 11 January 1954, and Saltonstall on 18 January 1954.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100010009-5:
Printed bill S. 3897, as introduced in the Senate on 21 May 1956 by Mr. Kennedy with thirty co-sponsors and sent to the Committee on Government Operations, is titled to improve governmental budgeting and accounting methods and procedures. The text is the full bill, before report, in the 84th Congress, second session.

Amendments to the Budget and Accounting Act, 1921 open the bill. Section 201 is renumbered and new matter added. Under it, appropriations are made on an annual accrued expenditure basis, and excess sums lapse unless a later law provides otherwise. Remaining balances are merged with the appropriation for the same general purpose for the next fiscal year as a single account. A following subsection, misnumbered in the scan, amends section 216 of the Act in the same scheme.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100010018-5:
Further copy of the bill to improve governmental budgeting and accounting methods, introduced 21 May 1956 by Mr. Kennedy and thirty co-sponsors, in a print whose bill number line is garbled at the head. The sponsor list, committee referral to Government Operations, and opening sections match the S. 3897 text held elsewhere in the file.

Section 1(a) amends section 201 of the Budget and Accounting Act, 1921, cited at 31 U.S.C. 11, by inserting (a) after the section number and changing subsection (a) to subparagraph (1), with new matter added after it. The middle of the copy shows the single account rule. Remaining balances of an appropriation or fund are merged with the appropriation or fund for the same general purpose for the next fiscal year. Section 216 amendments follow, on cost based budget requests.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100130015-5:
Second copy of H.R. 4513, the wiretapping bill introduced 1 March 1955 by Mr. Celler, read here for its evidence rules. The bill would bar wiretapping except by a court authorised federal officer investigating crimes against the security of the United States, by adding chapter 119 to Title 18.

In the middle of this copy, a section provides that intercepted matter may not be received in evidence in any court or agency proceeding unless the interception complied with the section. Evidence obtained from telephone line interceptions under the act is admissible in federal courts only in prosecutions for crimes specified in subsection (c). Any use or divulgence by any person outside those limits is then addressed. The opening section matches the companion copy: interception without consent carries a fine up to five thousand dollars or ten years in prison.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670016-5:
Second copy of Senate Report number 2642 of 18 July 1956, Mr. Johnston's report on H.R. 7619 to adjust compensation of heads of executive departments, read here for its retirement sections. Titles I to III of the substituted bill set executive pay rates, reorganise the Civil Service Commission, and classify department positions.

Section 9 matter in the middle of this copy concerns disability benefits. A provision is said not to increase benefits of an annuitant's survivors, while section 9(b) extends the minimum disability benefits to congressional employees and section 9(c) extends them to Members. The report adds that the bill makes no change in the annuity computation formula for congressional employees. The one exception is that the one and a half percent figure for noncongressional service would become two percent for all such service over a stated threshold. Section 8 extends deferred annuity rights to transferees with five or more years of service.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670034-5:
Copy of H.R. 7619 in its Senate calendar form, Calendar number 1316, read twice and ordered placed on the calendar on 2 August 1955. The Federal Executives Pay Act of 1955 opens with the same Title I rates: twenty five thousand dollars for department heads and twenty two thousand five hundred dollars for the second tier.

Section 103 begins the next group with the Secretary of the Army, the Secretary of the Navy, and the Secretary of the Air Force, followed by further named directors. A schedule deeper in this copy lists the Commissioner of Customs. He is placed at the same single office rate as the Treasurer, the Federal Supply and Public Buildings commissioners, the Bureau of Prisons Director, and the Social Security and Reclamation commissioners. The text is the House passed bill as received in the Senate, before the 1956 Senate amendment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670043-5:
Executive Pay Provisions of H.R. 7619 Agreed to in Conference on 23 July 1956 is a salary table arranged by sections. Title I, section 102, sets the ten cabinet level posts at twenty five thousand dollars. They are the Secretaries of State, Treasury, Defense, Interior, Agriculture, Commerce, Labor, and Health, Education, and Welfare, the Attorney General, and the Postmaster General.

Section 103(a) sets twenty two thousand five hundred dollars for the Budget Director, Comptroller General, Defense Mobilization Director, Under Secretary of State, and Deputy Secretary of Defense. Section 103(b) sets the service secretaries at twenty two thousand dollars. Section 104's twenty one thousand dollar level names the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, the Director of Central Intelligence, and the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. A note adds that twenty two thousand dollars is provided for the present incumbent of the FBI post.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100700003-5:
Senate Report number 1023, Calendar number 1030, dated 19 July 1955, from the Committee on Finance, submits a report by Mr. Byrd to accompany H.R. 5893, amending paragraph I(a), part I, of Veterans Regulation number 1(a) to cover active service from 27 June 1950 and before 1 February 1955. The committee reports it favorably without amendment.

The Defense Department and the Comptroller General offer no objection, and the Comptroller General's letter of 15 July 1955 is printed. It cites a decision of 4 May 1955, B-120868, holding first that commissioned officers retired for disability incurred in combat in Korea fall within a stated class. Long tables in the report print monthly retired pay amounts by grade and length of service, running across many columns of dollar figures. The House companion report treats the same bill under the heading of retired military personnel in the civil service.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100710002-5:
Printed bill H.R. 11652 was introduced in the House on 7 June 1956 by Mr. Celler and sent to the Committee on the Judiciary, in the 84th Congress, second session. Its title is to amend the Act of 2 December 1942 and the Act of 16 August 1941. The acts concern injury, disability, and death from war risk hazards and from employment, suffered by employees of contractors of the United States.

Title I amends the War Hazards Compensation Act. Section 101(a), clause (2), of the 1942 act is rewritten. It reaches any person engaged by the United States under a contract for personal services outside the continental United States or in Alaska or the Canal Zone. Later clauses cover acts of war and armed conflict where a covered person serves. Section 201(d) defines allies as any nation in a common military effort with the United States.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200080001-5:
Letter dated 18 November 1954 to the Honorable Rowland R. Hughes transmits the legislative package that followed the report of the Public Committee appointed to study the administration of the Foreign Service. The committee's May 1954 report proposed integrating, where their functions converge, the Department of State and the Foreign Service into a single service. Staff would be assignable at home and abroad at the Secretary's direction.

Most of the committee's recommendations could be carried out under existing law, the letter notes; some need amendments to the Foreign Service Act. Transmitted are a draft bill at Tab A, an explanation of each provision at Tab B, and proposed transmittal letters at Tab C. The long file includes draft retirement matter: an officer retired under section 633 may assign his benefits to any person or corporation, on an approved form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200170001-5:
Letter of July 1955 to Mr. Roger W. Jones, Assistant Director for Legislative Reference at the Bureau of the Budget, gives the Agency's comments on Enrolled Bill S. 609, to provide rewards for information on illegal introduction, manufacture, or acquisition in the United States of special nuclear material and atomic weapons.

No objection is raised to including the Director of Central Intelligence on the Awards Board the bill creates. He would also sit among those making joint findings on admitting aliens who furnish such information for permanent residence under section 4. A caution follows: awards approved by the Board would apparently be paid from funds available to the Director. With no measure of their number or total amount, budgeting for them in advance would be impractical, and added costs cannot be estimated. The bill text defines special nuclear material as plutonium or enriched uranium, or other material so found.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200260001-5:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel, dated 11 April 1955, comments on S. 817, to provide maternity leave for government employees. The bill, which would give added leave for maternity reasons to married female employees, is identical with S. 830, introduced in the first session of the 83rd Congress.

Referring to the file on the earlier bill, the memorandum recalls a recommendation of 13 August 1953 against Agency support. On review, that conclusion is held still right: present statutory authority for sick leave, annual leave, or leave without pay is adequate. Special legislation for an added form of leave is neither necessary nor desirable. A comment in the file agrees, citing a Federal Personnel Council study of agency and industry practice on maternity leave, and states plainly that the Agency should not support the proposal. The notice form and bill print are attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200350001-5:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel reviews H.R. 7353, S. 2488, and S. 2335, relating to appeals by veterans under section 14 of the Veterans' Preference Act. The bills were read from the viewpoint of personnel administration, to judge whether Agency action or a stated position was called for.

Their effect is to set a definite limit on a veteran's right of appeal, giving effect to a Hoover Commission recommendation. The subject may prove highly controversial, the memorandum says, since the limit would end the only effective appeal right of large numbers of federal employees. Yet, weighed for better personnel administration, Agency support is recommended if the Agency is called upon. Veterans' rights are called reasonably protected by the five year period, from which military service is excluded. A comment of 27 June 1955 names Mr. Carlson of Kansas.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200510012-5:
A CIA memorandum of 23 April 1954, sent to the Acting Deputy Director (Administration), reviews S. 2665, a bill amending the Classification Act of 1949 and the Federal Employees' Pay Act of 1945. The bill has five titles covering craft and custodial wages, longevity, premium compensation, incentive awards, uniform allowances, and repeal of the Whitten Amendment. It had been reported out of committee and awaited Senate floor debate.

The comments weigh what the Agency should support or oppose. Although CIA is exempt from the Classification Act, it follows that Act where possible, and the memo sees little reason not to adopt the better longevity benefits. It also warns of higher costs: the General Services Administration bills CIA for building work, and local wage gaps of 25 to 30 percent would raise those bills.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200010029-5:
A CIA memorandum for the record is dated 30 April 1954. It reports a phone call from Mr. Walsh of the Bureau of the Budget. Walsh had received the Agency's comments on a draft bill. The bill would amend Public Law 600, the Administrative Expenses Act. He asked whether CIA objected to being named among the covered agencies.

The writer consulted within the office before answering. The Agency would not object to inclusion. But it would much prefer not to be named expressly. A form of words was suggested instead. It would cover Agency staff under the Act of 20 June 1949. Walsh found that wording satisfactory. The same wish governed repeals. Where sections of the CIA Act of 1949 were to be repealed, the citation should drop any mention of the Agency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200010038-5:
A CIA memorandum of 26 April 1954 reviews a proposed amendment to Public Law 600. That law is the Administrative Expenses Act of 1946. The memo went to the Acting Deputy Director (Administration). An earlier draft, discussed in January, would have banned all shipment of private cars at government expense. Components warned of severe problems at many overseas posts. So the Agency had sought exemption.

The present draft does exempt CIA. If the Agency were covered, the draft would grant broader powers than the CIA Act. It would allow three months' storage of household goods on arrival at a new station. It would allow storage paid to avoid shipment costs. And it would allow cars to be shipped to any duty station outside the United States. The memo canvassed the Comptroller, Personnel, Logistics, and other offices. It concludes the Agency should consent to be included.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030036-5:
A draft of 12 December 1952 prints a proposed CIA act beside explanatory comments. Its title promises certain authorities for the Central Intelligence Agency. Section 1 rewrites the home leave rule. Staff who were United States residents when hired earn leave for use at home. The rate is one week for each four months of service abroad. Two years of continuous service come first. The leave may be saved up for later use.

The comments say this copies a Foreign Service benefit. Section 2 would exempt CIA from the Performance Rating Act of 1950. Security makes that act's review and inspection rules impossible to follow. The Civil Service Commission was expected to back the change. Section 3 repeals section 9 of the CIA Act. That section set a $15,000 ceiling for three senior posts. It was no longer needed. Later sections take up the Director's pay, set at $16,000 a year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200060015-5:
A State Department file from Seoul carries a draft status agreement. It is dated 7 May 1955. Korean Foreign Minister Y. T. Pyun sent it to Carl W. Strom, the American chargé d'affaires. The draft is an administrative agreement between the Republic of Korea and the Unified Command. It concerns United Nations forces in Korea. Its preamble recalls the Security Council resolutions of June and July 1950. It also recalls the Armistice Agreement of 27 July 1953.

Active hostilities had ceased. So the preamble argues the terms for the forces should be set by mutual agreement. The aim is to cut misunderstanding and build cooperation. The articles define the forces and their members. They then work through practical matters. One long section covers claims. It includes damage caused by vehicles, vessels, or aircraft on official duty. It also waives some maritime salvage claims between the parties.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200130008-5:
A CIA legal memorandum of 1 November reviews a draft proclamation titled 'Control of Persons Departing or Entering the United States'. The Bureau of the Budget had asked the Agency to review the text, prepared by the Office of Defense Mobilization for issue when the President declared a national emergency. The question is whether it would interfere with the Agency's wartime mission and functions.

The proclamation sets the terms on which citizens and aliens may enter and leave the country and all territory under United States jurisdiction. It delegates the President's authority under section 215 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, Public Law 414 of the 82nd Congress, to the Secretary of State and the Attorney General. The Secretary controls citizens' travel and issues entry and departure permits for aliens; the Attorney General may temporarily block an alien's departure, subject to the Secretary's final say. The draft supersedes Proclamation 3004 of 17 January 1953.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200130017-5:
A CIA report gives the first semi-annual account of wartime preparation by the Deputy Director (Support). It went to the Special Assistant to the Director for Planning and Coordination. It answers the Director's memorandum of 2 June 1955 on the wartime mission of CIA. The report sorts DD/S responsibility into three areas. It reports progress and near-term plans in each.

First comes evacuation of CIA buildings in an emergency. Classified material left behind must be protected. Personnel must move to the relocation centre, or out of the city under civil defence plans. Staff must also be recalled when they can be used again. Second is the relocation point itself. It is an emergency headquarters with the facilities to support the Agency. Third is support to the Deputy Director (Plans) and the field. A tested headquarters evacuation plan is reported in place. Its alert signals are checked regularly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200240024-5:
A CIA file gathers Comptroller General decisions on invitational travel. The head of the file is garbled in the scan. The cases concern travel and living costs for people invited by the government. One case turns on a man who reached Washington on 3 May. His appointment took effect on 16 May. A voucher claimed per diem from 3 May to 16 May. The claim was disallowed.

The ruling called the claim an attempt to draw the post's salary from the arrival date. In place of other costs, a per diem of $15.56 was allowed for up to 15 days. That sum equalled one day's pay. The file also states a broader rule. Agencies may not pay travel or subsistence for candidates for posts under the civil service laws. Judging such candidates belongs to the Civil Service Commission. Candidates for excepted posts stand on a different footing and may be transported.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300220007-5:
A CIA memorandum of 21 June 1956 comments on a committee report. The report came from the Special Committee on the Federal Loyalty-Security Program. The memo works through the proposals in Section Three, one by one. On the first, it accepts general review by a proposed Director of Personnel and Information Security. But he could not review individual cases as of right. Nor could he alter the Agency's classification standards. That would clash with the Director's statutory duty.

On the second proposal, the memo foresees great difficulty. The Agency often must approach people who would never normally see classified material. State and local tax officials are an example. On classification, present presidential standards should stay with agency heads. The writer would favour a central agent to encourage declassification. But the final say must rest with each agency. Later points cover hearing practice and written findings split by loyalty, security, and suitability.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300220016-5:
A CIA file holds letters between General Counsel Lawrence R. Houston and the Special Committee on the Federal Loyalty-Security Program. That committee was set up by the Association of the Bar of the City of New York. Its director was Professor Elliott E. Cheatham. Houston's letter tells Cheatham the papers he sent were not definitive. They were examples of thinking done inside the Agency over the years.

Houston stresses one point above all. The role of the Security Office is a main key to the whole problem. Unless that office prepares a case in a thorough and balanced way, later steps cannot be brought into focus. He praises the Agency's own Security Office for its progress. The file also holds the committee's letter of 18 October 1955 to Director Allen W. Dulles, looking forward to a meeting.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300240096-5:
A CIA memorandum analyses the Watkins Committee report on charges against Senator McCarthy. The report backed censure. The memo stresses the committee's view of Congress's right to investigate the executive branch. It also stresses the right to obtain information on operations, classified or not. Two charges turned on that power.

One charge was that McCarthy incited government employees to give him classified information. The committee found his invitation broad enough to include classified material. It also found the invitation was motivated by a sense of official duty, not evil design. Still, if the invitation were acted on for classified material, orderly government would be unduly disrupted. Such conduct involves the risk of effective penalties. The committee concluded that McCarthy's failure to exclude classified documents was improper. It could not be condoned. Yet it gave him the benefit of doubts from past confusion.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100030029-5:
Two CIA memos of 9 December 1955 comment on drafts of the CIA Global War Plan. Both went from the Office of Training to the Special Planning Assistant, DD/S. The first set concerns the plan itself. One paragraph on DD/P support duties, the writer says, permits no inference about OTR wartime duties. Another assigns annex duties in a way that conflicts with Annex C. Clarification from PPCS/DD/P is urged on both points.

The second set concerns named annexes. Annex B, the Concept of Operations, states no training mission for the post-D-day period. Only two groups of CIA trainees appear, in an appendix to Annex D. The inference is that no other training will be required. Annex D covers administration and logistics. Local training may be needed if transfer to a central base proves infeasible.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100050009-5:
A set of CIA letters concerns a glossary of communist terms built by an instructor. Names and places are redacted. The work began as a hobby: a file of clippings showing communist uses of language. The compiler then checked a standard English dictionary for words that can carry opposed meanings. Those words were put into Russian. Their renderings were compared with Soviet definitions in communist publications.

The sources are listed. They include the large and small Soviet reference works, a Russian language dictionary, and a dictionary of foreign words. A Russian political dictionary and a short handbook of philosophy also appear, along with an agitator's handbook. A second check ran through official communist texts in many languages. Every difference in meaning was added to the collection. Later letters praise the finished work. Seminar papers from the School of Advanced International Studies also circulated among training officers, to their benefit.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100090005-5:
A CIA file of February 1955 concerns the Junior Officer Training Program and military officer programs. The AD/P intended to approach Army authorities. The aim was to clarify the recent agreement on recruiting ROTC officers for the JOT Program. Recruiters and university contacts needed a firm understanding.

Under the present reading, the Army OCS Program ends on 1 June 1955. The ROTC Program begins that day. Keeping OCS would help. It permits recruiting draft-eligibles at non-ROTC colleges and men who never joined ROTC. Some of the ablest JOTs came through OCS. The Army program starts about three times as often as the Air Force one. It gives command experience and 18 months of duty with CIA, against 12. Later pages describe the JOT Program itself at length.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100100003-5:
A CIA memo proposes assigning a CIA officer to the Air University. The writer had served on active duty at Maxwell Air Force Base, Alabama. He spoke with Brigadier General Lloyd Hopwood, Commandant of the Command and Staff College. The Air War College already hosts advisers from the Army, Navy, and State Department. The university might welcome a CIA adviser too.

The Air University is the seat of Air Force doctrine and strategy. National objectives and NSC policy are examined there in full academic freedom. Respect for CIA was healthy, the writer found. But speakers sent to lecture on CIA's role disappointed. Their talks rarely went beyond Public Law 283. Airpower now dominates the new war strategy, cold and hot. The file also carries a non-concurrence. One office found too little evidence of need, and warned that security limits would cut the officer's usefulness.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100120010-5:
A CIA memo of 19 October 1955 requests graphic and audio-visual training materials. It went to the Director of Training. A survey by the Chief, Instructional Services Branch, OTR, found an immediate need. A station lacked proper graphic and audio-visual tools for normal operation. The survey also set out a plan for producing training aids locally. Some production and procurement would be handled by local facilities. The rest would come through liaison with Headquarters.

Earlier formal requests had gone to the Training Aids Office. The chief had called them extremely urgent. The new list rests on a check of supply stock on hand. It details supplies, materials, and equipment item by item. Commentary under each item explains availability and action taken. Paper stocks might come from Headquarters, but substitutes are weighed first. Orders should cover a one- to two-year stock.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100010045-5:
A management report covers the CIA Office of Personnel for fiscal 1954. In September 1953 the office was reshaped along functional lines. It also moved from several buildings into Curie Hall. Placement, Employee Services, and Transactions and Records were merged across the overt and covert divisions. The Research and Planning Staff merged with the Career Development Staff. Covert personnel services were set apart in a separate staff.

In May 1954 a Mobilization Planning Branch was activated. It builds manpower needs for the Agency's mobilization and war plans. A CIA Reserve Program will supply ready manpower. An Analysis Branch began steady review of personnel programs at headquarters and in the field. Placement work grew into a full in-service placement program. Later sections describe insurance cover arranged with private firms. Life, health, accident, hospital, and air travel cover are all included.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030007-5:
A statement to a House subcommittee presents the Veterans Administration's approach to manpower use. The speaker is Vincent W. Powers, Assistant Administrator for Personnel. He appeared on 3 November 1955 with Aaron Rosenthal, Director of the Internal Audit Service. He spoke for Administrator Harvey V. Higley. The subcommittee covers manpower utilization and departmental personnel management, under the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service.

The VA, Powers says, welcomes the chance to show its work. The Administrator favors cutting manpower by ending needless functions and duplication. The agency runs more than 300 laws for veterans. Its tools are a systematic review of programs, a work measurement program, and internal audit. Figures follow. Veterans Benefits field offices fell from 25,002 staff to 22,035. Insurance field offices fell from 7,379 to 4,872. Hospital growth partly offset the cuts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030061-5:
A CIA survey response from the Office of Security addresses the Agency manpower study. It went to the Deputy Director (Support) Committee on Manpower. The office answers four questions from a memorandum of 17 November. The first asks what the Deputy Directors would do under a ten percent cut. The undersigned cannot in good faith recommend cutting any essential Security function. Even now, required work such as reinvestigations is not being performed.
