A hidden factor shapes the office's workload. Employees of cover organizations such as RFE, CFA, and CAT perform Agency functions. They do not appear in Agency manpower figures. Yet they load the Security Office with investigations, clearances, and guidance. Contractual alien agents and emigre groups add more. The survey, the office assumes, will not cover those people. A cut falling only on counted staff would thus fall unevenly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100040006-5:
A House resolution, H. Res. 304, authorizes a broad investigation by the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service. Mr. Murray of Tennessee submitted it on 7 July 1955. It was referred to the House Calendar on 11 July 1955 as Report No. 1089. The committee may act as a whole or by subcommittee. Its subjects begin with the mails: transport and distribution, air carriage, and closing post offices and rural routes.

The resolution reaches far beyond the mails. It covers classification and appointment of postmasters and postal employees. It covers general and fiscal administration in the Post Office Department. It covers the malleability of articles and printed matter. It also covers federal civilian personnel management at large. That includes Executive Order 10577 of 22 November 1954 and the appointment system it created. Civil Service Commission practices are included as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100010032-5:
A CIA paper of 19 March 1957 lists the duties of a control section slated for abolition. Two tables give each task and its man-years. The first table covers one unit's work. Tasks include supervision and help to a reference branch with hard-copy intelligence logs. Daily handling of map materials takes 0.70 man-years. The Domestic Registry, covering stamps and related items sent to other units, takes 0.50.

The second table covers a successor unit. Screening and routing of hard-copy intelligence takes a full man-year. Other tasks are small: procurement forms, borrowed-item control, subscription forms. Inter-library loan channels run between CIA and the Army Map Service. Miscellaneous services include alerting analysts to new materials. The section also bird-dogs hard-to-locate and priority materials for requesters.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100020068-5:
A CIA briefing text of 9 July 1957 introduces geographic intelligence. It was prepared for a session on central support services. Geography, the speaker says, studies the location, identity, and areal links of physical and cultural features. The geographer locates and reads such elements as terrain, climate, and water. Cultural elements include industry, disease, and ethnic groups. Political and administrative units are also covered.

The geographer is chiefly a generalist. The map is his main tool. Geographic intelligence strongly supports operational and strategic planning. It records marked changes in landscape. Its products range from broad background studies to tight studies of targets, routes, and landing beaches. The store of linked data also serves policy choices, estimates, and current reporting. Photo reading, cartography, and map work are treated in more detail later in the briefing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410001-5:
A status table lists Geography Division projects as of 1 February 1957. The table is organized by branch. Columns give project number, title, analyst, requester, dates, and status of work. The Geographic Intelligence Review projects lead the list. MR-51 went to reproduction on 29 January. MR-52, begun 31 January 1957, is due in March.

Far East and Pacific entries follow. One text stands one-third complete and should finish during February. A regional analysis of Northeast Thailand is self-initiated. Its draft should be completed during the month. Other entries cover provisional overlays, collection of map materials, and photo cover requirements. A USSR section lists an urban area study of Stalingrad and work on Novaya Zemlya. Many analyst and requester names are redacted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490003-5:
Minutes record NIS Committee Meeting No. 237 of 5 February 1957. The chairman announced an Army appointment. Lt. Colonel David H. Smith became the Army's senior representative, replacing Col. Quintin S. Lander, effective 16 January 1957. Col. Sam A. Carnes was welcomed as the Air Force member designate. The Army member distributed revised outline guides for Sections 31, 32, and 33.

Action on those guides was deferred to the next meeting. The Navy member proposed a working group on Section 56, Intelligence and Security. He wanted a revised guide covering the internal security of foreign countries. The chairman read parts of Section 56 on Venezuela to illustrate present practice. The Navy member then asked that his proposal be tabled. Other items cover comments on principal sources in supplements.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490021-5:
Minutes record NIS Committee Meeting No. 255 of 26 November 1957. The committee approved the NIS Production Forecast for fiscal 1959-61, dated that day. Annual review at the fiscal year's end remains the rule. Maintenance shares of production were noted. They rise from 33 percent in fiscal 1959 to 41 percent in 1960 and 50 percent in 1961.

The Chapter I schedule was revised for State's Near East limits. Greece leads in August 1958, then South Korea and North Korea. Ireland, Albania, the United Kingdom, and East Germany follow into 1959. Afghanistan, Israel, and the Arabian Peninsula move to fiscal 1960-61, with Burma, Ceylon, and others. Wider dissemination of Chapters I follows. A chairman's list names top officials, from the Director of the Budget to the Federal Reserve chairman.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200100022-5:
A monthly report covers the Cartography Division for November 1957. The division accepted requests for 123 maps and charts. One hundred fourteen were for CIA, six for State, and three for the Air Force. OSI alone requested 50. The division completed 54 maps and charts. Sixty-one percent of completions concerned the USSR and Satellites.

Thirty-four items remained in reproduction. The NIS Map Coordinator received 23 final maps in November. One hundred seven final NIS maps stayed in reproduction. Orientation tours ran both ways between the division and D/GP. Personnel assignments shifted after a reorganization. A list of maps entered follows. It includes Ghana standard base and page-size sheets, Poland trade charts, and a Caucasus set. The Caucasus sheets cover climate, ethnic and religious groups, security and labor camps, and selected cities.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100050013-5:
A House committee volume, The Shameful Years, surveys thirty years of Soviet espionage in the United States. It was prepared by the Committee on Un-American Activities. The release date is 30 December 1951. John S. Wood of Georgia chairs the committee. Its narrative opens with Ludwig Martens. On 2 January 1919 he announced himself in New York as representative of the People's Commissariat of Foreign Affairs.

Martens admitted Communist Party membership, the volume says. He professed belief in establishing the Soviet form of government worldwide. He approved the work of the Third International. The volume then traces Soviet networks through the interwar years and beyond. Later pages follow named couriers and consulate inspections in 1944. Travel through Laredo and El Paso, and stops in Los Angeles and San Francisco, are detailed. The volume runs to hundreds of pages of case narrative.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100070002-5:
The full text of the Immigration and Nationality Act fills this file. Its table of contents opens the volume. Title I gives definitions and the powers of the Attorney General and the Secretary of State. Title II sets up immigration. Its first chapter builds the quota system on national origins, with minimum quotas. Later chapters govern qualifications for admission and the issuance of entry documents.

Section 212 lists the classes of aliens ineligible for visas. Section 215 covers travel control of citizens and aliens in war or national emergency. Section 252 governs conditional landing permits for alien crewmen. Section 253 covers hospital treatment of crewmen with certain diseases. A crewman who breaks the terms of a permit commits a misdemeanor. The fine runs to $500, or six months in prison, or both. The act's text runs to hundreds of pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100140022-5:
Pages from the Congressional Record of the Senate fill this file. A drought debate leads the visible text. Senators urge prompt action by the Department of Agriculture. The northern part of Mississippi is hit harder than the southern. Speakers join a plea for feed and practical assistance, not money relief alone. Senator Kerr of Oklahoma says the situation worsens daily. He charges the Department with utter indifference.

Senator Fulbright of Arkansas and Senator Stennis of Mississippi spoke before him. Senators Hill, George, and Russell are also named. Later pages turn to copyright. A list names groups supporting the Universal Copyright Convention and related legislation. The American Academy of Arts and Sciences heads the visible names. A procedural exchange notes the Senate is considering the House bill, not the Senate bill.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100190018-5:
Remarks by Lyman B. Kirkpatrick to the Third Agency Orientation Course on October 8, 1954, take stock of the Central Intelligence Agency as a whole. Kirkpatrick says he wants to give a balance sheet of where the Agency stands. He lists its relation to other intelligence agencies and the progress it has made. He adds a few of its weaknesses alongside its successes.

He warns that staff are too inclined to see the individual trees and miss the forest. They are too busy with the day's work to spare people for training. He defends the average government employee as loyal and hard-working. He says he resents the frequent attacks on federal workers by Congress and the Washington press. He also concedes that the Agency is becoming too bureaucratic.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100210060-5:
A 1953 legal opinion tests one clause of the standard overseas service agreement signed by Agency staff employees paid from confidential funds. The clause requires at least twelve months of service after travel to an overseas post at government expense. The question is whether that term lawfully binds employees who had already served overseas, or in a departmental post, before signing.

The opinion quotes the agreement's language treating early departure as a debt due to the United States. It then notes the strain in applying that wording: the statute speaks of the period following an appointment, and reading it as following a transfer is a stretch. The lawyers report that they could find no decision settling the point, which leaves the clause on uncertain ground for this class of employee.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100090011-5:
A memorandum to the Director of Training asks support for a project to build language training and area study inside the Agency. The sponsoring division states a plain need: intelligence officers who, beyond their professional skill, speak the language of the country they work against and know its people, their customs, taboos, and ways. A liaison relationship, with the partner's name removed in review, makes the gap critical.

The requested project would be built and then maintained for that purpose alone. The plan described has trainees serve a tour under supervision, with guidance and administrative support provided, and then return to headquarters. Those with enough interest and ability would move into straight operational duties with the sponsoring division.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200040024-5:
A brief history traces how the consultant program known as University Consultant Contacts came to be. In the summer of 1951, the Director of the Office of Training recommended that the Agency establish a systematic consultant service to complement its recruitment effort. The proposed University Consultant Program would be a joint venture of the Office of Training and the Office of Personnel.

After review and discussion, Matthew Baird, the Director of Training, and the Assistant Director (Personnel) reached agreement on the program's mission, organization, and administrative details. Final approval came from the Director of Central Intelligence. The rest of the paper works through the program's machinery, including boards of appeal and the steps by which candidates report for duty, with duties split between the two offices.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200080011-5:
Briefing suggestions prepare the Director of Training for a presentation to the Director of Central Intelligence on the Assessment and Evaluation Staff. The staff is described as a group of professional psychologists backed by a clerical staff. Their training is mixed: industrial psychology, clinical psychology, experimental design and psychological statistics, with some members from teaching, private business, the military services, and the Civil Service Commission. Consultants help them apply psychology to the Agency's unusual people problems.

The questions put to the staff, the paper says, run from whether to hire a man, through where to place him, to whether he can do a given job. Testing and assessment are now shaped to the real problem a supervisor or placement officer is trying to solve, which the paper presents as a gain in realism.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200100018-5:
A position paper on the Agency's Foreign Language Development Program completes a review promised earlier in 1956. The writers had sent an interim reply on August 17, 1956. They promised their position on the new basic policy soon after Labor Day. Now they set out their review of the whole language development problem. It includes the parts of the program that touch staff who expect overseas assignments during their careers.

Among the points made, two stand out. Study aimed at an overseas assignment should not by itself establish eligibility for money awards. Encouragement should be limited to those with real aptitude and suitable age and grade. Intensive voluntary language study should be backed in another way. Above all during an overseas assignment, it should earn substantial annual proficiency awards.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200230014-5:
Contract services are the subject of a memorandum to the Agency's Director of Training. It comes from the Acting Director of Security. It answers a proposal of October 28, 1955, to use contract help in place of work then done by staff employees. The reply turns on security. Given the nature of the work, its sensitivity and its classification, staff employees offer the greatest degree of security.

Only staff employees, the memorandum argues, should be used for some work. That is work requiring close and continuous access to highly classified information or training. People in lesser services could still be hired on personal service contracts for a set purpose. Controls would then have to keep their access to classified information limited. That limit would hold whether the access came by design or simply from the nature of the work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300010017-5:
Weekly Activities Report number 22 comes from the Acting Chief of the Agency's Plans and Policy Staff. It is addressed to the Director of Training and leads with a completed project. Clearance had been obtained from three offices: the CI Staff, the SR Division, and the FI Staff. The clearance allowed release of a reserve officer lesson plan titled Soviet Positive Intelligence. It was for use by the Strategic Intelligence School. The school's Chief of the Department of General Intelligence was told the clearance had come through. A revised, up-to-date copy would follow.

Other material in the report sets out the aims of a course of instruction. One aim is to trace a subject through its historical development and its growth since World War II. Another is to build understanding of the intelligence agencies. The course shows how they relate to one another and share responsibility within the community.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030006-5:
Weekly Activities Report number 38, dated September 25, 1958, from the Chief of the Language and Area School, begins with a senior visitor. Colonel White, the Deputy Director (Support), was given a report of progress over the two years since his last session with the school, together with an account of its new organization. He is described as relaxed, interested, and gracious rather than attacking.

The report also records agreement on the form and substance of a request to adjust contract salaries to Agency standards, awaiting the Director of Training's approval. Enrollment figures close the picture: German leads with 88 students and French follows with 84, then Russian with 57, while Chinese, at 23 students, draws more learners than Spanish or Italian.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300050004-5:
Covering October 1 to 7, 1958, Weekly Activity Report number 40 comes from the Registrar's office. The whole Registrar staff, the report says, was put to work on one job. They assembled the tabulations the Agency's Director of Training needed for a presentation. The staff also tabulated a report received from Chiefs of Station. They cautioned that the returns were in no way complete. The returns said nothing about the level or quality of the training actually received.

The Registrar also accepted an invitation to help in the first running of a course. He would give the scheduled talk on Personnel and Training. Its theme was the role of the training officer. That role, the report notes, is unfortunately often an extra duty. It is loaded onto the personnel officer. Other items cover arrangements made by the Standards Branch for special lectures.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300050013-5:
From the Registrar's office, Weekly Activity Report number 30 covers July 23 to 29, 1958. At the Deputy Director of Training's request, the Registrar was interviewed. The interviewer was John Hummon, a Civil Service Commission management intern. Hummon was then detailed to the Navy Department's training division. They discussed Agency participation in executive development programs. They also discussed the Office of Training's offerings in management and supervision. Hummon was pointed to a standard work on the training of federal employees. It would serve his dealings with other agencies.

A shorter item marks a milestone in the language awards system. The fifteenth list of successful candidates for language development awards had been submitted. With it, the program's running score is updated for the Director's information.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300050040-5:
Weekly Activities Report number 3, from the Registrar's office, covers January 15 to 21, 1958. The Secretary of the Joint Middle East Planning Committee had made a request. The committee belongs to the Joint Chiefs of Staff. It asked for information on the Agency's Middle East Survey course. Two Joint Chiefs officers were tentatively enrolled for the course beginning February 3. One was a Marine colonel and the other an Air Force colonel. Their security clearance papers were still pending.

The Registrar also explored a special briefing offer. It came from the Army's operations research leadership. Its executive director volunteered to brief in person within a few weeks. A training sponsorship case closes the report. An applicant was told that sponsorship would most likely be denied. Finishing a course at his own expense, though, would put a later request on stronger ground. He said he would do so.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300110034-5:
Weekly Report number 36 comes from the Assessment and Evaluation Staff. It covers September 3 to 9, 1958. The chief had visited a senior officer. He reported the results of a survey of supervisors' attitudes. The survey concerned the training evaluation reports for Operations Course number 6. He left the survey report behind. One recommendation was altered in the discussion. The chief proposed consolidating the report's two Eyes Only pages. That would remove the problem at issue.

The survey itself rests on interviews at branch chief level. The interviewees were the DD/P supervisors who had students in the course, all but one of them. A standard set of questions was used, for about an hour each. The survey's central difficulty is clear. Grades lack a frame of reference. Standards vary from course to course. No supervisor can be sure what Satisfactory or Excellent means.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000100050002-5:
A proposal for a personal services contract sets out a preliminary study. The study would examine how to select Agency personnel for foreign language study. Its background is waste. Large numbers of people in military and government agencies were being chosen for training. They were sent to learn modern foreign languages of strategic importance. Experience showed a problem. Many otherwise promising trainees failed to learn a language as well, or as fast, as was needed. Given the length and cost of the courses, the wasted effort was serious.

One cause, the proposal argues, is a lack of the needed abilities. This kind of learning demands certain aptitudes. The study would test which measures predict success. They include verbal abilities such as word fluency and rote memory. Above all, they include the power to distinguish complex speech sounds. Most tests for that power would have to be built from scratch.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000100100024-5:
A weekly summary report for the week of July 16 to 22, 1953, counts the students in Office of Training courses. On the full-time side, two groups carry the load. They are the Basic Intelligence Course and the phased basic training courses. Seventy-five students sat in Phase II and thirty in Phase III. A small interim training group sat alongside. Specialized entries list operations, tutorial, and covert training. Their numbers run in single figures and teens.

The part-time side covers courses run at Agency installations. It is headed by the Reading Improvement Course number 12, with fifty-five students. A management entry, the Human Resources Program, follows with twenty-nine. The report is a bare statistical return. It is one of a weekly series by which the training office tracked where its students sat.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000200050001-5:
An interim report of a management survey of the Agency's Office of Training states its problem at the top. The team was to study the organization, functions, and operations of the office. It was to recommend corrective measures. Those measures would reduce the present administrative demands on the Director. The survey team claims a free hand. It would identify problem areas and reach its own conclusions. Earlier surveys of the office might agree or not.

The interim findings turn on structure. The office's present shape, the team argues, lacks something. It lacks an adequate secondary level between the headquarters staff and the training elements. Responsibility for the administrative and support phases sits apart. It sits apart from responsibility for the training itself. A proposed new structure and concept are put to the Director. The survey can then proceed on an approved frame.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400020005-5:
A memorandum dated June 4, 1954, sends the Director of Central Intelligence the writer's comments. They concern the Inspector General's survey of the Office of Training. The survey had been the writer's own suggestion in May 1953. He wanted an objective analysis of the problems facing the office. He wanted recommendations on how the training effort could be improved. The Inspector General's findings, he reports, give guidance on many sides of the office's work. They raise further problems needing study and decision.

The comments answer the recommendations point by point. One stresses selection and placement. Many training problems dissolve if the right candidates are chosen. They dissolve if the trained are placed well. The office stands ready to give follow-up examinations to language graduates on request. Another concurs in using administrative training under simulated foreign field conditions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100060006-5:
Comments on the survey of the CIA Budget Staff come back from the Budget Officer in March 1950. He answers the Management Staff's recommendations item by item. He uses the survey's own citation numbers. The first item was a proposed man-year control card file for the Budget Staff. It had been argued over in the interval. The Personnel Division, the administrative staff, and the Machine Methods Division all took part. The comment reports what those talks justified.

On forms, the Budget Officer defends the present system. The information in question would be identical to what an Advice of Allotment Authorization already carries. Using two forms where one now suffices is no improvement. Looking ahead, budget analysts would prepare quarterly statements of funds. They would run through fiscal 1951. The change was expected to yield better procedure across the Agency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100080013-5:
The Agency Security Office's Annual Management Report is furnished to the Chief of the Management Staff on August 17, 1954. It opens with the problems the office cannot solve on its own authority. Budget limits and other restrictions keep the number of available personnel down. Chances to advance to higher grades are too few, above all in the lower clerical positions. And name checks with other federal agencies move at the speed of those agencies' own staffs, which the office cannot hurry.

Progress items follow. Investigators now get specific instructions for each assignment, and the unscheduling of stereotype leads is guarded against. The office had won firearms range time on set days each week, so training in the use of firearms could at last be scheduled firmly rather than fitted in.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100220008-5:
A staff paper on the Procurement Division of the Agency's Logistics Office revisits the division's March 1953 reorganization. That change created a branch with a new charge. It would inspect contractors' facilities and work in process. The change centralized the handling of contracts, purchase orders, and other means of procurement. The new proposal tightens the front door. It calls for tighter control over every document entering the division. Receipt, distribution, and internal control would all be covered. That work would be split off from a separate task, the handling of contract amendments and extensions of delivery dates.

The division's guard duties are spelled out too. It acts on patents, royalties, and copyrights to guard the government's interest in royalty-free license claims. It checks contractors' royalty claims with the Patent Office. It fields contractor requests for approval to subcontract, raise bonuses, or grant overtime and time extensions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200010019-5:
A proposal dated February 11, 1955, would establish a special courier service. It would carry official personnel files between Agency buildings. The file traces a winter of paper behind it. Memoranda of November and December 1954 and January 1955 covered the secure transport of personnel files to the annex buildings. A staff study and a task force report on the security of records are in the file too. The problem was control.

Files moved through the Records Integration Division. It distributed them internally to the area divisions and staffs. Instead of one hand on the files, the paper complains, three separate organizations now supply personnel material. The internal leg of the journey is not exactly controlled. A dedicated courier service is offered as the fix. It would be one channel, accountable end to end, for some of the Agency's most sensitive paper.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200040007-5:
Instructions for preparing the Personnel Information Card, Form 37-6, explain why the card exists. Efficient operation requires that current office and home information on each employee be available to the Telephone Service, the Mail and Control Section, and the other offices that keep locator records. A master file of the cards was therefore established in the Machine Records Branch of the General Services Office, with a card for every departmental employee assigned to headquarters in Washington.

Each card carries the employee's name, office location and telephone number, the Agency office of assignment, and the home address and telephone number. The administrative officer of each office is instructed to submit the information and keep it current. The card's printed blocks show present and new addresses, home telephone exchange and number, and a block an authorized officer must check.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200040016-5:
A fuller version of the locator card custody study argues the security side of the question. The file of Agency employee information cards sits in the telephone room. It sits under a real estate and facilities branch. Requests for home telephone numbers come in after duty hours. Moving the file to another jurisdiction might help. The Machine Records Division is among the candidates. A move would give a more efficient product for the operators who answer those calls.

But the study warns that a broad security interest rides on the file. The cards are restricted for a reason. They touch employees in semi-covert and covert status. Other data on them is sensitive in itself. It includes the symbols of organizational components. Those could be given away through a moment's carelessness. Custody, the argument runs, must be judged on protection as much as on convenience.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200100028-5:
A management study dated 11 August, signed by the Chief of the Organization and Methods Service, weighs a proposed table of organization for the CIA Office of Research and Reports. The examiner drew on talks with the Assistant Director, staff members, and division chiefs, on the office mission statement, and on a comparison with the current table. The problem set for the study was the merit of the new plan in structure, functions, and procedure.

The plan grouped the producing divisions under three Deputy Assistant Directors, cutting the number of units reporting direct to the top. A Deputy Assistant Director for Executive work would replace the former deputy role. The study backs the broad concept, expecting better long-range planning, tighter control of economic research, and a clearer chance to fill gaps in basic economic reporting.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200110027-5:
An analysis of production in the Office of Reports and Estimates asks why that CIA office produced what it did. Its central claim is that no single, precise mission was ever spelled out for the office. A broad duty to produce national material left a gap, and that gap was filled by ad hoc judgments, outside requests, and the habits of branch and group chiefs. Patterns set by repetition came to act like missions.

Later parts trace other forces shaping output. Long habit favored current periodical reviews, and producers relied on their own judgment and informed guesses about what might be needed. Doctrine and practice, the analysis argues, grew from below rather than from set policy. The study is a frank internal account of how an early Agency office drifted into its workload.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200180002-5:
An Office of Logistics memo gives recommendations for improving a photographic facility held for emergency plan use. Logistics staff reviewed a planned rearrangement of the plant and its equipment, judging the layout both for daily work and for the emergency role. Special weight was given to the chance that the Graphics Register file might have to be reproduced at the site in a crisis.

Printing technicians proposed a layout built on five ideas. They wanted smooth work flow with little lost motion, and room for up to twenty-five extra staff. They wanted fast conversion from daily to emergency use. Space for several unrelated jobs at once, or for one large job, and continued work during changeover completed the plan. An attached list, Tab B, names new equipment, including a printer, a dryer, and a rotary print washer, with counts for each item.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300020027-5:
A House conference report dated 22 May 1956 presents the agreed text of H.R. 9429, to be cited as the Dependents' Medical Care Act. The report, sent in by Mr. Vinson from the committee of conference, settles differences between the House and Senate versions. Its stated purpose is to keep morale high in the uniformed services by giving members and their dependents a better, uniform program of medical care.

Definitions open the act, covering the uniformed services from the Army and Navy to the Air Force and Marine Corps, with further services named in the full text. Later sections set when dependents of retired members, and of members who died in retirement, may receive care in service facilities. Such care depends on a request and on space, facilities, and medical staff capacity being free. Joint rules by the Defense and Health secretaries govern the program.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300030071-5:
Senate Congressional Record pages in this set range across several unrelated items, with the catalog title pointing to debate on an Advisory Commission on Intergovernmental Relations. One striking passage prints a July 1959 message from a railroad official to section foremen. It orders them to wire their senator against Senate bill 1425, using set wording on motorcar safety, and to pay the wire cost themselves for later refund. The speaker presenting it says the message speaks for itself.

Other pages give bill text on health benefit plans. They describe plans that pay for covered services in hospitals, in doctors' offices and patients' homes, and for tests outside hospital and preventive care. The plans were run by groups that had operated such plans before. The set is best used as a source for these separate fragments rather than as a single speech.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300170003-5:
A memorandum for the record dated 16 January 1959 notes a CIA briefing given that day at half past four in the afternoon. The visitors were Edwin Weisl, Sr., Cyrus Vance, and Edwin Weisl, Jr., briefed at the Director's arrangement with Weisl senior. Agency staff present included the Director and Messrs. Scoville, Sheldon, and Warner, among others named in the memo. Vance had phoned ahead to say Weisl junior would also attend.

Weisl senior explained that hearings were coming before the Preparedness Investigating Subcommittee, partly with the Space Committee, both chaired by Senator Johnson, and that the visit was a pre-hearing reconnaissance. Talk turned to Soviet missiles and the Bison aircraft, and the questions and answers are in an attached memo. The visitors planned next to call Secretary Quarles and General Twining, among others named in the closing lines.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020012-5:
A monthly report for the Map Library Division covers November 1958. The Reference Branch handled 1,273 map requests supplying 23,046 maps, and 145 requests for publications supplying 336 items. Map requests fell slightly from October, while publication requests rose. Thirty-three Department of State staff came in person for map material, and the branch answered 132 place name requests and 213 other reference questions.

Air Targets Material Program work added 2,540 charts sent out on 102 requests, plus text items on further requests. Holiday time, staff illness, and work pressure cut trips to vital storage to two, slowing that program. Later pages list new map receipts, including large series and sheets showing roads and pipelines, and maps and city plans for towns in Thailand and Vietnam.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020021-5:
October 1958 fills this monthly report for the Cartography Division. Requests accepted came to 147 maps and charts, 139 for the CIA and eight for the Department of State. The Office of Research and Reports supplied the largest share of Agency requests, followed by contributions to the National Intelligence Survey program. The division completed 147 maps and charts in the same month, and cancellations came to twelve.

The survey map coordinator received forty-three job requests, sent fifty jobs to reproduction, and took back sixty-eight maps, leaving a backlog of fifty-three requests. Other sections cover branch work, including steps toward standard specifications for survey base maps, which the report says would save time and smooth procedure. Personnel notes record a deputy chief acting during an absence and changes in the USSR-Satellites Branch.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020094-5:
July 1958 is the month covered by this Cartography Division report. Requests accepted came to eighty-four maps and charts, seventy-four for the CIA and ten for the Department of State. The Office of Research and Reports again supplied the largest share. Completions came to 121 maps and charts, 116 for the Agency and five for State, a higher output than the month's intake.

The survey map coordinator took in twenty requests, sent thirty-seven jobs to reproduction, and received sixty-four maps back, leaving one map in the office at month's end. Nine reruns were also handled for the map library side. The division held 447 maps and charts at the end of July, spread among its branches. Later notes mention a city plan project held up by security problems and a set period of overtime to meet deadlines after resignations cut staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100180015-5:
A status report on exchanges, dated August 1958 and tied to the Intelligence Advisory Committee's Ad Hoc Committee on Exchanges, is heavily garbled in the scan. Legible passages deal with the committee's widened duties, set in a paper of 12 August 1958. They also deal with the need for members to be ready to handle exchanges of persons as well as materiel. The report treats East-West exchange work as a standing coordination task across agencies.

One clear complaint runs through the middle pages. Projects begun by other parts of the government through private contractors had not reached the State Department in time for a coordinated government view to go out in reply. Many such projects touched intelligence interests, the report argues, so an orderly method was needed. Fine detail beyond that should be read with care because of the poor scan quality.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00423a000100010023-5:
A functions statement for the Administrative Staff of the Southeast Division covers its Budget and Finance Section, though the scan is garbled in many places. Legible lines assign the staff guidance and support work for components in budget, finance, accounting, and travel. They also give it responsibility to help where a division or another Agency part cannot support a budget and finance activity itself. Project plans and their approval also fall in this field.

Other readable items concern contracts and payrolls, including staff payroll handling and transfer of funds, and a procedure for approving draft regulations on budget and finance matters. A closing section names the Chief of the Administrative Staff and touches on undertakings expected in the near future, but names and figures there are redacted or unreadable. The statement is best used for the section's broad duties, not for fine detail.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000100190037-5:
Paper IAC-D-74/4, dated 16 August 1956, carries the Fourth Annual Progress Report of the Scientific Estimates Committee for fiscal year 1956. The committee's authority traces to its establishment on 14 August 1952 by a Director's directive under a National Security Council directive. Membership and method match later years: seven permanent member organizations and ad hoc subcommittees for particular subjects, with no permanent subcommittee structure. Three standing responsibilities under the founding directive govern the work, and the accomplishments section answers to them.

One item counts the committee's contributions to survey work, in sections of Chapter I of the National Intelligence Survey, with a tabulation at Tab B. Another records a detailed program, prepared with survey committee approval, for producing a full survey chapter through fiscal year 1959. It was based on an agreed list of Bloc and non-Bloc areas needing a basic scientific assessment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300050003-5:
Paper IAC-D-103/5, dated 18 July 1957, carries the Second Semi-Annual Report of the Ad Hoc Committee on Exchanges. A secretary's note explains that, for reasons given in the report, the period covered runs to eight months rather than the six last directed by the parent committee. The report itself is attached under a chairman's memorandum dated 17 July 1957.

Much of the visible text concerns technical consultants. Sponsors could make small adjustments to exchange proposals but had to tell the committee of any critical change. Through the consultant, continuing advice was given on itinerary, sponsors, delegation members, and briefing material, and the report calls that advice valuable. The committee's standing aim remained the one set in 1956: to gain the most intelligence value from East-West delegation exchanges while the exchanges themselves went forward under State Department handling.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300090018-5:
Minutes numbered IAC-M-352 record a committee meeting at a quarter to eleven on 15 July 1958, with Director Allen W. Dulles presiding. Members present are listed for State, Army, Navy, Air Force, the Joint Staff, the Atomic Energy Commission, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. One discussion item concerns friendly power activities in a named region, where the chairman suggested it might be wise to broaden coverage of relevant Turkish activities.

A long item follows on a joint review, with the communications intelligence board, of proposed Council intelligence directives. Draft Directive No. 1 and various proposed amendments were discussed in considerable detail. The minutes give only the fact and shape of each discussion, in the sanitized copy released, with some passages removed. Attendance notes mark which members were present for only part of the meeting.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300140003-5: A reference list headed SE's, NIE's and SNIE's sorts estimate numbers in columns, with no narrative text. Staff estimates, national estimates, and special national estimates are listed by their numbers alone. Some are marked with asterisks, and a few entries are marked illegible in the original. Later pages give estimate titles with publication dates in 1953. They include a Soviet statement in reply to a presidential speech and papers on the Soviet Bloc and Eastern Germany. The file is an index sheet for the estimates series.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000100010134-5:
A negotiated contract file, numbered TB-718 in the heading, names the David Clark Company, Incorporated, of Worcester, Massachusetts, as contractor. The signature page states that the contractor shall furnish all supplies and perform all services set out in an attached schedule, for the consideration stated there. Rights and duties of both sides are governed by the schedule, an appendix, and general provisions. Where schedule and general provisions clash, the schedule controls.

The contract number in the body is rendered TH-718, and the amount line is garbled in the scan, so no sum is quoted here. General provisions run to many pages. A termination passage provides that contractor personnel covered by a termination notice are paid the part of the fixed price earned for services rendered up to the notice date. Time needed under the clause is added. A file reference, DPB-0055-59, heads the copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000100020142-5:
Annex A sets a command concept for reshaping Agency air activities. Its aim is to organize all CIA air work so the Agency can respond quickly and well to needs across the whole Agency. Types of need considered are listed first. They include intelligence gathering overflights, such as photographic and electronic work. They also include airlift of very sensitive persons or gear where security demands special handling.

Contingency capability for clandestine work and a headquarters ability to monitor or control field work complete the list. On scope, the concept treats the Development Projects Division as mainly an action arm in support of the area divisions. Nearly all needs for clandestine air work would start with the area divisions and be levied on the division for completion. Its worldwide staff, facilities, and air assets would do the work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300020050-5: This declassified CIA document has no title. The nameless pages. Their story waits. The archive holds the file. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300030022-5: An account summary print lists project names and allotment accounts with current 1956, prior year 1955, prior years, and cumulative total columns. The name Aquatone heads the largest group: one account row shows 144,640.85 dollars and a group total of 165,267.39 dollars, while a Director's Project heading also appears. Other rows are small, down to a few dollars. The sheet is a raw summary table with no narrative text, and some digits are garbled in the scan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080009-5: An allotment ledger headed December 1958 lists Aquatone accounts in the 7-1004 series under expenditure issue, unliquidated obligation, total obligation, allotment authority, and unobligated balance columns. The 7-1004-10-001 account appears in both full and partial rows, with totals near five million dollars, and a 7-1004-10-004 account shows 676,479.97 dollars. The sheet is a raw year-end ledger print with no narrative text and partly garbled digits.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080036-5: An allotment ledger headed with a 1960 ledger line lists Aquatone accounts across the 7-1004 series, from the 10-000 head account through the 50 group. Figures include a 19,197.79 dollar row for a 30-010 account and seven-figure totals for the lead group. Column heads cover expenditure issue, unliquidated and total obligation requests, allotment authority, and unobligated balance. The sheet is a raw ledger print with no narrative text and heavy digit garbling.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080072-5:
Ledger pages for fiscal year 1957, marked Secret, record allotment accounts in the 7-1004 series, including an account headed Aquatone. Columns track amounts issued, unliquidated obligations, total obligations, allotment authority, and unobligated balances. Entries are dated September and October 1956 and carry account numbers such as 7-1004-50-012, with figures entered in dollars and cents.

Later pages break the same accounts down by voucher, showing payroll entries described as main roll and staff agents, plus adjustments dated in September and October 1956. Readers get the working level of Agency finance: how one large allotment was split among sub-accounts, how much had been obligated at each step, and how much authority remained unused.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00900a000100030003-5:
Confidential memorandum to the Deputy Director for Support takes up staff and non-staff elements within the Agency's DD/P Senior Staffs. It cites memoranda of 18 and 27 October 1955 and asks what names or personnel reporting changes would show the real functional alignment of those staffs. The study rules out organisational change and staff work inside Operating Divisions.

Staff work is defined in the paper as supervising policy, building policy where none exists, planning programs with Area Divisions, setting procedures, and reviewing proposed work. Findings were checked with the chiefs of FI, PPO, and TSS and the Deputy Chief of CI. The paper proposes reporting Senior Staff strength split between staff and non-staff elements instead of totals alone.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00137a000100140055-5:
Monthly report for September 1956 records a month of work in an industrial branch of the Agency's ORR. Part XIX, the economic sections of NIE 11-5-56, was completed and sent to the Guided Missile Intelligence Committee on 20 September. That 100-page contribution was approved with only a few changes, mostly of classification, which the branch was then preparing for distribution.

Other items look ahead. Planning was under way for study of economic aspects of nuclear energy, feeding requirements and contributions to the Joint Atomic Energy Intelligence Committee. A proposal was due soon for an international conference on Soviet Bloc motor vehicle industries, to be held in Washington. Work was also in hand to improve the adequacy and completeness of branch reports.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100010146-5:
Agency memo dated 21 March 1955 weighs a paper on freight transport speeds in the USSR and the USA. The paper deals with commercial and technical speeds. It is judged a good treatment of its subject. It meets the need laid on it in part. The reviewers advise that the comments go to the outside author. He should be free to revise where he sees fit. The paper should then be published for the intelligence community. A further paper on another listed topic should follow.

Pay is also taken up. Given the author's background, a rate of 125 dollars a week is advised. About two weeks is the guess for the time the work took. Long comments follow on the methods used for the speeds. Soviet and American speed figures rest on unlike bases, so the two sets cannot be set side by side.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020172-5:
Review dated 25 May 1956 works through economic needs for the Agency's OCI Periodic Requirements List. The list runs from 1 July to 31 October 1956. The review goes country by country. Algeria gains a new item. It asks for facts on arms supplied to Algerian rebels by Arab countries. British West Africa gains an item on Soviet Bloc bids to grow trade with Nigeria. Offers of technical help, loans, or credits are to be reported. Trade agreement talks are to be noted as well.

Liberia gains a like item on Bloc offers. It covers capital gear, technical aid, and long term loans. Later pages cover Near East countries. They include offers of credit and plant building by Bloc nations. A Jordan item asks about the shares of Syria, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia in funding a named railway project.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100050034-5:
Standing needs dated 1 July 1957 serve the Organizations and Management Branch of the Agency's Services Division, ORR. They open with the tying of Bloc economies. Wanted facts cover the make-up of the Council for Economic Mutual Assistance. They cover bodies such as the USSR State Committee for Foreign Economic Relations. Their programs and policies are wanted as well. So are the scope and the effects of tying national economic plans across Bloc countries.

Making production methods and products standard across the Bloc is also named. Ways of settling accounts between Bloc countries are named too. Set subjects then turn to labour. They cover the state bodies for labour affairs, such as the USSR State Committee on Labor and Wages. They cover the Chief Directorate of Labor Reserves. They cover trade unions, their people, and their policies. Labour law, social insurance, and welfare rules close the list.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180030-5:
Minutes in the Agency's files, ED/EC M-244, record a meeting on 4 June 1957 in Room 1533, Maiatico. They were issued on 7 June 1957. Mr. Hale chaired a full table from MDAC, Commerce, Defense, ICA, State, and Treasury. Notes cover hearings in Congress and a letter from Senator McClellan on the Paris talks. Main items are a report by the team on the CHINCOM meeting. A discussion of work to come is the other main item.

The hearings note has a Mutual Security Act presentation set for that day. It was to go before the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee. Talk on the Paris talks praised the work of the United States delegate. The United States had opened with support only from the Turks. Several countries later shifted toward the United States position. That shift was credited in large part to his presentation of the case.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180049-5:
Minutes ED/EC M-262 in the Agency's files, issued 2 August 1957, record the meeting at 2:00 p.m. on Tuesday, 30 July 1957, in Room 1213, Maiatico. A note covers a State Department proposal for a work program to carry out paragraph 21 of the revised economic defense policy. Numbered items are a memorandum to EDAC about the Joint Chiefs memorandum and a work program for paragraph 9 of the same policy.

State tabled its paragraph 21 work program paper at the meeting. Later talk turned to how control actions were read abroad. Commerce held that its actions had always been anti-frustration in intent, even when some governments read them as punitive, and that this had been explained to partner countries, at times with success. State answered that success had come at serious foreign policy cost.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180139-5:
Agency memo from the Chief, Analysis Division, to the Chief, Industrial Division, seeks added input for the Soviet National Intelligence Estimate. Recent draft papers rest on set ideas about the Soviet economy. They sit behind revisions of estimate figures against the past year. The ideas are admitted to be speculative. Hard facts must be brought to bear on them fast. An outside deadline of 15 August is named, with internal input due about 19 July. That leaves roughly three weeks of testing work to plan.

Background explains the stakes. Past forecasts rested on one open or hidden assumption. It was that Soviet will to push growth to the most was fixed, and with it the priority given to heavy industry. Later pages test how output rose from 1951 to 1955. They test it industry by industry. The rise came through new plant, through added labour, goods, and gear, or through better methods.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200010064-5:
Current Support Memorandum dated 20 September 1954 is an all-branch project of the Agency's Services Division, ORR. It assesses the impact of flood conditions on parts of Communist China's economy. China had suffered weeks of very wide flooding. The long range effect might badly hold back her economic program. Unusually heavy, steady rain had brought record flood crests on the Yangtze and Hwai Rivers. Flooding was reported from Tibet in the west to the Sungari, Liao, and Yalu Rivers in the northeast.

Damage in the Yangtze area was believed to match that of 1931. That year was, until then, the worst flood year in modern Chinese history. Water works built since 1951 in the Hwai basin had helped. But stress had been laid on dikes and channel works over holding reservoirs. That stress left river levels higher in flood periods than before.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200120008-5:
Agency Current Support Memorandum No. 618, dated 7 November 1958, reports that the Polish airline LOT was stressing international routes. A recent estimate by A. Skala, Director of Polish Airlines LOT, forecast a drop of 60,000 passengers on domestic routes for 1958 and a rise of 16,000 on international routes. The paper works through the route network behind those figures and the aircraft the shift would need.

Rumours are reported that the Poles might buy Viscount turboprop transports or Comet four-engine jets from the British, or receive IL-18 turboprops from the USSR, all types meant for longer flights. Poland's standing helped: it had been an ICAO member from the start and LOT a long-standing IATA member, so both could fully use the Bloc air expansion drive of 1955 to 1958.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200120035-5:
Agency Current Support Memorandum No. 563 reports military training of Middle East nationals in the Bloc. Since 1955, approximately 1,300 Middle East nationals had undergone military training there. Courses covered many phases of ground, air, and naval training. In the early period much of the arranging ran through Czechoslovakia, but since late 1956 the USSR had taken up direct negotiations for arms deliveries and the training that went with them.

Egypt and Syria supplied almost all the trainees sent to the Bloc. Afghanistan did not send students until December 1957, when it sent 50 for training in the USSR. Yemen, the only other country that had contracted for Bloc arms, had sent no trainees to the Bloc, though a number of Yemeni students attended Egyptian military schools.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200140006-5:
Secret paper in the Agency's files on Soviet Bloc aid and normal commerce opens with a public Soviet statement. The statement holds that the Soviet Union gives trade more for political than for economic benefit. That does not mean, the paper argues, that Communist countries run a giveaway program with no economic return. It means that where political gains are large enough, loan terms and financing will be set by politics rather than by commercial tests.

Features setting Bloc aid apart from normal commerce are listed: repayment periods and interest rates on Bloc credits run beyond the scope of commercial financing. Total Bloc credits, economic and military, to underdeveloped countries stand at well over 2 billion dollars. Grants-in-aid are called the chief feature of the Chinese Communist aid program. A full costing, the paper notes, would need item-by-item price data that were not available.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200140033-5:
Evaluation in the Agency's files takes up a Soviet pamphlet on fitting USSR railroad rolling stock with the SA-3 automatic coupler. The review begins with its origin. The SA-3 is not new, nor Soviet: it is a development of the Willison coupler brought out in the United States about 1900. It is a good design, with some gains over the Janney type used in America since 1887. It might have become the United States standard, but railroads had committed to the Janney type, with which it is not compatible.

The pamphlet is judged a shrewd exercise in self-praise in the guise of a technical paper. Little in Europe uses automatic couplers for freight cars, the screw and link coupler being the norm there, and the evaluator sees little chance of a late switch. The welding system is called very adequate for acknowledged Soviet capability in welding technology.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200140051-5:
Agency briefing outline on Soviet practices in aiding people sets out the political aim first, then the instruments. Under developed countries, credits are paired with trade offers or stated willingness to trade. Figures in the outline put Bloc credits spread across many countries, with a small group of countries taking the great bulk of the total, and military credits counted apart. Bloc trade with the nine major aid recipients is said to have increased 400 percent since 1954, with trade with Egypt up 4,130 percent since 1953 in the outline's figures.

Technician numbers follow: about 2,195 Bloc technicians in underdeveloped countries in 1955 are listed, with military specialists counted separately. Case notes then work country by country, including a mid-1957 Sudan case where cotton marketing trouble brought a token Soviet purchase, then offers of larger purchases and economic aid.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200160031-5:
Annual report for 1957 of the Agency's Services Division China Committee records a year of discussion rather than research. The committee held 47 meetings during 1957. Meetings were given to topics on Communist China. They were given to briefings by members and guests on research problems in their fields, and to briefings by the committee as a group. Briefing titles listed include Sino and East European Satellite trade relations, Communist China's balance of payments, and revision of the farm plan in Communist China.

Long range problems held a fairly rigid focus. They ran from economic signs of Chinese powers and aims in the Taiwan Straits to Five Year Plan goals and results. Population and farming stood as two problems. Factory growth in outlying areas, and railroad and highway building, closed the list. The committee served as a forum for swapping information and ideas, and for quick group action on Economic Research Area problems.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200180002-5:
Secret review in the Agency's files covers the Subcommittee on Transportation of the Economic Intelligence Committee and its work and results in fiscal year 1958. The subcommittee, TSC, kept no formal program for reviewing the quality of the transport intelligence product. Some of its work still served that end, chiefly joint effort on agreed basic transport statistics. Uniform methods for judging rail, highway, port, and inland waterway powers were part of it. The work ran in part through the Transportation Capabilities Estimating Group.

A growing practice is also noted: member agency research projects were coming under informal review by the subcommittee. Coordination of member agencies' research programs had no set program of its own. The review says setting one up could advance the subcommittee's functions in a marked way. A future program section then takes up the standing of TSC work and what should come next.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100120001-5:
Memo dated 31 December, the year in the mid-1950s in the scan, goes to the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence. It covers application of SD-MICC policy by the Agency. Since August 1951 the Deputy Directors had been weighing one use of that policy, that of the State Defense Military Information Control Committee. The use in view was releasing Agency non-military intelligence to foreign governments. A DDP and DDI examination of 2 September reached a conclusion, set out in an attached tab.

Their conclusion was plain: applying SD-MICC policy to non-military intelligence was neither practical nor fitting. They recommended that such policy be applied to military intelligence and information only. Release of non-military material would be decided, with the originator's consent, by the Agency officers already charged with dissemination duty. Later pages weigh the value of a release against the return expected.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100140171-5:
Catalogue of overall country studies in the Agency's files covers research on communications habits, stereotypes, exposure, and attitudes. An Indian study, Communication of Ideas in India, is listed in three parts. The parts are channels of communications, public opinion in Lucknow, and communications and the background of opinion in the village. Polls by local groups add data, analysed by the sponsoring office with program use in mind.

A Japanese poll by the Japanese Public Opinion Research Institute is listed in six parts. Its topics are the United States and Soviet conflict, the Korean hostilities, rollback policy, Japan's security, world peace and war, the United Nations, and rearmament. Other entries include French attitudes toward the United States, an audience evaluation of a film called Without Fear, and a study of Philippine puppet films as a message medium. Credibility studies on candor in broadcasts to West Germany close the set.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000200080014-5:
Agency briefing paper for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, TCS-1858-57, dated 26 August 1957, sets out what coverage of certain Soviet targets within range of U-2 aircraft was expected to yield. The object is intelligence of critical value to major national intelligence objectives. The paper states plainly that precise target information for applying strategic weapons, though of vital interest, is not one of the critical objectives of this briefing.

Its theme is the unique role of AQUATONE-type photography in producing National Intelligence estimates, the basis for major national security decisions. Principal targets fall in the fields judged most significant in the Soviet ability to strike at the United States: the guided missile system, the long range bomber force, and nuclear energy production. Photography of medium bomber home bases, and of special weapons storage and handling sites found on earlier operations, would sharpen estimates of nuclear delivery capability.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400100037-5:
Top Secret CHESS message in the Agency's files is a photographic frame log with its own camera prefixes. Numbered items list frame pairs marked SL, V7, and 6R, each rated good or fair and classed by geometry: extreme oblique, far oblique, medium oblique, near vertical, or vertical. Early entries read SL 420, good, extreme oblique; SL 426, good, far oblique; and paired SL 414 and SL 416 frames, good, far oblique.

Later items run past nineteen numbered entries in the portion shown, with V7 frames rated vertical and SL frames in medium oblique. The log records the usable photography of a mission frame by frame. No targets are named in the text; identification rests on frame numbers held elsewhere.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400100046-5:
Message in the Agency's files, cite Whiskey-0101, carries photo report No. 1384. Its date of information is 6 July 1957. It covers Lebanon, with Syria items later in the text. Beirut International Airfield showed 7 C-47 type and 13 C-54 type aircraft. It showed 2 Viscount, 2 Convair 340, and 3 Scottish Twin Pioneer aircraft. It showed 6 liaison type aircraft. Beirut Harbor showed 1 passenger ship and 8 cargo ships. Estabel, Metulla, and Riyaq airfields each showed no aircraft. Kleiat showed no aircraft, though its northeast extension was completed. Sidon Harbor showed 1 tanker, its dimensions garbled in the scan.

Syria items include Dumeir Airfield. The field was in the grading stage of construction. Its runway was to be about 7,800 by 135 feet. The runway runs west-southwest to east-northeast. A parallel taxiway sits on the north side. A west alert apron of about 450 by 155 feet is given. An east alert apron entry follows, cut off in the scan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000500150022-5:
An Army memorandum dated 2 June 1958 asks the Director of Central Intelligence to grant Chalice clearances to named Army personnel. Sent through the Army staff, it cites minutes of a 26 May 1958 meeting as its basis. The request is grouped by duty. One group covers Army staff members with policy, decision, and research and development duties tied to operations and their support. Senior generals head that list, each entry giving rank, service number, and existing top secret clearance date.

Further groups cover intelligence staff officers with policy duties, and officers who would handle and administer Chalice material inside a secure area. Each entry follows the same pattern of name, rank, and clearance record. Personal details printed in the lists are left aside here. The file shows how access to a sensitive program was extended service by service, person by person, with a paper trail for each grant requested.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600060003-5:
A final report dated 25 May 1956 reviews how intelligence requirements and collection tasks line up with priority national objectives under DCID 4/5. The review was done with staff from member agencies, after notice to the Intelligence Advisory Committee in January 1955. It first describes existing practice. Priority objectives, approved by the committee and noted by the National Security Council, set the broad direction for production and collection work across the community.

Those objectives are not the only guide, the report stresses. Research and collection offices also serve departmental needs, which often overlap the national list. In research, gaps in available information become requests for collection. Committees coordinate some fields: atomic energy, science and technology, guided missiles, economics, and basic intelligence. Collection offices, meanwhile, work inside set spheres of duty and face real limits on staff, reach, and timing when they plan their programs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600090064-5:
A draft global war plan for the deputy directorate for intelligence area, dated 28 June 1955, fills the file. Opening pages define key terms. Intelligence production means national intelligence and any weighed information used for national security. Services of common concern are tasks CIA performs for the whole community under the National Security Act of 1947. The plan warns that the peacetime shape of the Agency may not fit wartime needs.

Its concept of organisation follows. Command and staff for production would sit at a wartime headquarters in or near Washington. Overseas work tied to production or to support of secret operations would fall under a CIA field commander. Other field production would sit under the theater commander, with no Agency control over officers lent to it. Later sections set out phases: building and testing wartime methods in peace, training staff for them, then carrying out evacuation and redeployment plans once war begins.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600110034-5:
An operating instruction for electronic intelligence work in CIA fills the file, though parts of the scan read poorly. Early sections list the authorities behind it. They cite National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 6 and the manual of United States signals intelligence work. Terms are then defined with care. Operational control covers assigning and changing tasks. Technical control covers the methods and steps used to carry a task out.

The mission section sets the Agency's duty plainly. CIA will carry out electronic intelligence tasks assigned by the Director of the National Security Agency. Those tasks must rest on the cited authorities and win agreement from the Director of Central Intelligence. Work proceeds within Agency resources and under both forms of control. Later sections take up liaison channels. Closing pages begin a list of support duties the Agency owes the wider effort.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700050021-5:
A status list tracks problems in the hands of the Office of Intelligence Coordination. Entries are short and numbered, each giving the state of one matter. One settled item covers post-mortems and gaps. By agreed steps, the estimates office now passes found gaps to this office once its own work ends. Follow-up with collectors then sits here.

Requirements work fills much of the list. Staff have joined committee talks on covert needs and checked that offices grasp the current setup. Economic needs for open Foreign Service collection are being joined up with State. Committee requirements also reach the operations side, to alert its divisions to like material. Agency demands on the foreign documents arm are under study as part of a wider look at foreign writings as a source. Another entry reviews support for open scientific collection.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070047-5:
A first three-year report of the Watch Committee, dated 4 November 1953, reviews December 1950 to November 1953. Its first part traces legal roots. On 7 December 1950 the Intelligence Advisory Committee ruled that the Joint Intelligence Indications Committee should serve as its Watch Committee. Terms were cleared days later. The mission: gather, weigh, study, and report signs of Soviet-Communist hostile intent.

Roots run back through a G-2 indications file group, which gained Navy and Air Force members over time. In August 1950 the joint committee took it over and invited CIA, State, and the FBI to sit in. That path explains why the chair and secretariat sat where they did. Later pages track output growth: copies of the report rose from 113 in December 1950 to 225. Type, paper, and layout all improved, spurred in part by word that President Truman found the early report hard to read.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070083-5:
A memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence traces how the Intelligence Advisory Committee is made up. Its roots reach to the Lovett Committee, which urged in 1945 that a new central agency hold an intelligence board. That board would join the service intelligence chiefs with heads of the main civilian arms. President Truman's order of 22 January 1946 took a like path for the Central Intelligence Group.

Under that order an advisory board of top military and civilian chiefs counselled the Director. The memo draws a fine line: the board served the Director in his community role, not as agency head. The National Security Act of 1947 said nothing on such a body. That silence, the memo argues, carried no clear meaning either way. Later pages weigh whether central seats could harm the committee's work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100360002-5:
A short memorandum dated 8 October 1956 chases a late report. Its subject is a Soviet inquiry for a West German sheet steel testing device. The source report, IR-195-56 from an Air Force unit in March 1956, had moved slowly. Commerce flagged the delay to the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee on 17 September. Embassy Bonn had also sent the item in a despatch dated 4 June.

Routing facts fill the rest of the memo. The report bears no date beyond a collection date of 5 March. It does not say which Washington offices stood on the Air Force list. One office logged receipt on 3 May, then passed the paper on through a panel. One desk was left off the routing, the memo notes. Bonn's despatch, by office records, never arrived at all. The file holds the memo twice over, in two near-like copies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490080-5:
A progress report dated 28 January 1955 tracks a survey aimed at lowering the grading of COCOM papers. All papers in the numbered allied series now carry a secret stamp. The plan would drop most to confidential. A Paris cable of 10 December said Washington would list, within ninety days, the papers that must stay secret. This report is the first on the survey.

Work so far is basic. A card index of every allied paper on hand has been built. Missing papers are being hunted into one central file. Draft tests sort the pile: papers stay secret if they expose bloc demand or supply for set goods. The same holds for papers showing a good's strategic weight, secret trade, or sources and methods. Early findings close the report, with more work urged.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100510014-5:
A memo dated 24 July 1958 puts a merger plan before the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee. The plan would fold it into the Economic Intelligence Committee as a subcommittee. Letters swapped between that committee's vice chairman and Admiral Walter DeLany, who chairs the parent advisory body, ride along. Personal soundings of members had already run in the plan's favour.

Admiral DeLany's terms are spelled out. The change would suit his body so long as the new subcommittee keeps serving its needed role in economic defence. A formal vote is set for 13 August 1958 in Room 1121, M Building. Background notes explain why the link is close already. One CIA office, led by Dr Otto Guthe, supplies chairmen and secretariats to both committees. The letters add that defence work has in fact drawn growing support from the wider economic intelligence community, even as this committee's own pace eased.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300030002-5:
A memo urges a standby force for the Office of Communications, with top approval noted in September 1959. The problem is stated first. The headquarters signal centre needs a dependable, cleared pool it can call at once. Such a pool would cover surges that outrun the staff on hand. Little progress, the memo admits, has been made in lining up skilled staff for that surge need.

The plan would build the pool inside the communications office itself. Personnel staff would screen the pool in liaison with that office and others. One hitch gets frank treatment: family strain. A note from the communications director suggests capping the grade range of members' husbands as one way to ease admin friction, a sign the pool draws on staff wives. Cover notes show the deputy director for support backed the set-up on 14 September.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300030011-5:
A personal letter dated 27 March 1959 tries to lure a man home to a new post. Larry writes to Chick, and admits the job can only be sketched in guarded terms. Its core is watching several large research and development efforts, the development side above all. The holder must keep his chiefs posted on progress and needs. 

Contract running rides with the post, with help. So does judging each fresh proposal for feasibility, timing, and cost. The holder must track wider research and American policy in the field, so he can urge fresh projects worth backing. Sharp grasp of advanced technique is a must. Travel inside the United States will be frequent. The present holder leaves very soon, so overlap is vital. Three questions close the plea: can Chick break away fast, be in post by 15 June, and meet his new chief about 15 April?
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300040001-5:
A legal memo dated 25 August 1956 answers how to handle gifts from foreign governments. It goes to the Director of Personnel. The constitutional bar is quoted first. No federal office holder may, without the consent of Congress, take any present or title from a king, prince, or foreign state. A statute then routes such goods through the State Department. 

Practice under those rules fills the rest. Gifts are turned in, and a call is made on whether the Agency keeps a piece, or passes it to a charity body. The statute also forces a report to every other Congress, listing retired staff whose gifts State still holds. A presidential order of 23 April 1954 enters the account. The memo ends with patience: fresh law is hoped for next session, and no new fix should be tried till Congress acts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300140037-5:
A memo dated 2 May 1957 asks whether the Veterans' Preference Act binds CIA. The act gives veterans first claim when federal staff are cut. Its rules shape how a cut is run for all staff, veteran or not. In practice, the memo notes, CIA has kept to the act on firing, rehire, and like steps.

One class of case stands apart. Firings under section 102(c) of the National Security Act, the Director's own power, have not been run by the act. No court has yet ruled whether the act binds the Agency at all. The Justice Department holds, in loose terms, that 102(c) firings escape the act. Special law, in its view, beats general law. Two court cases are tabbed for support. One rests on a Commerce appropriation act of 1953, the other on a State act of 1950. Neither case raised veterans' claims head-on.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300150009-5:
A memo dated 22 July 1959 reports good legal news on a planned staff cut. Lawrence Houston writes to the deputy director for support. His staff had talked with Donald B. MacGuineas, a Justice Department litigation chief. The topic: may CIA run a reduction in force by tests of its own, apart from the Veterans' Preference Act, and what law would say?

MacGuineas gave a firm steer. If the Director deems his own tests needed in the national interest, Justice will defend the firings in court. He believed each defence would hold. Two strings come with that pledge. The scheme must be rational and specific. And the Agency must follow its own rules to the letter. On pure law, then, the path is open.
