Politics and practice are another matter, Houston warns. They must be weighed with great care before such a scheme is so much as launched.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300200012-5:
A note to Houston passes on a rough translation from a German book on CIA. The clip treats legal tangles from the spy hunts of 1952. A well-known professor stood charged with false swearing, on words sworn to a Senate panel. The book's own tale, told loosely and with gaps, runs as follows.

Two Agency men, the book says, told a Seattle travel office the man meant to flee to the Soviet Union. That tale helped sink him. Yet the book also notes a limit in law: the Agency holds no home security role inside the United States. When a court sought the men's own words, the Director of the day, Bedell Smith, barred them from the stand. A Seattle court found both in contempt and gave them fifteen days. They never served the time. President Truman pardoned both, a rare grace for so small a slight, the book remarks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300210011-5:
A memo dated 26 January 1955 from Matthew Baird, Director of Training, presses a push for fresh writing on intelligence work. His office had opened a program the past October. Its aims run two ways. First, spur Agency staff to do first-hand study of how intelligence is done. Second, print the best of that work, plus strong pieces recast from office files.

Two study bids have come in so far, Baird reports. Panels of Agency officers are vetting them. A few papers may be reshaped for a planned book line, Studies in Intelligence. The first of those books should go out early this year. More raw stock is wanted. Chiefs across the Agency are urged to send study bids and names of staff with a bent for the craft. The head of the Intelligence School and his aide stand ready to call and talk through the plan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300220010-5:
A memo dated 22 January 1960 sets the table for the Agency Publications Board. Its next meet is set for eleven on Thursday, 4 February. The note tells members what the Board's staff has done since the last meet. 

A draft staff study on video dissemination is going round, with a sketch for its facts part. If notes and fixes land in time, a fresh draft will face the Board on the fourth. Counsel's office is at work on one part of that facts part. A fresh USIB panel on intelligence publications met on 19 January; its notes and a data form reached all members. The panel takes up two hard words next month: which journals are vital, and which ones merely twin each other. A White House board asked for those views. Our Board must judge if it can speak on its own journals by then.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100030008-5:
A memo of October 1959 reports back on a West Point meet that shrank in the plan. The seminar as set was never held, he learned. In its place, one day of a June meet took the theme up.

The host meet ran 17 to 19 June at the Military Academy. Its theme was the social sciences and the safety of the state. One day-part went to gaming as a way to teach. Paul Nitze held the chair. Hans Speier of RAND led the talk, drawn from his own piece in World Politics. His main line: gaming is no stand-in for hard study. It is a help at its side, and a strong tool in the class room. A game should not try to call how men will act. Its worth lies in how it trains men to weigh a hard call.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100040016-5:
A review in hand takes stock of the Agency's tongue scheme as a whole. Its word is not last word, the writer grants. The check is still in train. Yet points of weight have come up that earn a first air at this stage. 

The scheme's shape is set out plain. It runs in three arms. One arm is set tongue study, laid on a man by his shop. The next is free tongue study, taken up by choice. The third pays cash prizes for skill won and held. The training chief holds the scheme's helm and owns its school rooms. Each branch chief, in turn, fixes what tongues his own work calls for. The staff chief keeps a live roll of the tongue skill of all hands, built with the school's help.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100080067-5:
Panelists for the Personal Effectiveness Abroad seminar received this reference list of readings tied to each session of the course. Entries give author, title, publisher, and date, plus short notes on what each work covers. Starred items were required reading, held in the Language and Area School library, while the rest could be signed out from another Agency library for short periods.

The list opens with work on orientation and training for government service overseas, then moves through books on culture, history, and human relations. Later entries treat the biological roots of emotion and personality, and how cultures grow and change. Together the readings show the broad base of study behind a course on working well in foreign societies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200050001-5:
Goods controlled for trade with China are set out in a China Special List dated 13 July 1955. The list is sorted by class and number. Metal-working machines come first. Then come chemical and petroleum gear, power gear, general plant gear, and transport goods. Later classes cover electronics, fine tools, metals, chemicals, and rubber goods.

Each entry gives an item number, a short plain name, and a source note. The first entry covers machine tools and their parts. It allows narrow limits for machines made for plain goods such as needles, pins, and buttons. Fine measuring bridges and map-making tools appear in the electronics class. The list gave allied officials one shared guide for holding back key goods from China.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200070018-5:
A glossary of terms used in allied controls on trade with Communist China opens this reference volume. Entries define the China Committee itself, set up in the fall of 1952, and the International China Embargo List built from Coordinating Committee lists plus the Consolidated China Special List. Differential controls are explained as the gap between treatment of the European Soviet bloc and treatment of China, North Korea, and North Vietnam.

Beyond definitions, the volume serves as a working index to committee business. Long runs of entries list China Committee documents by number, year, and subject. German memoranda on generator spare parts and liquid nitrogen cold boxes for China sit beside British papers on crawler tractors and records of talks on roller bearings. Officials could use one volume to fix both the language and the paper trail of the embargo.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000100020119-5:
Research support for unconventional warfare planning was debated at a meeting recorded in January 1959, with staff from geographic and target analysis work present. One office reported studies already used in feasibility work, including material tied to an airborne assault problem assessed with the Air Rescue Service. Location studies for airfields and smaller strips formed part of that support.

Published studies from the Target Analysis Branch were shown, the most recent dated September 1958. Argument followed over who should produce such studies, with one speaker tired of the constant battle to meet needs on thin support. The sharpest complaint was that the most serious flaws in the studies came from gaps between what planners asked for and what the research offices could actually supply.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000200260004-5:
January 1959 service figures are reported for the Map Library Division. Staff forwarded 22,371 map sheets in answer to 1,135 map requests, plus 277 items against 111 requests for atlases, gazetteers, and other publications. Most map requests came from Agency staff, led by research offices outside the geographic area branch and by the plans directorate.

One request came from the White House staff, for city plans of every United States city with fifty thousand people or more. Staff also answered 1,127 place-name questions and hosted twenty-nine State Department visitors. Processing tables compare cataloguing for 1957 and 1958. Overseas procurement notes close the report, covering map buying in Portugal, the Netherlands, and Germany, and a mapping project in East Jordan whose scope was being revised.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000500040023-5:
A full Inspector General survey of the Office of Personnel fills a bound report with a detailed table of contents. The survey set out to examine the office's functions closely, record the strengths and weaknesses of the Agency's Career Service, and make recommendations. An opening section paints the wider Agency picture before turning to the office itself.

Division by division coverage follows: contract personnel, benefits and services, personnel operations, records and services, salary and wage work, military personnel, and a clandestine services personnel division. Annexes add an organisation table, the Agency reserve training program, and assignment material. One criticism recorded from senior supervisors targets the training program's rule that five per cent of staff strength be kept in training at all times.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200010016-5:
Suppliers to a secret development project receive their governing rules on releasing project information to the Department of Defense in a memorandum dated 11 December 1956. Security standards come first. Knowledge of the project was confined to cleared people with a valid need to know. The memo admits that some erosion of those standards had already occurred as the circle of work grew.

Specific rules then guide how subsystem information may be handled so that no one can piece together the whole weapons system. The existence of the U-2 aircraft itself had been acknowledged in carefully worded press releases. Those releases implied a range of perhaps eighteen hundred nautical miles and a ceiling of about fifty-five thousand feet, figures suppliers were to treat as the public line.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200040040-5:
Forces, bases, and targets for the AQUATONE and OILSTONE effort are weighed in a project paper. The text survives in rough form. Good weather seasons are noted for Europe and Siberia from April through October. Units are shown in place and at work. One unit in Europe has planes. One in Japan has three planes and flies some weather flights. A third unit covered the Middle East at times.

An Air Force unit with like planes is also shown, still in training. The paper weighs a long target list. It asks what flights are needed to cover the most urgent targets. A closing debate takes up control of the work. Civil pilots and folded-in planes could support a claim that the United States was not involved. Others held that army units under army cover could run such work just as safely.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200110015-5:
Photographic supplies, processing, and exploitation equipment for Project CORONA are the subject of a 17 December 1958 memorandum carrying a series of recommendations. Weeks of meetings and exchanges sit behind it, involving project staff, the Photographic Intelligence Center, and contractors including Eastman and Lockheed. Reference papers from December 1958 are listed, among them an ITEK proposal for a ground data handling system.

The recommendations ask approval for a program of equipment buying and contracting. Contracts would be negotiated and run by the project's procurement staff, with ITEK and Eastman named as sources for the gear in question. Clearance of several new contractors would be needed, with no tie to the project shown inside or outside the Agency. Cost figures in the released copy are blacked out.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200130095-5:
A draft memorandum dated 31 December 1958 asks the Director of Central Intelligence to approve a new approvals procedure for Development Projects Staff projects. For four years, spending approvals had run under a procedure based on the AQUATONE project outline of 7 January 1955. That outline had made the writer the approving officer and project director for AQUATONE.

A paper approved on 12 August 1958 had stretched the same procedures over CORONA, GUSTO, and other projects, with provisional budget approval, but the original outline had never been formally amended. The proposed changes are defended as worthwhile in themselves. They also gain urgency, the draft notes, from the writer's new duties and the need to cut the volume of paper crossing his desk by pushing decisions downward.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100020098-5:
June 1955 work by the Industrial Division is summed up in a monthly report. The report came from the Assistant Director for Research and Reports. It passed through the Chief of Economic Research. Branch work sent in includes a study of floor space at the Kiev airframe plant. It also includes a survey section on making and building in Poland.

Other work covers power use in the Soviet Union. An index of Soviet factory output is listed. So is a study of Soviet army spending. Parts went into a national estimate as well. Sixty-five man-hours went to special research in the month. New topics were put forward for future collection notes. They include a possible Mi-6 helicopter at one airframe plant. They also include Soviet radar and rail car output.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100110133-5:
Detailed comments on Project 30.2043, a draft study, run from wording queries to hard questions about steel accounting. The first note catches a figure of 7,100 yuan and asks whether 'million' must be added. A summary passage is called too detailed, an introduction is said to read more like a foreword, and one section's past plans need past tense in place of conditional phrasing.

Steel draws the longest discussion. The relationship between crude and finished steel output should be checked, the reviewer writes, since most scrap seems to consist of billet chips recirculated as crude steel. Steel castings made inside machine-building plants often escape both crude and finished counts entirely. Investment priorities and problems structure the draft's later parts, with one section on excessive non-productive investment flagged as repeating an earlier discussion.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100120015-5:
Creating a senior planning and review board inside the Economic Research Area is argued in a November 1959 proposal discussed by the area's chief. The paper under discussion, sent by a senior officer whose name is redacted, urges a fresh look at the area's procedures and practices. Running such an area well, the chief notes, is a highly technical business, and the proposal had the merit of starting that discussion.

The board proposed would gather the division chiefs, acting through the area staff, and would in effect form an informal advisory board to the chief. Together they would advise on policy for the area as a whole, on planning of the research program, and on the division of research effort. A side benefit is urged: senior staff plainly needed better shared understanding of what the area does and why.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100120024-5:
October 1959 work is summed up in a monthly report dated 4 November 1959. The report comes from the Industrial Division. Material went into a half-year report to the President's Board of Consultants. That report covers foreign economic and map work from 1 April to 30 September 1959. A branch officer briefed the photo branch on register work. He also covered a change meant to speed photo reading.

Staff spoke for the Agency at a joint meeting in San Francisco in early October. The meeting judged a collection program. A study of the Soviet machine tool trade is named among the work done. The chief travelled to back United States talks at the 1959 review of the trade list. That list is kept by the allied trade control body. Talks also opened with a Dutch output agency. The aim was to obtain data the division wanted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100120097-5:
Leading Soviet machine-building plants are listed by industry in a July 1959 paper of personalities prepared for the Nixon trip. Each entry gives the plant, its place and line of work. The names of its senior people, so the travelling party could know who ran the sites it might visit or discuss. Aircraft plants open the list, starting with the Fili plant in Moscow, numbered 82.

Calculating and analytical machinery, the state bearings plant named for Kaganovich, described as the largest anti-friction bearings plant in the Soviet Union, and makers of multi-spindle automatic lathes follow. Later sections cover the ZIL motor vehicle plant, a shipbuilding plant that builds submarines, a television plant. The Nevskiy machine-building plant, noted as one of the largest builders of steam and gas turbines and of axial compressors that might serve in gaseous diffusion plants.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100130014-5:
Comments on earlier comments about estimate NIE 11-8-59 are filed on 3 November 1959. The writer is the Chief of the Industrial Division. He answers a paper of 14 October 1959 from the Aircraft Branch chief. The first point takes up bomber and missile output. Would the Russians give up making both bombers and tested missiles? Would they rely almost wholly on a Badger force for a long stretch? That stretch would last while they waited on solid fuels.

The branch's own estimate answers no. The Soviet Union would make the tested missile, at least for a spell. It would do so until something better was at hand. Or its stance would stay weak. A wording point is agreed. 'A direct copy' is the right phrase, in place of 'an adaptation'. One sentence is marked for cutting. It claimed that short Soviet lead times showed a high-priority effort.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100130023-5:
Romanian plants are set out in sheets revised through 30 September 1959. The first sheet covers a tractor plant at Orasul Stalin, also called Brasov. The plant is the Uzinele de Tractoare 'Ernst Thalmann'. It was once the IAR aircraft works. Part of the tractor plant was used to make planes. That part is the sheet's real subject.

Facts wanted are listed by number. Proof of plane assembly or parts making is wanted. Names and marks of planes made are wanted too. Photos are asked for, with full side views if they can be had. Types repaired, and a count of planes by type, are also sought. Staff numbers and shifts are listed. A second sheet covers another Romanian aircraft plant. It asks whether shops exist for airframe study. It tells collectors to listen for wind tunnel sound. Tunnels often ran at night, when power was free.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00346a000100250005-5: Lead production in the Sino-Soviet bloc is presented as a bare statistical table in metric tons, with no narrative text. The first table gives bloc output by country across the 1950s, from Bulgaria and Czechoslovakia to the Soviet Union, Communist China, and North Korea, with footnotes on metal content of ores mined. Further tables cover world production of refined lead, primary and secondary, country by country, including the United States, Canada, and Australia.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100040133-5:
Soviet aims at the Administrative Radio Conference in Geneva are weighed as of 14 September 1959. The Soviet team spoke much of working together. That talk prompted a fresh look at the Soviet place in world radio links, and at the points raised so far at the talks. The sum-up finds a pattern. Soviet plans and stands aim to push set Soviet gains. Or they back stands that harm the United States.

One running case is the air radio bands. At the first United States and Soviet meeting on the point, the Soviets said their plan meant nothing. Since then they have explained more. What they want is a shift in the spacing of two route classes. The shift would make room for world air routes into and out of the Soviet Union. That aim is read as sound and helpful. Other plans are tested with more doubt.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090002-5:
A lecture on the Soviet economic system, part one of two, is delivered at the Army War College at Carlisle Barracks in 1959. The speaker jokes that two hours on the subject deserve a peacetime counterpart of the Purple Heart, a 'Purple Ear.' He begins with a sketch of the Russian economy in 1913, the base year for many Soviet studies and claims.

Much misinformation surrounds the size of the economy the Communists inherited from the Tsars, he argues. The Soviets picture prerevolutionary Russia as the counterpart of Black Africa today, a myth of backwardness deliberately created so that Communist achievements since then appear even larger. The lecture then walks through the planning machine: Gosplan, whose new chairman Kosygin is also a deputy chairman of the Council of Ministers. The state committees, all of lesser rank than Gosplan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090057-5:
The World Situation is a declassified Agency speech text that reads the Cold War as the latest round of an old contest. It opens with the Greeks at Thermopylae and moves through Tours, Lepanto, and Vienna. Each stand is cast as a defense of a way of life, not just of land.

The speech then turns to Soviet aims in its own day. It describes Moscow buying time for fast forced growth of the Soviet economy. It also describes new room for political and economic pressure on the West. Spending on science and arms sits at the core of the argument, and the close urges the free world to pool its strength.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090084-5:
Khrushchev's Challenge is a declassified Agency address on the Soviet threat, framed for a Chamber of Commerce audience. It states that over one billion people then lived under Communist rule. The early postwar gains, it says, came through military action and political subversion.

The address treats trade and aid since 1953 as a fresh weapon of the same drive. It then looks back at how the Soviet Union was built. Forced industrial growth under Stalin stressed heavy industry above all else. That drive turned a mainly farm economy into the second largest economy in the world, and its costs and gains are weighed in turn.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090147-5:
An untitled speech text in declassified Agency files opens with the claim that history is one long chain of conflicts between rival camps. Greeks at Thermopylae, Charles Martel at Tours, and the Turks turned back at Vienna serve as its early cases. Each fight is cast as a defense of a way of life.

The text then argues that the current struggle cannot be read as a simple clash of national pride. It notes that the Soviet Union stokes national hopes in other lands for its own ends. Pan-Arab feeling is named as one case. Talk of overwhelming retaliation places the speech in the nuclear age, though its main stress stays on ideas and allegiance.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100019-5:
The Challenge of Soviet Power is an address by Allen W. Dulles, Director of Central Intelligence, to the Edison Electric Institute in New Orleans on 8 April 1959. Dulles opens with Lenin's line that Communism is the Soviet system plus electrification. The first Soviet plan of the early 1920s made a modern power system a chief goal.

The address tracks how that lead held. Soviet primary energy output is put at 47 percent of the United States level in 1958, rising close to 60 percent by 1965. The steel gap had also shrunk for five years. Dulles warns against the comfort of assuming the absolute gap would keep growing on its own.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100046-5: Declassified CIA material on penetration and subversion in underdeveloped nations. The red assault. The file covers the subject. The archive holds the paper. Its pages add detail to the Cold War story. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100055-5:
The Challenge of Soviet Power survives here in a rough scanned copy of a declassified Agency address to an Edison Electric Institute convention. Legible passages repeat Lenin's line that Communism is the Soviet system plus electrification. Electric power is called vital to both military strength and intelligence work.

Power runs the radars that watch against surprise attack, the address argues. It also makes nuclear weapons production possible, and it speeds the handling of the flood of facts that reach Washington each day. Later legible lines turn to Soviet investment and civilian output. Those shares are put well below United States levels, even as Soviet effort in key fields ran high.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100080003-5:
An untitled study fragment in declassified Agency files, with a missing page notice at its head, takes up special latitude in free world trade controls. West Germany and Portugal are named as the notable cases. West Germany let goods under quota control move to East Germany outside COCOM quotas and procedures.

West Germany also gave COCOM no delivery figures for strategic goods in interzonal trade. Its defense was political: East Germany was part of Germany, so the trade counted as internal, not foreign. Later pages turn to the Battle Act and aid cutoffs. A waiver for top class goods is explained as a guard for United States security interests, not a blank pardon.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100160004-5:
U.S. Policies on Enforcement of Controls is Staff Study No. 16 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 7, 1955, prepared in consultation with the State and Commerce Departments. Its first section covers COCOM enforcement, starting with present control arrangements and understandings among the partner nations.

Later pages trace how hard joint enforcement was to build. Agreement on TAC and United Kingdom transactions controls formed part of the bargain for the August 1954 list reduction. Five more months of talks passed before those controls took effect. Cool allied enthusiasm for the whole program is named as a standing drag on its growth. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100200009-5:
Political Impact of Free World Controls on Trade with the Sino-Soviet Bloc is Staff Study No. 20 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 17, 1955, contributed by the Defense Department. Its first conclusion is stated with care. A review of the signs in available intelligence strongly supports one view of the controls.

That view holds that free world controls cost the Sino-Soviet Bloc more, in strategic terms, than they cost the free world. By the same logic, the highest possible strategic cost would come from a total embargo. The study also notes the system's base in selectivity, and a recent trend away from that base is flagged for the reader. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100020063-5:
Tabbed replies in declassified Agency files answer, one by one, the Inspector General's recommendations on training. Tab 1 takes up clerical usage. The Directors of Personnel and Training, with operating offices, are urged to take a fresh look at the whole problem, and the reply concurs.

Tab 3 sets a three year tour as the standard for instructors. One third of the instructor staff would be replaced each year, in a planned and staggered flow. The reply concurs, with room left for single exceptions. Tab 20 turns to how junior officers are chosen: a JOT Selection Panel with line officers from the three Deputy Directorates.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100020072-5:
Office of Training Response to the Inspector General's Survey of the CIA Training Program, dated August 1960, is a long and full reply. Its author calls the survey timely and useful, while granting that many of its points are not new. Four broad observations on Agency training as a whole lead the reply.

The deepest question is put first: should training stay permissive, taken by choice, or become planned and directed? Staffing any program, the reply argues, turns on who shall be trained, in what, when, and for what purpose. A senior officer program is also urged, to grow officers able to frame and judge policy as a whole.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200020035-5:
Proposed Changes in a language regulation set out three aims for a pending revision. First, the parts dealing with the overall language program should be strengthened and made plain. Language growth is the true goal, the draft states, and awards are only inducements toward it.

Second, award ideas should turn from broad, undirected interest in study toward the use of that study to the Agency. Third, award costs should be brought into line with current budget trends. Set proposals follow: split the rules into two regulations, cap awards at five years at one skill level and ten years in all, and require tests for all in directed training.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200020125-5:
Areas of Duplication in Training Programs Conducted by CIA/OTR and Other Government Agencies is a memorandum dated 11 April 1960 to the Deputy Director of Training. Its sources are listed first. They include the CIA Act of 1949, the Government Employees Training Act, course catalogs, and the training lists of State, the Army, and other agencies.

Management training shows the overlap in concrete form. The Agriculture Department ran a forty hour personnel management course for mid level staff. The State Department ran forty hours of advanced executive studies for higher grades. Institutes and conferences by other bodies crowd the same ground. The memo even asks whether such talking affairs count as genuine training at all. The memo survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200020134-5:
Determination of Training Requirements is a memorandum dated 18 January 1980 from the Plans and Policy Staff. Written ahead of expected Inspector General interest, it reports a survey of 1959-60 files. The aim was to find hard cases of action taken to draw out statements of what training the Agency truly needed.

Two findings lead. The training office worked on a continuing basis to keep abreast of, or ahead of, stated needs. It also held its programs to what clear need could justify, while trying to head off crash demands by spotting future needs early. Before 1958, formal requirements forms did that work. Later pages credit direct liaison with the customer for the shape of the orientation courses.
cinq-mars-volume-5:
Alfred de Vigny stages the reckoning of conspiracy in Cinq-Mars, Volume 5 of the English edition. De Thou, the hero's friend, confronts Cinq-Mars in a room. His charge is plain: the plot now means banishing or slaying a minister, and bringing a foreign army into France. Assassin and traitor are the words he forces his friend to hear.

The treaty with Spain, France's enemy, has carried the favorite far past pride into treason. Cinq-Mars leans at the chimneypiece, while his friend crosses his arms and judges him. Love for Marie de Gonzague, ambition, and hatred of Richelieu all get weighed in the scene. De Vigny slows the action to let conscience speak at full length. Readers near the end watch friendship do what armies could not: strip the plot of its romance. The scaffold casts its shadow, though the arrests and trial wait in the last volume.
clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of-a-you:
Clarissa Harlowe — Volume 5 of Richardson's novel in letters runs on plots within plots. Lovelace writes Belford about his ipecacuanha scheme, a feigned sickness meant to work on Clarissa's feelings. The servant Dorcas is coached to act surprise and terror on cue.

A greater fraud follows. A Captain Tomlinson arrives with a pretended commission from Clarissa's uncle John Harlowe. A general reconciliation is offered, if Tomlinson can be convinced the pair are actually married. Clarissa insists that the truth be told to him, and carries her point. Lovelace, foiled in one private view, still draws hope from the effects of his drug plot.
cupboard-love-the-lady-of-the-barge-and-:
One comic tale, Cupboard Love, fills this fifth part of W. W. Jacobs's set The Lady of the Barge and Others. The scene is Negget's farm, in a room half parlour and half kitchen. Three folk sit at tea on a November dusk, wary of a servant at the door.

Mrs Negget's gold brooch has been stolen. Her uncle, Mr Martin Bodfish, an ex-policeman with a pension and a small legacy, hides under a bed to catch the thief at a second try. Talk turns to Mrs Pottle, Mrs Driver, and a wedding ring that may be the true prize. Jacobs builds the joke on village talk and sly hints. The part stands alone as a short, dry farce of farm life.
curtius-history-greece-vol-5:
Fallen cities and rising Macedon fill the fifth volume of Curtius's History of Greece, in Ward's 1899 version. Philip builds an army and a kingdom in the north. Alexander then carries Greek arms to the ends of the known world.

Freedom fades as the city-states pass under kings, yet Greek culture conquers its conquerors. The Hellenistic world spreads language, art, and learning far and wide. Curtius closes his great work on that rich paradox. Readers leave with a full arc, from tribal legend to world empire, told by a scholar who loved Greece in its glory and its fall alike.
dialstone-lane-part-5:
The last stretch of W. W. Jacobs's novel fills this fifth part of Dialstone Lane, chapters eighteen to twenty-three. Month by month the Fair Emily creeps south. The Great Bear gives way to southern stars, and Mr Chalk tries not to feel let down by the Southern Cross.

Pressed by Brisket, he owns it is as much like a cross as the other is like a bear. Chalk takes to a drill suit, bare feet, and a Panama hat, the one joke aboard for the bored Mr Stobell. Captain Brisket tells the mate that something big, not pleasure, brought Stobell so far. A cable from Auckland, all safe and coming home, ends the wait in Binchester. This file holds part five, the close of the tale.
diana-of-the-crossways-volume-5:
The fifth and final volume of George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways covers chapters thirty-six to forty-three. Champions of the stricken lady gather at Diana's door each morning. Sullivan Smith and Arthur Rhodes keep their punctilious rival watch. Diana, accused and ill, passes through convalescence of a distraught mind.

Nature receives one of her cultivated daughters in a short country excursion. The penultimate chapter shows a final struggle for liberty, run into harness at last. A nuptial chapter closes the book, as a barely willing woman is led to bloom with married feeling. Meredith rewards Diana's long defence of her honour with the steady Redworth. The volume completes a novel about talk, scandal, and a woman's claim to judge her own life.
dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-5:
The fifth Loeb volume of Dio Cassius, in Earnest Cary's translation, holds books forty-six through fifty. The republic is dead with Caesar, and now his heirs fight over the body. Dio, writing around 230 CE, tells how Octavian, Antony, and Lepidus carved up the Roman world.

The second triumvirate posts its death lists and crushes the tyrannicides at Philippi. Octavian then wars on Sextus Pompeius at sea and turns west against Antony. Dio keeps the senate debates and street feel of the crisis. These books carry the story to the last clash at Actium, told in the next volume.
doe-osti-3014668-lahaina-energy-partners:
NREL staff prepared this poster set for the Lahaina Energy Partnership. Evan Rosenlieb, Ben Polly, Amanda Farthing, and co-authors wrote it. The posters cover Tasks 1 through 5 of a technical assistance engagement with the Maui community. They were written for public discussion. Lahaina's energy planning had taken on new urgency. Each task poster ends with questions posed back to residents.

Task 1 assesses generation options. Community priorities rank low-impact hydropower, distributed energy resources, and community solar highest. Waste-to-energy, agrivoltaics, and floating solar rank lower. One subtask examines hydropower from treated wastewater. It may need new reservoirs. Later tasks cover microgrids and resilience. They ask what residents worry about in outages of three hours, twelve hours, and three days. They also ask what community ownership should mean.
ethics-part-5:
Benedict de Spinoza finishes his Ethics, in Elwes's translation, with part five, Of the Power of the Understanding, or of Human Freedom. His preface promises to show how far reason can control the emotions and what mental freedom, or blessedness, really is. The wise man, he says, proves far more powerful than the ignorant.

Spinoza argues that understanding an emotion clearly already loosens its grip, and that the mind's intellectual love of God is eternal. Things distinctly understood, the scholia insist, outweigh confused impressions in shaping a life. The Ethics ends on its highest claim: blessedness is not virtue's reward but virtue itself. These closing propositions complete the geometric system begun with definitions of God.
evan-harrington-volume-5:
Volume five of George Meredith's Evan Harrington covers chapters twenty-six to thirty-one. Mrs. Mel, the tailor's widow, comes forward to make a bed for herself and her family. Her early rising and sharp accounts open the portion in the shop. Meanwhile Rose Jocelyn shows generalship in the campaign of the courtship.

Evan performs on the second fiddle, socially and literally, at Beckley entertainments. Tom Cogglesey brings a proposition that threatens the family's schemes. The battle of the bull-dogs, told in two parts, supplies rough comic relief. Meredith alternates the widow's shop, the great house, and the cricket world of the county. Evan's secret presses harder as engagement nears. Pride, money, and mother-wit drive this middle-late stretch of the novel.
fbi-vault-9-11-attacks-investigation-and:
Part 5 of the documents freed under Executive Order 14040 comes from the Federal Bureau of Investigation probe into the September 11 attacks. The order sent old case papers through a fresh review, and a key at the front of this part lists why some lines are still held back. The pages that follow are dated case entries.

The sampled entries trace goods seized from Khalid al-Mihdhar. Log books note flights in a Cessna 172 from fields near San Diego in May 2000. A store receipt lists two aviation headsets, a chart kit, and a log book, paid for with his card. An entry for September 13, 2001, records a car search. Redactions cut through the part, and many names are masked by codes.
following-the-equator-a-journey-around-t:
India arrives in Following the Equator, Part 5, by Mark Twain, and boyhood dreams of the East take over. Twain writes that the old visions rise in a luscious moonlight: barbaric gorgeousness, princely titles, and names that taste good in the mouth. He lists them with delight, from the Nizam of Hyderabad and the Maharajah of Travancore to the Begum of Bhopal and the Gaikwar of Baroda.

Chapter XXXIX opens with a calendar maxim about learning to endure another man's adversity, which suits the imperial tour ahead. Even the great god Vishnu, Twain jokes, carries one hundred eight holy names for Sunday use, of which he once memorized all and now retains only John W. The Indian chapters that follow mix pageantry with hard reporting on famine, plague, and caste, but the doorway is this wonder: a famous humorist admitting the East still dazzles him.
freeman-norman-conquest-vol-5:
Effects, not events, fill the fifth volume of Freeman's Norman Conquest, from 1876. Freeman asks what Norman rule did to English institutions over the long term. Culture, law, and national identity all bear the Conquest's stamp in his judgment.

The volume reflects on his life's work like a summing up for a jury. He weighs loss and gain across eight centuries of consequence. English freedom, he argues, survived by absorbing its conquerors. Readers get the reflective close of a vast history. The year 1066 stands as the hinge on which England's later story turns. Scholars still test their own views against his bold claims today.
froude-history-england-vol-5:
Elizabeth takes the throne as the fifth volume of Froude's History opens, in the 1860 printing. Scotland's crisis presses at once on the young queen's council. Catholic Europe watches, while Knox's fiery Scotland offers both threat and chance.

Froude's Elizabeth emerges here in full, brilliant and self-possessed. She moves with a caution far beyond her years among great dangers. Plots at home and pressure abroad test her nerve from the start. The volume launches the reign that dominates the rest of his history, and it shows a queen determined, above all, to survive and to rule.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-5:
Charles Bohlen's shorthand notes of July 17, 1945, capture Truman's first meeting with Stalin at Potsdam. They are an unnumbered item following document 710 in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. Bohlen served as interpreter, and his notes are telegraphic jottings, not a polished record.

Even in fragments, the agenda-setting shows through. Molotov reads out items: the German fleet's division, reparations, and the Polish question. Trusteeships and the Italian colonies come up, as does Franco's Spain. Stalin insists Yalta did not decide Poland's frontiers. On Spain, he argues the Franco regime was imposed by Germany and Italy and shelters fascist remnants. Light touches survive too, in talk of meeting hours and late rising habits. The notes are prized precisely because they are raw, taken down as the words were spoken.
gao-gaoreports-b-291307-5:
Veolia Water North America Operating Services, LLC, is the protester in GAO decision B-291307.5 and B-298017, issued May 19, 2006. Veolia protested how the Naval Facilities Engineering Command ran talks under two requests for proposals. The aim was to privatize water and wastewater systems in North Carolina, Virginia, and West Virginia. GAO denied the protests. The agency had read 10 U.S.C. 2688(f)(2) to bar Veolia's scheme. Under it, Veolia would run the systems but pass title at once to a third party.

The second digest point turns on estoppel. GAO said the Competition in Contracting Act of 1984 lets it decide protests only on claims of law or rule breaches. A reliance claim alone would not be heard.
gao-gaoreports-b-293435-5:
Career Quest returns in file B-293435.5, dated April 13, 2005, this time seeking its protest costs. The General Services Administration had taken corrective action after the firm's first protest over the A-76 study. GAO denied the request for reimbursement. The agency's corrective action, it held, was prompt. The protest itself was not clearly meritorious. Both points must favor the protester before costs can be granted in such a posture.

The ruling is short, and it states a rule that recurs in cost cases. A protest that forces a quick fix is not, by that fact alone, a well-founded one.
gao-gaoreports-b-294121-5:
A request by the Department of Commerce for a second look is the matter of GAO file B-294121.5, dated April 12, 2005. Commerce sought to reopen a ruling that had sustained Saltwater, Inc.'s protest. The contract covered fisheries observer services for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. It had been awarded on a sole-source basis to NWO, Inc. GAO denied the request for reconsideration. The rule stated is plain: a party may not hold back material it could have shown the first time.

Commerce claimed the earlier ruling held both factual and legal errors. GAO found no ground that met the test for reopening a decided case.
gao-gaoreports-b-294980-5:
The protest in file B-294980.5 reached GAO's ruling on July 27, 2005, with Cooperativa Muratori Riuniti, an Italian builder, as the protester. The Navy had rewritten its solicitation for two facilities at Aviano Air Base in Italy. The rewrite came after GAO sustained the firm's earlier protest of an award to Impresa Pizzarotti. GAO's ruling here backs the agency's course. The changes rested on sound grounds, and offerors could revise their offers in reply. This copy is a redacted version cleared for release.

A second point widens that leave. When a solicitation changes after closing, offerors should in general be free to revise other parts of their offers too.
gao-gaoreports-b-295126-5:
DRS Fermont returns in companion GAO files B-295126.5 and B-295126.6, dated December 7, 2007. This time the firm protested its exclusion from the competitive range in the same generator purchase. It claimed flawed scoring and unfair talks. GAO denied the protest. The record backed the agency's scoring of the offers and of the prototypes shown in an earlier phase. Talks were fairly shaped to each firm's own offer.

A third claim, that the talks misled the firm, came too late. The firm knew during talks that the questions clashed with the written terms. It waited more than 10 days to object.
gao-gaoreports-b-295352-5:
A fee question from the Abidjan guard case is the matter of GAO file B-295352.5, dated August 18, 2005. The Department of State asked whether Inter-Con Security Systems should be paid legal fees above the standard cap of $150 per hour. The firm had won its protest and then defended the ruling. GAO said yes: a higher rate could be recommended. The firm's claim to the agency had shown a reasonable basis for an adjustment tied to the rise in the cost of living.

The decision is short and narrow. It does not set a new rate in the text given. It clears the way for one, on the proof the firm filed.
gao-gaoreports-b-295451-5:
The protest in file B-295451.5 reached GAO's ruling on June 22, 2005, with Chenega Technical Products, LLC, as the protester. The Army had passed the firm over in a purchase of support base services within the continental United States. The firm attacked the scoring of its past performance. It also said the award choice rested on a mechanical match of ratings. GAO denied the protest. This copy is a redacted version cleared for release.

Two digest points carry the ruling. The past performance scoring was sound and tracked the stated criteria; mere disagreement proves nothing. The award choice, in turn, weighed prices and performance risk in a real way.
gao-gaoreports-b-296435-5:
Nu-Way protested its loss in the Forest Service mobile food contest in GAO decision B-296435.5, dated September 28, 2005. The work was meals at field sites for fire crews. The firm was marked not fit on its gear. It said the agency missed facts near at hand. It also sought talks to clear a vague point.

GAO denied the protest. The bid was vague on a key gear need. That doubt was fair to hold. Gear facts shift by call, so facts outside the bid need not be used. The fix sought would have been talks, not a mere clear-up. The agency had warned it might award on first bids. No talks were due.
gao-gaoreports-b-296493-5:
Advanced Technology Systems protested a Housing and Urban Development award in GAO decision B-296493.5, dated September 26, 2006. The winner was Pyramid Systems. The deal backed the Tenant Rental Assistance Certification System. The work was system support and fix work. The firm hit tech marks and past work marks.

GAO denied the protest. Marks on both points fit the stated tests and were sound. One flaw did occur. The agency drew weak claims on the winner's staff counts. But those claims were not key to the pick. The winner won as the higher rated, higher priced best value. No harm to the firm was shown.
gao-gaoreports-b-297381-5:
SI International protested a Homeland Security deal for records work in GAO decision B-297381.5, dated July 19, 2006. The winner was Datatrac Information Services. The work was to digitize records. The files were Alien Files held at sites round the land. Both bids had an emergency plan. Price for the plan sat in each quote.

GAO denied the protest. Both plans met the aims and terms of the call. Talks in a fix phase were fair. They hit flaws GAO had named in a past round. They also hit weak spots in quotes. Strong points need not be raised. With tech tied, the low price pick was sound.
gao-gaoreports-b-298751-5:
Philadelphia Produce Market Wholesalers, LLC protested a later award on the same commissary produce buy. This time the Defense Commissary Agency picked Military Produce Group, LLC. The region and store group matched the firm's prior case. GAO decided B-298751.5 on May 1, 2007.

The firm urged that the winner be shut out for a conflict. It said the winner's like work in a second region shaped the current terms. GAO found no proof the firm helped draft those terms. The firm also attacked past-record scores and the award call. GAO found the review fair and in line with the terms. It denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299145-5:
Lockheed Martin Systems Integration-Owego and Sikorsky Aircraft Company protested Air Force corrective action in the rescue aircraft case. The agency had changed its terms after a prior ruling backed their protests. The award to The Boeing Company was again at stake. GAO ruled in B-299145.5 and B-299145.6 on August 30, 2007.

The new terms dropped the traits of each design from the cost count. A broad judgment on upkeep gains took their place. Yet firms could not broadly revise their bids. GAO held that bar flawed. When tests change in a material way, firms must get a fair chance to reply. That chance was denied here. GAO sustained the protests.
gao-gaoreports-b-310301-5:
Re-Engineered Business Solutions, Inc. lost its protest under GAO decision B-310301.5, dated April 4, 2008. The Army sought works and supply services at Fort Hamilton in Brooklyn. Past protests had stung the buy. The Army fixed its call and asked for fresh bids. The fix was the point of this new fight.

GAO denied the protest. The call had a plain flaw at its core. It framed a cost-based deal but asked for price bids. It set a price test in place of a cost test. Fixing that flaw by amendment was fair. A flawed call may be mended mid-race when the flaw is real.
gao-gaoreports-b-311245-5:
A plea to change a fix is refused in this GAO decision, B-311245.5, dated August 4, 2008. Metro Machine Corporation won a deal, then saw a protest shake it. GAO told the agency to hold frank talks with both sides. One talk would hit split work hours in a bid. One would hit a low cost cap and its risk. The winner asked GAO to rethink that fix.

GAO denied the plea. The winner showed no flaw in the fix or its base. It just clashed with the call GAO made. The low-cost risk ties to the cost test the call set. It was fair game for a talk. Bare clash earns no fresh look.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-5:
Moving service jobs abroad can cut prices and displace workers at the same time. Report GAO-06-5, issued November 28, 2005, gives an overview of services offshoring. Offshoring means buying goods or services from abroad that were once produced at home. Debate covers gains such as lower prices and higher productivity. It also covers costs such as job loss for some U.S. workers. GAO acted under the Comptroller General's authority.

GAO sums up expert views on likely effects. It describes types of policies proposed in response. It highlights areas where more research could advance the debate. The Commerce Department generally agreed with the findings. Readers get a balanced issue overview.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-5:
Paying disability representatives from claimants' benefits is studied in GAO report GAO-08-5, dated October 15, 2007. The Social Security Protection Act of 2004 widened this fee withholding beyond attorneys in Disability Insurance cases. It now covers attorneys in Supplemental Security Income cases and qualified nonattorneys in both programs.

Eligible nonattorneys proved the most seasoned group, averaging over 240 claimants represented in 2 years, against fewer than 90 for others. Judges rated them about equal to attorneys, while ineligible nonattorneys scored lower. Most judges and eligible nonattorneys liked the system but faulted the entry bar, which can be met after as few as five claims in 2 years. GAO also flags overpayments to representatives that need watching. The Social Security Administration agreed with the advice.
gargantua-and-pantagruel-illustrated-boo:
Book 5 closes Rabelais's five-book tale of the giants, in Peter Antony Motteux's English version. Pantagruel's ship sails on from isle to isle toward the Oracle of the Bottle. Panurge still hopes for a firm word on marriage. The prologue asks why folk say men are less foolish now than in days of yore, and plays with the word sot, or fool.

Strange courts and rites greet the crew, among them a hall where dancers move like chess pieces at war. Cats, clerks, and wine all get mocked in turn. At last the travelers reach the temple of the Bottle and hear its word. The voyage ends the long joke on quests for certain truth.
godolphin-volume-5:
Joy and Despair is the title of chapter forty-two, where the fifth volume begins. Lucilla pauses at the door of Godolphin's rooms, then gathers courage and enters. His favorite servant, amazed and glad to see her, says his master is out but that they leave the next day. Lucilla flushes with delight that her letter worked so fast.

Trunks lie half-packed, and the rooms show all the bustle of a departure. Lucilla, the idol of all who know her save the one man whose love she lives for, has staked everything on this visit. The volume carries the Roman thread of the tale toward its crisis. Lytton's high, fervent style suits a heroine who acts from the heart alone.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r:
Edward Gibbon's fifth volume, with Milman's notes, opens at chapter forty-nine with the worship and persecution of images in the east. The revolt of Italy, the popes' temporal dominion, and the Frankish conquest follow. Charlemagne's character and coronation close that great chapter's survey of the restored western empire.

The volume then turns to the rise of Islam, the Prophet's life, and the Arab conquests of Persia, Syria, Egypt, Africa, and Spain, before reaching the eastern empire's later centuries. Gibbon's treatment of Mahomet and the caliphs mixes admiration with skepticism. Russian audiences and Persian kings appear in the notes. By the close, the story approaches the Crusades and the shrinking Byzantine state.
humboldt-cosmos-otte-vol-5:
The fifth volume of Humboldt's Cosmos, in Otté's English translation, is the last, left unfinished at his death in 1859. The Bohn set had begun in 1849. Humboldt, near ninety, was still adding to it, on the geology of the earth and the distribution of life.

The volume returns to volcanoes and the making of rock, then closes on the geography of plants, the seed Humboldt planted with his Andean plant zones. Even unfinished, it completes the arc: from nebulae to the moss on a single mountainside. Cosmos as a whole was the Victorian age's grandest picture of one connected nature. Its author died the same year as Darwin's Origin appeared.
humboldt-personal-narrative-williams-vol:
The fifth volume of Humboldt's Personal Narrative, in Williams's translation, came out in 1821. The expedition is now in the Andes of New Granada and Quito. Humboldt climbs the great volcanoes, measuring their height against the sea and snow line.

On Chimborazo in 1802 he reached higher than any European had climbed, until thin air and a ravine stopped him short of the top. The volume's pages on altitude, plant zones stacked by height, and ancient Inca roads made seedbeds for whole sciences. Humboldt also copies and ponders the ruins and calendars of the peoples before the conquest. The Narrative's seventh volume would end the set in 1829.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-5:
Julian the Apostate, the emperor who tried to restore pagan worship, strides through Ibsen's vast double drama Emperor and Galilean. The fifth volume of Archer's 1908 edition presents both parts. Ibsen called the sprawling work his masterpiece, above even the famous social plays.

Two worlds collide in Julian: the beauty-loving pagan past and the Galilean faith he renounced. Philosophy, politics, and mysticism crowd the stage across decades of one reign. Rarely performed whole, the play reads like an epic of the spirit in crisis. It marks Ibsen's most ambitious reach as a thinker. Readers who know only the drawing-room dramas will find a different, grander Ibsen here.
ihne-history-rome-vol-5:
Caesar and civil war close Ihne's History of Rome in this fifth volume, from 1871. The republic's last giants fight for mastery of the Roman world. From their wars the Empire is born, and the free state passes into one-man rule.

Ihne ends his five books at the hinge of Western history. His German thoroughness carries the tale from Marius's heirs to Augustus's dawn. Readers see both the glory and the cost of the change. The full history served as a standard account for a generation, and its final volume shows the sober craft that earned that standing in full.
isbe-1915-vol-5:
Volume 5 closed the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia in 1915, completing the set edited by James Orr. The project had set out to give Bible readers a full, conservative reference in English. By the final volume, thousands of signed articles by scholars covered the whole field of biblical study.

The closing volume carries the alphabet to its end and adds maps, lists, and indexes that tie the set together. Readers could trace a name, a place, or a doctrine across all five volumes. The encyclopedia became the standard companion to Bible study for pastors and students of its era. Though later works replaced it, its articles still reward readers who want the learning of 1915 in one place.
j-s-le-fanu-s-ghostly-tales-volume-5:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu's Ghostly Tales, volume five, opens with Laura Silver Bell of 1872. Dardale Moss, a bleak Northumbrian moor of black peat and heath, is her home ground. Mother Carke's stone cottage stands a mile from the meanest neighbor. Its hollow thatch and stingy peat smoke suit the wild place, Le Fanu writes.

Stories of Lough Guir, a child taken by fairies, and Dickon the Devil fill the volume. Little Billy is lost with no grave to mark him, one tale laments. Wicked Captain Walshaw and Tom Chuff's vision add range. This last volume mixes fairy lore with haunting.
jataka-cowell-vol-5:
The fifth volume of Cowell's Jataka, published in 1905, nears the end of the 547 birth stories. E. B. Cowell edited the set at Cambridge, and several hands translated from the Pali. Only one volume remained after this one in the 1895 to 1907 series.

The tales here are among the longest in the collection, full of travel, war, and royal intrigue. The future Buddha, born as prince or sage, holds to truth and mercy when courts reward neither. Each story still ends with the Buddha naming the cast in their present lives. The volume carries the cycle's growing weight toward its famous finale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-s-rod-5:
Aaron's Rod was the rod of Aaron, the high priest, said to hold miraculous power during the plagues before the Exodus. The entry recounts that it swallowed the rods of the Egyptian magicians. It also blossomed and bore fruit in the Tabernacle. That sign proved the tribe of Levi's sole right to the priesthood, and the rod was kept before the testimony.

In rabbinical writing, the Haggadah makes this rod the same staff as the staff of Moses. Tradition in the entry links it to Jacob, Judah, and David, and says kings used it as a scepter until the Temple fell. It was said to be made of sapphire, to weigh forty seahs, and to bear the initials of the Ten Plagues.
joshua-volume-5:
Volume five of Georg Ebers's Joshua opens at chapter twenty-four, on a prisoner transport bound for the mines. The captain of the guards has never had a harder trip. One prisoner, Ephraim, has escaped, and his faithful hounds are lost. Two storms have drenched and terrified the troop, the second fiercer than any in twenty-five years of service.

Fever struck prisoners and guards alike after their wet nights in the open. Two dead prisoners had to be buried on the road. Hosea, linked to the bold lad who fled, suffers most from the captain's ill humor. Yet he bears every hardship in silence, without complaint or oaths. This volume follows the Hebrews' suffering as Pharaoh's army meets its end.
journeys-through-bookland-vol-5:
Volume five of Journeys Through Bookland, in the 1922 new edition, turns toward heroes and legends for young readers. Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels opens the contents. King Arthur follows, with Balin and Balan, the Holy Grail from Malory, and Arthur's passing. Tennyson supplies Geraint and Enid and The Passing of Arthur in verse.

Shakespeare enters through Polonius's advice, and Cardinal Newman's Lead, Kindly Light as a hymn. James Whitcomb Riley and Michael Drayton add lighter and patriotic verse. Later pieces tell of Henry Hudson's fourth voyage and Robert Bruce and the spider. Sylvester steers older children from story toward history and national legend in this volume.
lawyer-quince-odd-craft-part-5:
W. W. Jacobs wrote Lawyer Quince as part of his story collection Odd Craft. Quince is a bootmaker in the village of Little Haven. His neighbors gave him his nickname for a clear reason.

From a few old law books, Quince gained much legal lore. He offers that lore freely to anyone with a dispute. Jacobs opens on a sunny, sleepy village street after the London coach. Footsteps and raised voices then promise a fresh quarrel. Jacobs tells such village tales with dry, affectionate humor. Jacobs sets the tale among his Little Haven villagers. Quince's book learning meets village cunning with comic results.
lecky-england-18th-vol-5:
Revolution shocks England in the fifth volume of Lecky's History, from 1890. France's upheaval kindles reform hopes at home and loyalist fears beside them. The younger Pitt fights to hold the nation together through a decade of passion and panic.

Radicals and loyalists battle for the country's soul in Lecky's pages. Trials for treason, cheap pamphlets, and volunteer corps mark the divide. He maps the passions of the seventeen nineties with wide learning and calm judgment. The volume shows Britain's great political split at its sharpest, a crisis that set the terms of debate for the century to come.
life-of-george-washington-volume-1-of-5:
Washington Irving opens his five-volume life of Washington here. Chapter One traces the Washington family's ancient English genealogy. The family held landed estates in the county of Durham. Its roots reach back to the century after the Norman Conquest.

William the Conqueror rewarded followers after wasting the northern country. The shrine of St. Cuthbert made Durham a rich, privileged see. Camden's Britannia supplies Irving's early authorities and color. From these deep roots, Irving builds toward Washington's Virginia youth. St. Cuthbert's shrine drew princes and gentry as a titular defence. William increased Durham's extraordinary privileges after the Conquest.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-5:
Part Five opens with Twain receiving his pilot's license. Chapter 21 calls itself a section in his biography. Steady work followed, and he hoped to die at the wheel. Then the war came and suspended river commerce entirely.

Twain became a Nevada silver miner, then a newspaper reporter. Gold mining, San Francisco reporting, and Sandwich Islands correspondence followed. Twenty-one years drifted before he saw the pilot-house again. Chapter 22 then returns him to the river he loved. Lecture platforms and New England authorship ended his wandering list. A poet companion joined the return trip down the river.
lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-5:
Volume 5 closes George Meredith's Lord Ormont and His Aminta with Book 5. It opens with 'Lovers Mated,' as Lord Ormont thinks of Aminta as his countess. Yet the old soldier still broods on how wives should be ruled, in Napoleon's way.

Farewell visits and a marine duet lead toward the plighting, the lovers' pledge. A chapter gives Aminta's own words to her lord before the conclusion. Meredith ends the long contest of pride and patience on the coast. The volume settles whether love or pride rules this marriage. It completes one of Meredith's most searching stories of married life.
marion-arleigh-s-penance-everyday-life-l:
Marion Arleigh's Penance was number five in Chicago's Everyday Life Library. Charlotte M. Brame, also spelled Braeme here, wrote it. She was the author of Dora Thorne and other beloved tales. The story opens at three o'clock on a warm June afternoon in London.

Heat lies on the city like a purple haze over a sapphire sky. No breath of wind stirs the leaves or cools the workers. Against that sultry opening, Marion's story of love and penance unfolds. Brame wrote for the great public that devoured weekly fiction. Her tales joined high romance to humble life. Penance, in her world, is the price of a proud heart's lesson.
matrimonial-openings-sailor-s-knots-part:
W. W. Jacobs placed Matrimonial Openings in his Sailor's Knots set of 1909. Mr. Dowson sits by the kitchen fire and smokes in peace. His wife talks hot and fast while he gives mild answers.

She fears their daughter Flora will wed as her sister Jenny did. Jenny's match, she says, left her worn with work. Flora walks out with Charlie Foss, a man her mother calls good for nothing. Ben Lippet, who will one day be his own master, is her mother's pick. Jacobs lets the wife's sharp talk clash with the man's calm replies. The humor rests on that clash more than on the courtship itself.
memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-montesp:
Book five of Madame de Montespan's memoirs opens at the waters of Bourbonne. Few guests had come that year when the tale starts. The Prince de Mont-Beliard of Wurtemberg soon arrives to pay his respects.

He had lost his wife less than a year before that visit. French officers held his states, and he feared the hold would last. He dared not ask her plainly what the King meant to do. Chancellor Hyde, who had swapped houses with her, brings word of his wish. A note from the King and a letter from her husband follow. Land in Navarre, promised to her, hangs in the air.
merivale-romans-empire-vol-5:
Government, not emperors, fills the fifth volume of Merivale's History, from 1863. Merivale pauses his tale of courts and camps to show the working Empire. Tax men, roads, courts, and provincial towns reveal how Rome was actually run from day to day.

Daily business replaces drama in these instructive pages. Grain fleets, post roads, and local councils keep a world in motion. He shows the slow rhythms that held millions in one system. The volume gives readers the Empire's machinery in full view. Most histories of Rome stop at the palace door, so the turn is rare and valuable.
nasa-tm-19640008185-satellite-situation-: Volume four, number five of NASA's satellite situation report series is preserved here. Reports in the series were compiled by Goddard Space Flight Center with NORAD and the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. They catalog satellites and other objects in orbit, with launch and orbital data. The hosted sample preserves only garbled table data with no readable text, so this issue's date and listings cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19710010490-msc-apollo-13-invest:
Panel 5A of the Apollo 13 Investigation Team owned corrective action for the Command and Service Modules. Its study, dated June 12, 1970, began right after the flight that lost its number two oxygen tank. Panel leader A. C. Cahen approved the report, which covers both studying fixes and putting them into effect.

The contents map three jobs. First comes the cryogenic oxygen tank failure, then an accidental fuel cell reactant valve closure. A third section compares configuration differences among service modules 108, 109, and 110. Appendices cover oxygen quantity gaging, stratification, heater analysis, and service procedures prepared for Apollo 14. The scope section says the panel also assessed possible problems flagged by a related systems evaluation panel. Together the sections form the corrective action record for the next CSM flights.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-5:
Augustine's anti-Pelagian writings fill volume five of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, first series, from 1886. Philip Schaff edited the set. Pelagius, a British monk, had taught that humans can choose the good by their own strength. Augustine spent his last twenty years fighting that teaching.

The treatises here argue that grace is not a reward for merit but the source of every good act. Original sin, infant baptism, and predestination all come under his hammer. The fight fixed the West's doctrine of grace for good and ill. Augustine's late severity still sparks argument; few sets of pages have shaped more sermons.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-5:
Gregory of Nyssa, youngest of the three great Cappadocians, fills volume five of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890, with his dogmatic treatises and other works. Gregory was Basil's brother and the deepest thinker of the three. Philip Schaff and Henry Wace edited the series.

His Great Catechism teaches the faith's whole frame to new instructors. Against Eunomius he defends the Trinity with careful logic about names and knowledge. His life of his sister Macrina, and his talks on the soul and resurrection held as she lay dying, give the volume a human close. Gregory's teaching on the soul's endless growth toward God still draws readers.
night-and-morning-volume-5:
Book the Fifth, the last book of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning, fills volume five. A Latin line from Petronius heads chapter one, about the mysteries and ministerings of the gods. A note in the copy points readers to a corrected full set in Project Gutenberg.

Mr Roger Morton stands behind his counter on a drizzling, melancholy day. Morton is an alderman, twice mayor of his native town, and a thriving man grown portly. Nightly brandy and water have deepened the roses on his cheek. His digestion troubles him, and he blames joint, pudding, vegetables, and cigars in turn. The brandy he never thinks of dropping.
northern-lights-volume-5:
Volume five closes Gilbert Parker's Northern Lights with three tales: The Error of the Day, The Whisperer, and As Deep as the Sea. The first opens with a definition from an Admiralty note. The error of the day is the gap between the range set on a gun's sights and the true range.

A great naval gun, Parker notes, never fires twice alike. Air, ammunition, and wear shift its aim, so allowance must be made each time. Talk then turns to Kowatin, in the Saskatchewan country. Billy Goat, really William Goatry, sings a street song about a fatherless child. Parker mixes sea gunnery and prairie talk in one volume.
one-of-our-conquerors-volume-5:
George Meredith closed his novel in this fifth volume. Book five opens with Nesta and her father. Victor rides with Lady Grace Halley in her carriage. She flatters him that together they might rule the world. The thought exposes the poor value of his aim.

Mother and daughter meet in the next chapter. Nataly, Nesta, and Dartrey Fenellan share a key scene. A chapter stands in the shadow of Mrs. Marsett. An expiation and a great undelivered speech follow. The last chapter ends Victor's campaign of ambition. Meredith ends with irony, pity, and hard self-knowledge.
pahlavi-texts-west-vol-5:
West closed his five-volume Pahlavi Texts with a final volume in 1897. It appeared as volume forty-seven of the Sacred Books of the East. The volume translates books eight and nine of the Dinkard.

The Dinkard, meaning Acts of Religion, is Zoroastrianism's great encyclopedia. Book eight summarizes lost Avestan texts book by book in detail. Book nine expounds selected passages with commentary and moral teaching. West's rendering closed his long labor of preservation in 1897. Together the five volumes gave English readers a Zoroastrian library. The series stands as the last word of a monumental Victorian project. Later scholars still build on West's foundations.
palfrey-history-new-england-vol-5:
Palfrey closes his great History of New England with Volume 5, from 1858. The story runs through the eighteenth century to the eve of revolt. Five volumes end as the Puritan world gives way to an American one.

New wealth, new ideas, and new wars loosen the old tight bonds. Town faith yields ground to trade, print, and wider horizons each year. Palfrey keeps his calm, full style to the final chapter. His work stood for decades as the standard history of the region. The close feels earned: a world ends, and another waits offstage.
pausanias-description-greece-frazer-vol-:
Volume five of Frazer's Pausanias gathers the maps and plans of the edition. Frazer's 1898 Description of Greece used text, commentary, and now cartography. Readers can walk the traveler's routes with these sheets in hand.

Plans of sanctuaries and cities show walls, temples, and excavated remains. Topographical essays argue how routes ran between ancient sites. The visual companion turns armchair reading into a field expedition. Frazer believed ancient texts should be tested against the ground itself. His maps embodied that belief for a generation of travelers. Archaeologists carried these volumes to Greece in their luggage for decades. The volume completes the working apparatus of the great commentary.
personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-volume-: The sample hosted for this entry shows only the front matter of Part 5 of volume 2 of Sheridan's memoirs, the contents pages, with no chapter text visible. The contents run from the battle of Dinwiddie Court House and Five Forks through Sailor's Creek to the meeting of Grant and Lee and the surrender. Later chapters take Sheridan to Texas, the Rio Grande, and the French invasion of Mexico, then to Reconstruction duty in Louisiana and Texas.
personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-5:
Part 5 of Grant's memoirs opens at chapter fifty-two, the battle of Spotsylvania in May 1864. Grant explains the ground with an engineer's care: the Mattapony River and its four little parent streams, the Mat, the Ta, the Po, and the Ny. Lee's army comes up by the Catharpin Road while Warren and Hancock take the Brock Road.

Burnside crosses the Ny and holds against a furious attack. Grant reads Lee's movements and prepares to strike his right and get between him and Richmond. The part is the Overland Campaign at closest quarters, generalship written as plain narrative.
pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-far-n:
The fifth and last volume of Gilbert Parker's Pierre and His People contains Antoine and Angelique, The Cipher, A Tragedy of Nobodies, and A Sanctuary of the Plains. These closing tales stay in the far north world of the earlier volumes, where winter, distance, and small settlements press hard on the people in them.

Antoine and Angelique opens as quiet dialogue between husband and wife watching birds go south early, a sign the winter will be long. Angelique has heard a child cry in the night and felt a cold hand at her heart; Antoine answers each fear gently, blaming devil-birds and wild geese. The exchange builds a mood of dread before she asks that they, too, go southward before the great winds come.
plato-dialogues-jowett-vol-5:
The fifth and last volume of Plato in Benjamin Jowett's translation is given wholly to the Laws. The Laws is Plato's longest work and the last he wrote. Gone is Socrates; an unnamed Athenian stranger talks with two old men on a walk through Crete.

The three design a new colony, Magnesia, law by law: its gods, its schools, its marriages, its courts, and its drinking parties. The tone is stricter and more pious than the Republic's, with heavy stress on law as teacher. Some editions add Plato's letters to the volume's plan. Reading the Laws shows Plato in old age, trading the ideal city for one men might actually build.
ranke-history-england-vol-5:
Volume 5 of Ranke's History, from 1875, brings the Stuarts to the throne. James I rules first, with his claims of divine right held high. The long road toward civil war opens across these careful pages.

Ranke traces the deep clash between king and parliament step by step. Money, faith, and law feed a crisis neither side can calm. His long view, the hallmark of his work, holds the whole span. Small slights grow into fixed camps and armed camps in time. The storm gathers slowly, and the historian misses none of its signs. Readers watch a kingdom drift toward a breaking point it cannot see.
rhoda-fleming-volume-5: The fifth volume of Rhoda Fleming by George Meredith is preceded here only by the standard header of its plain-text publisher. It supplies the title, the author's name, and English as the language of the text, and it counts the item as the thirty-first in a series of Meredith's works. No memoir of the story follows it in the pages shown: neither a contents list nor an opening scene is printed. Only the facts of title, author, and volume five can be reported from this front matter.
roughing-it-part-5:
Part 5 of Mark Twain's Roughing It, in an 1880 printing, opens at Chapter XLI with Captain Nye sick with spasmodic rheumatism, a joint disease marked by sharp pains. Nye is kind and pleasant when at ease. When a spasm hits, he groans, wails, and swears with great force and fancy. The narrator bears it gladly, since he had seen Nye nurse a sick man with patience when the roles were reversed.

While Nye raves, the narrator's mind stays busy night and day with grand plans. He redraws his house, weighs a billiard-room in the attic, and picks between green and blue cloth for the drawing-room. He plans servants, a fine home for his mother, and a grand trip through Europe. He writes home each day with orders about land and money.
samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-5:
Part 5 of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren, written as Josiah Allen's Wife, opens at Chapter XVIII with Samantha reading her husband's face. Josiah's face was smooth and placid, and he had not taken a mite of sense of what she had been saying, and she knew it. Men, she reflects, know at most that it is only talk, since women have not got it in their power to do anything. His accent was mildly wondering and gently sarcastic. How a steeple would look pointing down, he said: that is a true woman's idea. A picture of Sister Filkins is printed in the passage.

Samantha answers that she would have the steeple point down toward the depths of darkness in the heart of the man who raised it up.
sandra-belloni-volume-5: Volume 5 of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni, marked v5, is presented here through header matter only, as number 23 in a series by the author. The title line names the work and the author, and a release date of September 2003 is given. The file was first posted on January 4, 2002, as Etext number 4417, in Edition 10, in English and ASCII. A credit line names Pat Castevans and David Widger as producers of the electronic text. Nothing from the novel's pages appears in the portion shown here.
satapatha-brahmana-eggeling-vol-5:
Eggeling's fifth and final Satapatha Brahmana volume appeared in 1900. It closed the Sacred Books of the East rendering of the great Vedic ritual manual. Eggeling had spent nearly two decades on the translation project.

The closing books contain a famous jewel, the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. There, talk of ritual turns into deep thought about the self. Teachers like Yajnavalkya debate the nature of the soul and ultimate reality. Sacrifice gives way to philosophy across these chapters. The volume thus marks the hinge between old Vedic worship and Indian thought. Eggeling's completion of the set was a major scholarly achievement.
sketches-new-and-old-part-5:
