Mark Twain's sketches new and old continue in this fifth part, opening with The Siamese Twins, written about 1868. Twain claims close knowledge of the joined brothers and promises private details never before in print. The twins, he reports, stayed fast bound to each other through decades of travel and fame.

Even as children they played together always, so that their mother hunted for one when both were lost, sure the other stood near. Twain turns their bond into a rebuke of civilized brothers who quarrel and part. Tenderness and satire share the sketch in equal measure.
stepping-backwards-night-watches-part-5:
Stepping Backwards belongs to Night Watches, a set of comic tales by W. W. Jacobs about working men talking in pubs. Mr. Simpson has just had new teeth fitted at dinner-time, and his friend Mr. Jack Mills praises the change, saying the lisp is gone and the teeth make him look far younger than his fifty-three years.

Mills then pushes a fuller make-over: shave the whiskers, dye the white hair black, and do it all at once at a barber's shop in Bird Street. Simpson hesitates, half tempted and half afraid of being laughed at, and the humor grows from vanity, friendship, and the wish to seem young again at the warehouse.
stories-by-american-authors-volume-5:
Stories by American Authors, Volume V, dated 1884, holds A Light Man by Henry James, Yatil by F. D. Millet, The End of New York by Park Benjamin, Why Thomas Was Discharged by George Arnold, and The Tachypomp by E. P. Mitchell.

James opens the volume with a diary-like tale. A man home again after years away feels bored and low. He resumes his old notes in April 1857. He weighs what he seems to friends, to a woman he may love, and to himself. Around it sit tales of war, work, and a famed speed machine, giving a mixed shelf of serious and fanciful American writing.
symonds-renaissance-italy-vol-5:
Volume 5 of Symonds's Renaissance in Italy, from 1875, treats the Catholic reaction. The free world of the early age meets a sterner church. Discipline returns, and the spring of Italy fades toward dusk.

Councils, censors, and new orders press on thought and art alike. Symonds closes the age proper with Rome's firm reassertion of rule. Painters and thinkers learn to work within tight, watched bounds here. He mourns the lost freedom while granting the new order its strength. Freedom yields to order in his sad, balanced telling of events. The sunset he paints has shadow, gold, and grief in it.
talleyrand-memoirs-vol-5:
The fifth and final volume of Talleyrand's memoirs brings his long career to its close. After the July Revolution of 1830, the aged diplomat took one last post: ambassador to London. Beaufort's translation completes the 1891 set.

Talleyrand recalls the July Monarchy and his London mission, where he worked to keep peace between France and Britain. Belgium's future and Europe's balance fill these final chapters. He writes as a man summing up a life spent in every regime. Few memoirs span so many governments with one cool, constant voice. He died in 1838, soon after the London years this volume recalls.
the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-volume-: No prose by Meredith stands here for volume five. The book is The Adventures of Harry Richmond. A Gutenberg wrapper stands in its stead. The part is numbered 54 in its set. It is filed as 4448. Release is dated September 2003. First posting was January 31, 2002. David Widger is named as the file's maker.
the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-5:
Part five of Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer opens at chapter eighteen by giving away Tom's great secret. He and his brother pirates schemed to come home and attend their own funerals.

The boys had paddled on a log to the Missouri shore at dusk on Saturday and slept in the woods at the town's edge. They then crept through back lanes and dozed in the church gallery amid broken benches. At Monday breakfast Aunt Polly and Mary shower Tom with love and care. Polly grants the joke was fine, yet calls him hard-hearted for letting her suffer near a week. Readers get the funeral scene and Tom's brief glow of fame.
the-amazing-marriage-volume-5:
Book Five closes George Meredith's 1895 novel in this fifth volume. Its chapters run from The Red Warning from a Son of Vapour onward. A last chapter ends with a parting word by the Dame. Along the way come a retarded courtship, a road to an act of penance, and a meeting of earl, countess, and her brother over a silver cross.

The opening finds Fleetwood at his leased estate of Calesford, worn down by tradesmen rushing to make the house fit for grand London parties. At dinner Gower Woodseer, acting as secretary, forces him to hear how bad Countess Livia's money troubles have grown, with gambling debts bleeding her dry.
the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-of-tw:
Volume five of Gilbert Parker's romance opens at chapter thirty-one on a dark night at St Aubin's Bay. Ranulph returns home to find no light, no drawn blinds, and no fire. He fears something has happened to his father before he reaches the door.

Dormy Jamais hurries round the corner, plucks his sleeve, and refuses to talk indoors because stone walls have ears. Dormy says he has Ranulph's father safe and chuckles at his own cleverness. Speaking in Jersey patois, Ranulph humours the shrewd little man. Dormy then runs toward the shore, his wooden shoes clacking, whispering that there has been trouble in St Heliers.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-5:
October 1885, volume three, number five, opens with a portrait of William W. Crapo and a sketch by Edward P. Guild. Crapo of New Bedford is presented through his father first. Henry Howland Crapo, son of a Dartmouth farmer, taught himself with so little help that he once set out to make his own dictionary.

Henry became a teacher, surveyor, city treasurer, and library trustee, with interests in the whale fisheries. After timber purchases in Michigan he moved there, entered politics, and served four years as governor from 1865. William, born in Dartmouth on May 16, 1830, was his only son among ten children and shared his love of learning.
the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-volum: Volume 5 of Charles James Lever's Confessions of Harry Lorrequer covers chapters XXIX to XLI, printed at Dublin in 1839. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The chapters promise Captain Trevanion's adventure, difficulties, an explanation, Mr. O'Leary's first and second loves, a duel, and early recollections of a first love. Later titles turn to wise resolves, the proposal, and thoughts on matrimony in general and in the army in particular. No chapter text follows.
the-convert-deep-waters-part-5:
W. W. Jacobs tells The Convert as part of his Deep Waters stories. Mr. Purnip walks arm in arm with Mr. Billing, a new recruit to his cause, and praises him warmly. With Billing won over, Purnip says, the others will follow like sheep, and his friend will shine as a bright lamp in the darkness.

Billing is pleased but unsure of the rules. He has given up fighting, yet he asks what to do if somebody hits him. Turn the other cheek, Purnip answers, and smile; shame will hurt the striker more than a blow. Billing doubts it, noting he can hit a man pretty hard and that a good smack in the jaw saves a deal of arguing. Purnip paints the sway a first-class fighting man gains by refusing to fight.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-p:
Part five of Purgatory in Dante's Vision holds cantos twenty-six through thirty-three, in Cary's verse. Walking single file along a rim of flame, Dante casts a shadow that makes the fire burn redder. Spirits marvel that he seems no mere shade, and one begs to know how a living man can block the sun.

Poets of love pass through the fire and greet each other with joy. Past the flames, an angel sends Dante on to the earthly paradise. There he meets a lost love, confesses his faults, and is made clean for the stars.
the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-5:
An essay on Isaiah opens volume five of The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations. It calls Isaiah the first and most sublime of the four greater Hebrew prophets, son of Amoz, who spoke under four kings of Judah. It also notes that many critics give the last twenty-seven chapters to a later writer, since Cyrus is named there.

Next comes the ruin of Sennacherib's host, when an angel slew a vast Assyrian camp in one night. Text and plate pairs fill the volume. Doré's portrait of the prophet is judged here to fit the later voice better.
the-elson-readers-book-5: The Elson Readers, Book Five, by William H. Elson and Christine M. Keck, is present here as title matter and a contents list. A tale called The Crystal Glass opens the book. Then comes a part named Nature, Humour, Home and Country. Animal pieces name Samuel White Baker, Ernest Harold Baynes, and Theodore Roosevelt. Bird and flower poems follow. No lesson text appears in these pages.
the-gilded-age-part-5:
Part 5 of The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today is dated 1873. Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner wrote the novel. This part opens with Chapter XXXVII. Laura Hawkins looks for a committee chairman. He is nowhere to be found. She makes a new plan. She sends a note to the Hon. Mr. Buckstone. She asks him to call that night.

Buckstone comes, and the two trade smooth praise. Laura plays on his fame as a man not fond of women. He replies with fine words about her own fame. Each one flatters the other. Each one seems pleased. The talk shows how charm works as a tool in Washington. A bill there can turn on a smile and a well-placed call.
the-great-conspiracy-volume-5:
John Logan wrote The Great Conspiracy: Its Origin and History. This record is Part 5 of that work. It opens with Chapter XVIII, Freedom Proclaimed to All. Logan takes up the question of emancipation as it came to a head. Much of Lincoln's thought, he says, turned on one perplexity. Lincoln assumed that the physical difference between the black and white races barred their living together in one land as free men and equals.

Logan traces that idea through Lincoln's speeches and acts. It was advanced in the Lincoln-Douglas debates. As President, Lincoln held out a hope to the border-state delegations on July 12, 1862. The freed people, he suggested, might go to his projected colony in South America. On August 14 he appealed to the colored free men on the same plan. The chapter shows emancipation weighed against colonization in Lincoln's mind.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Vol. 2, No. 5 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated February 3, 1898. It is also numbered No. 65 of the whole run. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a publisher's notice of rates. The paper comes from 3 and 5 West 18th Street, New York, every Thursday. Single numbers cost five cents each. The trade is supplied by the American News Company.
the-history-of-rome-volumes-1-5: Theodor Mommsen wrote The History of Rome. The record holds a compilation of the five volumes. William Purdie Dickson translated the work with the author's sanction. A note lists the five books in order. Book I covers the period before the end of the monarchy. Book V ends with the establishment of the military monarchy. The note adds that each volume stands on its own as well. Only the compilation note and title page are present here. A dedications heading also appears.
the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1620-m: Volume 5 of The Mayflower and Her Log, by Azel Ames, is represented here only by its Project Gutenberg front wrapper. The wrapper records a June 2003 release, etext number 4105, and production by David Widger. Its paragraphs concern license cautions, donations, and the volunteer labor behind the project. The book's own pages never begin, so this record can tell a reader the volume's identity and source file, but nothing of what Ames wrote inside it.
the-money-master-volume-5:
Volume 5 of Gilbert Parker's The Money Master contains Epoch the Fifth, chapters XXII to XXV, and an epilogue. Chapter XXII, Bells of Memory, follows Jean Jacques far from the Manor Cartier, unable to escape signals from his past. At Montreal he had briefly regained his lost Carmen, then turned from her grave.

Carmen Dolores is remembered in a long, tender reckoning. She had known passion in Granada with Carvillho Gonzales, smothering homesickness, and a final betrayal by the man who abandoned her during the last year of her life. He took not only her last hope but small treasures, including rings given by Gonzales in Cadiz and by Jean Jacques himself, and money she knew she would not long need.
the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volume-5: Volume 5 of George Meredith's novel The Ordeal of Richard Feverel shows only its Project Gutenberg header in the pages present here. The header gives the etext number 4410. It gives a release date of September 2003 and a first posting on December 28, 2001. No title page or story text appears. The file was produced by Pat Castevans and David Widger and stands sixteenth in the Gutenberg series by Meredith. Only the book's title, author, and etext source can be stated.
the-poetical-works-of-edmund-spenser-vol: Volume V of The Poetical Works of Edmund Spenser, dated 1860, is given over to miscellanies and an appendix. Here only the contents and the heading of the first section appear, so the poems themselves are absent. The miscellanies collect the Complaints, including The Ruines of Time, The Teares of the Muses, and Virgils Gnat. Mother Hubberds Tale and Muiopotmos appear there too. Later entries name Daphnaida, the Amoretti, Epithalamion, Prothalamion, and the Fowre Hymnes. The appendix promises variations from the original editions and two letters from Spenser to Harvey.
the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-5:
Part 5 of Mark Twain's The Prince and the Pauper opens at Chapter XV, Tom as King. Foreign ambassadors come with gorgeous trains, and Tom, throned in awful state, receives them. The splendour delights him at first, but the long, dreary addresses wear the pleasure into homesickness. He says the words Hertford puts into his mouth and looks like a king, yet cannot feel like one. He is cordially glad when the ceremony ends.

Most of Tom's day is spent in labours of royal office. Even two hours of princely pastimes are fettered by ceremony. Only his private hour with his whipping-boy counts as clear gain, bringing both entertainment and needful information. By the third day he is growing used to his chains. One dread still looms over the fourth day: dining in public, alone, under a multitude of curious eyes.
the-seats-of-the-mighty-volume-5:
Volume five of Gilbert Parker's The Seats of the Mighty holds chapters twenty-five to thirty of Captain Robert Moray's memoirs. Its headings include The Secret of the Tapestry and Master Devil Doltaire. An appendix excerpt from The Scot in New France follows the final chapter.

The twenty-fifth chapter, In the Cathedral, opens at dawn. Moray looks out over ruined Lower Town roofs at dawn. A bell calls to prayers at the Jesuit College. Starved peasants creep about the cathedral, eager for crumbs. Yet the Intendant's Palace holds abundance and revelry, Moray notes. He descends to the room where Labrouk's body lies. Candles burn at the dead man's head and feet. Labrouk's widowed wife enters, and Moray whispers his sympathy.
the-sisters-volume-5:
Volume five of Georg Ebers's The Sisters opens at chapter twenty-two, on a tower roof. An astrologer stood on the pylon tower by the gate of the Serapeum, Ebers writes. He had mounted to observe the stars. Swift black clouds kept sweeping across his field, though. At last he laid aside his instruments impatiently. No translator is named in the pages shown for this volume.

The gate-keeper, father of poor little Philo, answered with a shrug. It is a night of horror, he declared, and great disaster threatens. In fifteen years in his place he had seen such a night only once before. The next day Antiochus's soldiers plundered their treasury, he recalled. Tonight is worse, he insisted. The sacred bulls seemed to rise from the dead in the Apis-cave, butting at the door with their horns.
the-tales-of-the-heptameron-vol-1-of-5: Margaret, Queen of Navarre, wrote the Heptameron, and the Society of English Bibliophilists printed this five-volume English version in London in 1894, newly translated from the text of Le Roux de Lincy. George Saintsbury supplied an essay on the work. Here only the opening leaves of volume one are present, showing the shared title page, a frontispiece portrait of Margaret, and a contents list. That list promises a memoir of the queen, Saintsbury's essay, and the dedications and prefaces of the original editions, but the tales themselves do not appear.
the-tales-of-the-heptameron-vol-2-of-5: Volume two of the Heptameron of Margaret, Queen of Navarre, carries the same 1894 London title page as its sister volumes, with George Saintsbury's essay and engravings by Freudenberg and Dunker. No more than the front matter and the start of a contents list are present in this record. The contents continue the first day of storytelling and name Tale VIII, the misadventure of Bornet, before breaking off. Readers learn where this volume picks up the company's tales, while the stories themselves stay outside the pages shown.
the-tales-of-the-heptameron-vol-3-of-5: The third volume of Margaret of Navarre's Heptameron repeats the common title page of the 1894 Society of English Bibliophilists edition. It was translated from Le Roux de Lincy's text, with an essay by George Saintsbury. Front matter is all that this record holds, plus a contents heading that places the volume in the second day of the tale-telling, continued. No individual tales are named and none are printed in what is shown. The volume's place in the five-part set is clear, its stories are not.
the-tales-of-the-heptameron-vol-4-of-5: Margaret, Queen of Navarre, is the author behind the Heptameron, and volume four of the 1894 London edition shares the set's title page, Saintsbury essay credit, and Freudenberg engravings. This record gives front matter and a bare contents opening only. The contents announce the fourth day and its prologue, then stop, so none of that day's tales can be read or described from these pages. What survives is the volume's identity, its place in the five-volume set, and the point where its storytelling resumes.
the-tales-of-the-heptameron-vol-5-of-5: Volume five closes the 1894 London Heptameron of Margaret, Queen of Navarre, printed for the Society of English Bibliophilists with George Saintsbury's essay and the set's engraved illustrations. The pages present here stop at the front matter and the first line of the contents. That line announces the sixth day and its prologue, nothing further. So the final volume's tales remain unread in this record, even though its position as the set's conclusion and its shared title page are plain to see.
the-three-cities-trilogy-lourdes-volume-:
Volume five of Zola's Lourdes, in Ernest A. Vizetelly's translation, covers the fifth day, and readers should note that no fourth-day volume sits among these records. Pierre again cannot sleep at the Hotel of the Apparitions. He has inquired after Marie, who sleeps soundly after the procession, and he worries that her father has not returned from Gavarnie. With the hare-brained M. de Guersaint, every mischance seems possible.

The last night of the pilgrimage fills the hotel with pilgrims hurrying to and from the Grotto, doors slamming and floors shaking. Pierre keeps rising, mistaking corridor noises for de Guersaint's return. Zola closes his Lourdes inquiry with a doubting priest kept awake by the very fervour he cannot share, while the cured and the unhealed prepare to leave.
the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-volume-5:
Book Five of Zola's Paris, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, opens with Guillaume bent on witnessing the execution of Salvat, the anarchist. Pierre tries to dissuade him, fails, and resolves to spend the night at Montmartre watching over his brother. The guillotine can be seen from a Socialist deputy's house, so Pierre offers himself as guide. The brothers sit up in the workroom until two o'clock, then start out into a serene, moonlit night.

Paris below them sleeps like a spell-bound city, its labour and suffering lulled until dawn, while in a far district a knife is being raised to kill a man. The Sacred Heart basilica looms white and domeless over the roofs, a symbol of dominion. Zola sends his priest and his revolutionary to watch the state kill, testing both men's faiths at daybreak.
the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-volume-5:
Part Five of Zola's Rome, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, opens on the evening of Pierre's long-awaited papal audience, fixed for nine o'clock. He waits in the Borgo, early, his heart gripped by infinite emotion and grief. That afternoon he spent beside the dead Dario and Benedetta, who now lie in one another's arms. The lovers' pitiful end has left him unable to eat, longing only to hide and weep.

Walking slowly across the dark Piazza of St. Peter's, lit only by lamps around the obelisk and colonnade, he feels an anguish of charity for all who suffer. Zola brings his priest to the Pope carrying grief for Paris and Rome alike. Whether the audience heals or ends his dream of a rejuvenated Christianity is the trilogy's Roman question.
the-works-of-edgar-allan-poe-volume-5: A contents list is all that appears for volume five of the Raven Edition of Poe's works. Tales include Hop-Frog, The Man of the Crowd, and Some Words with a Mummy. The Poetic Principle represents his criticism. Poems follow, headed by The Raven and The Bells. Annabel Lee, Ulalume, and Eldorado are listed among poems of later life. Poems of manhood, including Lenore and The Haunted Palace, close the list.
thirlwall-history-greece-vol-5:
Volume 5 of Thirlwall's History, from 1845, gives the Peloponnesian War itself. Athens and Sparta lock in a long, grinding death struggle here. Thirlwall follows Thucydides closely, and he follows him very well.

Plague, revolt, and the Sicilian disaster crush Athens by slow degrees. Sparta's patience and Persia's gold wear the sea empire down at last. The bishop's steady narrative never flinches from the war's waste. Greek disunity, not foreign arms, breaks the city-states in his telling. Readers feel the tragedy build year by grim campaigning year. His calm voice makes the horror land harder, not softer.
un-ga-res-a-69-5:
One state's trade laws can reach too far, argues Resolution A/69/5, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text defends a set of Charter-era rules: states are equal, none may meddle in the home affairs of others, and trade and shipping must run free. Heads of Ibero-American states had already called for an end to one-sided trade steps by one state against another.

The named target is the U.S. Helms-Burton Act of 12 March 1996, part of the U.S. embargo of Cuba. Its reach past U.S. borders, the text says, harms the rights of other states and of firms and people under their law. Year by year, this vote is the Assembly's standing rebuke of that law.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/5, adopted in the autumn of 2014, is the General Assembly's annual call to end the United States embargo against Cuba. The Assembly reaffirms sovereign equality, non-intervention, and freedom of trade and navigation. It expresses concern at laws with extraterritorial effects, such as the 1996 Helms-Burton Act. It again urges states that maintain such laws to repeal or invalidate them as soon as possible. It asks the Secretary-General to report on implementation at the seventieth session.
un-sc-res-5:
Soviet troops in Iran gave the young Security Council one of its first tests. Iran had reported that it could not yet confirm a full Soviet withdrawal. The statement came in a report dated 6 May 1946. Council rules set in April required that check. On 8 May 1946 the Council chose to wait rather than press on.

It deferred further proceedings on the Iranian matter. Iran needed time to verify the facts through its own officials. The government in Tehran had to report what it found. The Soviet Union was absent from the vote. The case showed the limits of the Council when a great power was itself a party.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Soviet troops remaining in Iran gave the newborn Council its first great test. Moscow had promised to withdraw by spring 1946. Iran reported on 6 May that it could not yet confirm a full pullout. Resolution 5 was adopted on 8 May 1946 by ten votes. The Soviet delegation was absent from the chamber.

Members chose to pause rather than escalate. Proceedings on the Iranian case were deferred. Tehran gained time to check through its own officials. A complete report was demanded as soon as possible. If Iran still lacked answers by 20 May, it had to report what it knew. The Council would then decide its next steps.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s11-5: Section 11.5 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers the Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States. It sits in Part 11, on subscriptions to Federal Register publications. The rule is a single sentence on the sale of the work. Copies of the yearly clothbound volumes are sold at a price set by one officer. That officer is the Superintendent of Documents, who acts under the broad direction of the Administrative Committee. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s2-5:
Section 2.5 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers the publication of statutes, rules, and kindred documents. It sits in Part 2, on general information about the Federal Register system. Part (a) names the officer in charge of central filing. The Director of the Federal Register holds that charge for the original acts passed by Congress.

The charge also covers the original documents that hold executive orders and proclamations of the President. Other presidential documents, rules, and notices of proposed rulemaking fall under it as well. Such matter is sent to the Director by officials of the executive branch. Part (b) of the section builds on that filing role, as the text goes on to state. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s301-5:
Section 301.5 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers the Office of the Chairman of the Administrative Conference of the United States. It sits in Part 301, on the organization and purpose of that body. The Chairman is the chief executive of the Conference. He presides at meetings of the Council and at each full session of the Conference.

Among his powers is the power to press federal agencies to take up the advice of the Conference. The Chairman is also cleared to make inquiries into matters he holds to be of weight for the Conference. Such matters may be put forward by persons inside or outside the body, as the text goes on to state. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s304-5:
Section 304.5 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations deals with the time of replies to calls for records. It sits in Part 304, on the release of records, for the Administrative Conference of the United States. As a rule, the agency will reply to calls in the order in which they came in. A second clause deals with a two-track way of work. The agency in the main uses two tracks, one for plain calls and one for hard calls.

In the choice of a track for a call, the agency weighs a set of points. They are the count of records called for and the count of pages in the work. The need for talks with other bodies, or for the send of the call to them, is a point as well.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s425-5:
Section 425.5 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers disclosure of records to persons other than the person they concern. It sits in Part 425, on the President's Commission on White House Fellowships. Records under the Privacy Act that are asked for by any person other than the person they concern are not to be made open. A set of exceptions then follows in the text.

The first exception lets records be passed to fit officials for a set end. That end is the placing of Fellows in work assignments for the Fellowship year. The section also calls for a record of each such disclosure. That record covers the date and nature of the disclosure and its purpose, as the text goes on to state. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s602-5:
Section 602.5 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets the terms for Freedom of Information Act requests. It sits in Part 602, the FOIA rules of the National Capital Planning Commission. Part (a) calls for a named officer. The Commission is to name a Chief Freedom of Information Act Officer. That officer is cleared to grant or deny any request for a record of the Commission.

Part (b) states where requests are to go. Requests for records not at hand in the reading rooms of the Commission, in person or online, go to that officer. Part (c) adds that all FOIA requests are to be made in writing. Rules for requests sent by mail follow in the text. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026.
vittoria-volume-5: Volume five of Vittoria by George Meredith carries number 45 in the Project Gutenberg series of his works, as its header states. Only that header is present in these pages, a few screens of license terms about copying, sharing, and the rights of the archive foundation. The novel itself is not shown, and no chapter titles for this volume appear. The set runs to eight such volumes, each fronted by the same header, plus a companion record that lists the whole contents.
watch-dogs-ship-s-company-part-5:
W. W. Jacobs tells Watch-Dogs as one of his Ship's Company tales, in the voice of the oldest inhabitant of a waterside village. The tale opens at the Cauliflower inn. The old man takes a long, slow draught of beer, and calls it almost the only enjoyment he has left, that and a pipe of tobacco. Neither wants chewing, he notes. That is a great thing when a man has little left to chew with.

He lights his pipe with infinite care, cupping the match though the summer air is still. Then he lectures the wayfarer who bought his pint. Kindness to animals is all very well, he says, but kindness to your fellow creatures is more. A given pint earns thanks even once it is gone. When the landlord refills his mug unasked, the old man starts with pleasure and spills two spoonfuls.
